ON THE PSALMS IV (last)

[EXCELLENCES OF THE LAW OF GOD] PROLOGUE I explained with the help of God and as I could, partly by preaching to the people and partly by writing, all the psalms contained in the book that we call the Psalter according to the custom of the Church. However, Psalm 118 differed, not so much because of its known length as because of the depth it contains, which is known to few. As my brothers resented the fact that only the exposition of this psalm was missing from my writings to complete the entire exposition of the Psalter, and they insistently urged me to pay this debt, I did not agree for a long time to their prayers and supplications, because as many times as I tried to think about it, as many times I realized that it exceeded my desires and strength. For the simpler it seems, the deeper it usually seems to me; to such an extent that I cannot declare its depth. On the contrary, other psalms that are difficult to understand, although they hide the meaning due to darkness, nevertheless this same darkness is made evident; It is not perceived in this one, because it presents such an aspect or appearance that it is thought that it only needs a reader or listener and not an expositor. Even now as I begin his presentation, I am completely unaware of what he may say about him. However, I ask and trust that God will help me so that I can do something, because that is what I did in all the

Psalmos ornnes caeteros, quos codicem Psalmorum novimus continere, quod Ecclesiae consuetudine Psalterium nuncupatur, partim sermocinando in populis, partim dictando exposui, donor Domino, sicut potui: psalmum vero centesimum octavum decimum, non tam propter eius notissimam longitudinem, quam propter eius profunditatem paucis cognoscibilem differebam. Et cum molestissime ferrent fratres mei, eius solius expositionem, quantum ad eiusdem corporis Psalmos pertinet, deesse opusculis nostris, meque ad hoc solvendum debitum vehementer urgentent, diu petentibus iubentibusque non cessí; quia quotiescumque inde cogitare tentavi, semper vires nostrae intentionis excessit. Quanto enim videtur apertior, mucho mihi profundior videri solet; ita ut etiam quam sit profundus, demonstrare non possem. Aliorum quippe, qui difficile intelliguntur, etiamsi in obscuritate sensus latet, ipsa tamen apparet obscuritas; huius autem nec ipsa, quoniam talem praebet surfacem, ut lectorem atque auditorem, non expositorem necessarium habere credatur. Et nunc quod tandem ad pertractationem eius accesso, quid in eo possim, prorsus ignoro: spero tamen, ut aliquid possim,

things that I have stated at length when they seemed difficult or almost impossible to explain or understand. I determined to expound this psalm through sermons preached to the people, which the Greeks call "homilies", since it seems very fair to me that the faithful who attend church should not be deceived in the knowledge of this psalm, with whose song they usually delight as with the others. But let's leave the prologues behind and talk about the psalm, about which I thought it appropriate to make this preamble. SERMON

1 [v.l]. This great psalm, my brothers, from its beginning exhorts us to blessedness, which no one despises. Who can, could or will ever find someone who does not want to be happy? If the one who exhorts does nothing more than move the will of the one he persuades to follow what he suggests, what need does the human soul have of exhortation for the happiness, which it craves by nature? Then why are we encouraged to want what we cannot help but want if it is not because, while everyone desires happiness, many do not know the way to achieve it? This, then, is what he teaches who says: Blessed are those who are without spot in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord. This is as if he said: Be what you want: you seek bliss. If you want to be happy, be immaculate. Everyone wants happiness, but adfuturum atque adiuturum Deum. Sic enim fecit in ómnibus quaecumque sufficienter, cum prius mihi ad intelligendum vel explicandum difficilia ac penis impossibilia viderentur, exposui. Statui autem per sermones id agere, quí proferantur in populis, quas Graeci ójjuXía; vocant. Hoc enim iustius esse arbitror, ​​ut conventus ecclesiastici non fraudntur etiam psalmi huius intelligentia, cuius, ut aliorum, delectan assolent cantilena. Sed sit huc usque prooemium: iam de ipso est loquendum, de quo istuc visum est praeloquendum. s ERM o i 1 [v.l]. Ab exordio suo magnus psalmus iste, charissimi, exhortatur nos ad beatitudem, quam nemo est qui non expetat. Quis enim usquam vel potest, vel potuit, vel poterit ínveniri qui nolit esse beatus? Quid igitur exhortatione opus est ad eam rem quam sua sponte appetit animus humanus? Nam proferto qui exhortatur, id agit, ut excitetur voluntas eius cum quo agit, ad illud propter quod exhortationis adhibetur alloquium. Utquid ergo nobíscum agitur, ut velímus quod nolle non possumus; nisi quia omnes quidem beatitudem concupiscunt, sed quonam moda ad eam perveniatur, plurimi nesciunt? Ideoque hocdocet iste, qui dicit: Beati immaculati in via, qui ambulant in le ge Domini. Tanquam diceret: Scio quid velis, beatitudinem quaeris; si ergo vis esse beatus, esto immaculatus. Illud enim omnes, hoc autem pauci volunt, sine quo non pervenitur ad illud quod omnes volunt. Sed ubi erit quisque im-

Few want to be immaculate, without which it is not possible to get what everyone wants. But where will man become immaculate if not on the way? On what path? In the Lord's. For this reason we are exhorted and not in vain are we told: Blessed are those who are undefiled in their way, who walk in the law of the Lord. What kind of good it is, for which many lazy people show themselves, to walk undefiled along the path, which is the law of God, is made known when it is indicated that those who do this are happy; so that what many reject must be done to get what everyone wants. Indeed, being happy is such a great good that the good and the bad want it. And it is not surprising that the good are good for achieving it, but it is surprising that the bad are bad for wanting to be blessed, since anyone who gives himself over to lust and is corrupted by sensuality and rape, seeks bliss in this evil, and considers himself unhappy when he does not achieve the pleasure and delight of his desires, and does not hesitate to consider himself happy when he achieves them. Likewise, he who burns himself with desires of avarice, gathers wealth in any way in order to be happy: and everyone who desires to shed the blood of enemies, and he who desires to dominate, and he who feeds his cruelty with the calamities of others, seeks happiness in all these crimes. Well, to all these strays, who seek false happiness with true misery, this divine voice calls to the path, if it is heard: Blessed are those who are undefiled on the path, those who walk in the law of the Lord. This is as if he were saying to them: Where are you going? You get lost and ignore it. Does it not go where you walk to where you want maculatus, nisi in via? In qua via, nisi in lege Domini? Ac per hoc, Beati immaculati in via, qui ambulant in lege Domini, non superfluo nobis dicitur, sed exhortatio necessaria nostris mentibus adhibetur. Quid enim boni sit ad quod multi pigri sunt, id est, immaculatos ambulare ín via, quae lex est Domini, sic ostenditur, cum beatos esse qui hoc faciunt, indicatur, ut propter illud quod omnes volunt, etiam hoc fiat quod plurimi nolunt. Beatum quippe esse, tam magrmm est bonum, ut hoc et boni velint et mali. Nec mirum est quod boni propterea sunt boni; sed illud est mirum, quod etiam mali propterea sunt mali, ut sint beati.

Nam quisquís libidiníbus deditus, luxuria stuprisque corrumpitur, in hoc malo beatitudem quaerit, et se miserum putat, cum ad suae concupiscentiae voluptatem laetitiamque non pervenit, beatum vero non dubitat iactare cum pervenit. Et quisquís avaritiae facibus inardescit, ad hoc congregat quocumque moda divitias, ut beatus sit: ínimicorum sanguinem fundere quicumque desiderat, dominationem quisquís affectat, crudelitatem suam quisquís alienis cladibus pascit, in ómnibus sceleribus beatitudem quaerit. Hos igitur errantes, et vera miseria falsem beatitudem requirentes, revocat ad viam, si auditatur, vox ista divina, Beati immaculati in via, qui ambulant in lege Domini: tanquam dices, Quo itis? Peritis, et nescitis. Non illac ítur qua pergitís, quo perveníre desí-

arrive, because you certainly want to be happy; but the paths on which you run are deplorable and lead to greater misfortune. Do not seek such a great good by such a bad path. If you want to reach it, come here, walk along this path. Abandon the malignancy of the evil path, those of you who cannot detach yourself from the desire for happiness. You tire yourself in vain walking where, once you arrive, you defile yourself. For those who, contaminated with error, walk in the perversity of the world are not blessed, but those who are undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord. 2 [2.3). Hear, furthermore, what follows: Blessed are those who search his testimonies, those who seek him with all their heart. It seems to me that by these words no other type of blessed is commemorated other than that of which he spoke before. Because to search the testimonies or precepts of the Lord and seek Him with all your heart, is to be immaculate on the path and to walk in the law of the Lord. Then he continues and says: for those who work iniquity have not walked in their ways. Therefore if those who walk in the way, that is, in the law of the Lord, are those who search his precepts and those who seek him with all their heart, surely those who work iniquity do not investigate his testimonies. However, we see that the perpetrators of evil dedicate themselves to investigating the testimonies of the Lord in order to be rather learned than righteous. We also observe that others search the precepts of the Lord, not because they already live righteously, but to know how they should live. These do not yet walk undefiled in the law of the Lord, and, therefore, they are not yet happy. Then how is it to be understood: deratis: nam utique beati esse cupitis; sed misera sunt, et ad maiorem miseriam ducunt itinera ista qua curritis. Tam magnum bonum quaerere per mala nolite: si ad illud pervenire vultis, huc venite, do ite. Viae perversae relinquite malignitatem, qui non potestis relinquere beatitudeinis voluntatem. It frustrates tending fatiguemini, quo pervening inquinamini. Non autem beati inquínati in errore, qui ambulant in perversitate saeculi; sed, Beati immaculati in via, qui ambulant in lege Domini. 2 [v.2.3]. Quid porro adiungat attendite: Beati qui scrutantur testimonia eius, in toto corde exquirunt eum. Non mihi videtur aliud his verbis commemoratum beatorum genus, quam illud quod ante dictum est. Nam scrutari testimonia Domini, et eum in toto corde exquirere, hoc est immaculatum in via, in lege Domini ambulare.

Denique sequitur et dicit: Non enim qui operate tur iniquitatem, in viis eius ambulaverunt. Si ergo ambulantes in via, id est in lege Domini, ipsi sunt scrutantes testimonia eius, et in toto corde exquirentes eum; proferto qui operate tur iniquitatem, non scrutantur testimonia eius. Et tamen novimus operarios iniquitatís ad hoc scrutari testimonia Domini, quia malunt docti esse quam iusti: novimus et alios ad hoc scrutari testimonia Domini, non quod iam recte vivant, sed ut sciant quemadmodum vivere debenant. Blessed are those who search their testimonies, while we see men who search their testimonies and are not happy, because they are not immaculate? The scribes and Pharisees, who sat on the seat of Moses, and of whom the Lord said: Do what they say, do not do what they do, for they say and do not do, undoubtedly searched the precepts of the Lord to know what good they said, even if they did what was bad. But let us leave these aside, since it will be declared to us that these did not investigate the precepts of the Lord, since they did not seek these precepts, but something else through them, that is, to be praised by men or to become rich. It is not scrutinizing the precepts of the Lord not to love what they teach and not want to get to where they lead us, that is, to God. Furthermore, if these same ones search the precepts of the Lord in order to obtain and attain through them not God, but something else, undoubtedly they do not seek Him with all their heart, which we see was not added here in vain. Knowing the Spirit, who said these things, that many would investigate his precepts for a purpose other than that established, he not only said: Blessed are those who search his testimonies, but he added: those who seek him with all their heart, as teaching in what way or why the precepts of the Lord should be searched. Finally, Wisdom herself, speaking in the book of Wisdom, says: The wicked search for me, and do not find me, because they hate Wisdom. And what is this if not that they hate me? They look for me, he says, and they don't find me, because they hate me. And why will it be said that they seek what they hate if it is not because they do not seek Wisdom, but rather something else in it? They do not pretend to be wise for the glory of God, but rather they try to appear wise by attending to the glory of men. How ac per hoc nondum beati. Quomodo ergo intelligendum est, Beati qui scrutantur testimonia eius; cum videoamus homines eius scrutari testimonia non beatos, quia non immaculatos? Nam Scribae et Pharisaei super cathedram Moysi sedentes, de quibus Dominus ait, Quae dicunt, facitel quae autem faciunt, faceré nolite: dicunt enim, et non faciunt (Mt 23,3); utique scrutabantur testimonia Domini, ut haberent quae dicerent bona, quamvis facerent mala. Sed hoc omittamus: recte quippe responderbitur nobis quod isti non scrutantur testimonia Domini. Non enim quaerunt ipsa, sed aliud quaerunt per ipsa, id est, ut glorificentur ab hominibus, vel ditentur.

Non est hoc sctutari testimonia Dei, non diligere quod ostendunt, nolle pervenire quo ducunt, id est ad Deum. Aut si et ipsi scrutantur testimonia Dei, quamvis non ut ipsum, sed ut aliud ex his inveniant et acquirant; certe non in toto corde exquirunt eum, quod non utique frustra hic additum cernimus. Will they not hate Wisdom, which commands and teaches that what they love must be despised? Therefore, blessed are those who are undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord. Blessed are those who search his testimonies, those who seek him with all their heart. Thus, then, we will say that those who, searching his testimonies, search for him in such a way that they seek him with all their heart, walk undefiled in the law of the Lord. Did he not search his testimonies or seek him who said: Good Master, what good must I do to obtain eternal life? But how did he seek Him with all his heart, when he preferred his riches to the advice that the Lord gave him about abandoning them, and, therefore, he turned away full of sadness? Therefore Christ is certainly not sought in this way, since Isaiah says: Seek the Lord, and when you find Him, let the wicked forsake his way, and the perverse man his evil thoughts. 3. The impious and wicked seek God in such a way that by finding Him they cease to be impious and perverse. But how are those who still search his testimonies and seek him blessed, if the impious and wicked can do this? What man will say, however impious and wicked, that the wicked and the wicked are blessed? Therefore they are blessed in hope, as are those who suffer persecution for righteousness; not for what is present, when suffering evils, but for what is coming, since theirs is the kingdom of heaven; not because they have inveniunt; oderunt enim sapientiam (Prov 1,28 et 29). Quod quid est alium, quam, Oderunt me? Quaerunt ergo me, ait, et non me inveniunt qui oderunt me. Quomodo igitur dicuntur quaerere quod oderunt, nisi quia non hoc, sed aliud ibi quaerunt? Non enim volunt esse sapientes in Dei gloriam, sed volunt viderí sapientes propter hominum gloriam. Quomodo enim sapientiam non oderunt, quae iubet et docet conternnendum esse quod diligunt? Proinde, «Beati immaculati in via, qui ambulant in lege Domini. Beati qui scrutantur testimonia eius, in toto corde exquirunt eum. Sic enim scrutando testimonia eius, ut in toto cotde exquirant eum, immaculati ambulant in lege Domini. Numquid tamen Ule non scrutabatur testimonia eius, nec quaerebat eum, qui dicebat, Magister bone, quid boni faciam ut vitam aeternam consequar? Sed quomodo eum in toto corte quaesivit, cuius consilio divitias suas praetulit, quo audito tristis abscessit? (Mt 9,16.22).

Nam et propheta Isaiah dicit, Quaerite Dominum; et cum inveneritis eum, derelinquat impius vias suas, et vir iniquus cogitationes suas (Is 55, 6 et 7). 3. Quaerunt itaque Deum et impii et iniqui, ut eo inventiono non sint impii, nec iniqui. Quomodo ergo iam beati, cum adhuc testimonia eius scrutantur et exquirunt eum, cum hoc faceré possint et impii, possint et iniqui? Beatos autem esse impíos et iniquos, quis vel impius dixerit aut iniquus? Ergo spe beati, sicut beati qui persecutionem patiuntur propter iustitiam: non propter quod adest, quamdiu mala patiuntur; sed propter quod aderit, quoniam ipsorum est regnum caelorum; et beati qui esuriunt et sitiunt iustitiam, non quia esuríunt et sitiunt, sed

hunger and thirst, but for what follows: and they will be satisfied. Likewise blessed are those who cry; not because of crying, but because of what follows: because they will laugh. Therefore, blessed will be those who search his precepts, those who search for him with all their heart, not because they search and search, but because they will find what they seek, since they do not search carelessly, but with all their heart. If you are happy in hope, perhaps only in hope will you be blameless. For in this life, although we walk in the law of the Lord, although we search his precepts and seek him with all our heart, if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves and the truth is not in us. This must be investigated with the greatest care taking into account what follows: those who work evil did not walk in their ways. For it may seem that those who walk in the way of the Lord, that is, in the law of God, searching his precepts and seeking him with all their heart, may already be blameless. Those who work iniquity have not walked in his ways. And Saint John writes: He who sins works iniquity; and adds: Sin is iniquity. But this sermon must now end so that such a great issue is not confined within narrow limits. SERMON

1 [v.3]. It was written in this psalm and it is read, and it is true, that those who work iniquity did not walk in their ways. But propter quod sequitur, quoniam ipsi saturabuntur: et beati qui plorant; non quia plorant, sed propter quod sequitur, quia ridebunt (Mt 5, 10.6.5). Proinde, Beati qui scrutantur testimonia eius, in toto corde exquirunt eum; Non quia scrutantur et exquirunt, sed quia inventuri sunt quod exquirunt: in toto enim corde, non negligenter exquirunt. Si ergo spe beati, fortassis etiam spe immaculati. Nam proferto in hac vita, licet in lege Domini ambulemus, licet scrutemur testimonia eius, et in toto corde exquiramus eum, si dixerimus quia peccatum non habemus, nos ipsos seducimus, et veritas in nobis non est (1 lo 1,8). Sed hoc diligentius inquirendum est. Sequitur quippe, Non enim qui operantur iniquitatem, in viis eius ambulaverunt. Ex quo videri potest, qui ambulant in via Domini, id est in lege Domini, scrutando testimonia eius, et in toto corde exquirendo eum, iam esse posse immaculatos, hoc est sine peccato, propter verba sequentia: Notn enim qui operantur iniquitatem, in viis eius ambulaverunt. Qui autem peccatum facit, et iniquitatem facit, ait beatus Ioannes; et addidit, Peccatum iniquitas est (ib. 3,4). Sed iam sermo iste claudendus est, nec in angustum tanta quaestio coarctanda. SERMO

We must strive with the help of God, on whom our words and ourselves depend, so that we do not disturb the reader or listener by misunderstanding what is well said. We must avoid thinking that all the saints, from whom this voice comes: If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves and the truth is not in us, they do not walk in the ways of the Lord, because sin is iniquity, and those who commit it certainly have not walked in his ways. And also, on the contrary, it is believed, which is clearly false, that they have no sin, because it is true that they walk in the way of the Lord. It was not written: If we said that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, in order to avoid arrogance and pride, otherwise it would not be added: and the truth is not in us, but it would be said: humility is not in us; and, above all, clarifying this meaning and removing all doubt what follows, since, after having said what Saint John referred to previously, he adds: But, if we confess our crimes, God is faithful and just to forgive our sins and cleanse us from all iniquity. What do you say to this? What does this oppose the arrogance of detestable impiety? Yes, to avoid arrogance, but not to confess the truth, say the saints who have sins, what do they confess in order to obtain forgiveness and be purified? Or does someone also confess to avoid arrogance? So how will forgiveness of sins be achieved with a false confession? Be silenced and the weak arrogance of the proud is consummated, which deceives itself by saying in the ears of man, with feigned humility, that it is a sinner, and saying in its heart, with perverse arrogance, that it has no sin. Those who say this deceive themselves and the truth is not in them. When they whisper this in the ears of man, se randum est, opitulante Deo, in cuius manu sunt et nos et sermones nostri (Wis 7:16), ne recte dictum, non recte intellectum, lectorem auditoremve perturbet.

Cavendum est enim, ne omnes sancti, quorum illa vox est, Si dixerimus quia peccatum non habemus, nos ipsos seducimus, et vertías in nobis non est; aut non putentur ambulare in viis Domini, quoniam peccatum iniquitas est (1 lo 3,4), et qui operantur iniquitatem, non utique in viis eius ambulaverunt; aut quia dubium non est eos ambulare in viis Domini, non credantur habere peccatum, quod procul dubio falsum est. Ñeque enim propter arrogantiam superbiamque vitandam scriptum est, Si dixerimus quia peccatum non habemus, nos ipsos seducimus. Alioquin non adderetur, Et veritas in nobis non est; sed diceretur, Humilitas in nobis non est: praesertim quia sequitur unde iste sensus clarius illustretur, omnesque auferat dubitationis ambages. Cum enim hoc beatus Ioannes dixisset, adiunxit: «Si autem confessi fuerimus delicta nostra, fidelis est et iustus, qui dimittat nobis peccata nostra, et mundet nos ab omni iniquitate» (ib. 1,8 et 9).

They deceive not only themselves, but also others with the perversity of perfidious doctrine. But, when they say it in their heart, there they deceive themselves, there is no truth there; and therefore they deceive themselves in their hearts and the light of truth disappears from it. Exclaim, then, the holy family of Christ, which grows and bears fruit throughout the world, humbly truthful and truthfully humble; exclaim, I will say, with these words: If we said that we have no sins, we deceive ourselves and the truth is not in us; But, if we confess our crimes (God) is just and faithful to forgive us our crimes and cleanse us from all iniquity. Just as this is said, he sits down. For there will be true humility if it is not displayed only in words, but, as the Apostle says, we are not haughty in thought, but we feel with the humble. And it does not say "we speak", but we feel, which is executed with the heart, not with the mouth. Hypocrite, if you say that you have sin believing that you lack it, outwardly you feign humility and inwardly you embrace vanity. Then you lack the truth in your mouth and in your heart. What good is it for you to appear to men that you are humble, because that is what you tell them, if God sees that you are haughty, as you feel? An ideo mens altitudine inflatur, ut humilitatem lingua mentiatur? Legis, vel audis, Noli altum sapere, sed time: et tu in tantum sapis altum, ut te peccatum existimes non habere; ac per hoc, quia non vis timere, nihil tibi aliud remanet quam tumere. 2. Regarding this, he answers: "Have you not read what I confess saying: I do not do the good that I want, but I do the evil that I do not want"? We have heard it. (Phil 3,15.14). Postremo in qua alia via cucurreram, quando dicebam, Bonum certamen certavi, cursum consummavi? (2 Tim 4:7). Et hoc audimus: iam itaque illud interrogamus, Quomodo in viis Domini ambulabas, si malum quod nolebas hoc agebas; cum Psalmus sanctus insonet dices, Non enim qui operantur iniquitatem, in viis eius ambulaverunt? 3. Here someone will say: "How did he carry out the evil that he did not want and how did he not perpetrate it, but rather the sin that lived in him? While we are elucidating this question, let it be established that it has been proven by the authority of the canonical Scripture that it can happen that those who walk in the ways of the Lord, although they are not without sin, nevertheless do not commit it. For those who work iniquity, that is, sin, since sin is iniquity, did not walk in his ways. Then to explain how it can be understood that he works through the body of this death, in which the law of sin dwells, and that he does not commit sin, since he walks in the ways of the Lord, another sermon is necessary, since this one must conclude here.

1 [v.3]. Sin being iniquity, according to Saint John, arose from what is recorded in this psalm: Those who work iniquity did not walk in their ways, a difficult question, namely: how the saints could not have been in this life without sin, since what is recorded is true: If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves and the truth is not in us, and, nevertheless, they walked the ways of the Lord, which Those who work iniquity walk. go, walk the ways of the Lord, which those who do it do not walk, because it is no longer he who commits it, but the sin that dwells in him. This issue was resolved; However, another even more difficult one arises from it, namely: How does man do what he does not do, since both things were said: I do what I do not want; and also: Not I, but the sin that dwells in me? Therefore, we must understand that, when the sin that dwells in us works in us, if our will does not consent to it and restrains the members of the body from obeying its evil desires, then we do not act. For what does sin do if we do not want it? Only the movement of illicit desires. But, if the will does not give its consent, certainly many affections are excited, but no act is permitted. This is what the Apostle himself ordered where he said: Let sin not reign in our mortal body, so that it obeys its appetites; nor lend your members as weapons of iniquity to sin. Then the Apostle forbade us to obey the desires of sin. Sin, indeed, works these desires; If we obey him, we also act. On the contrary, if, obeying the Apostle, we do not obey them, it is not we who act, but the sin that dwells in us. If we lacked all disordered movement, neither we nor sin would work any evil in us. However, it is said that we execute the movement of illicit desire, and that by not obeying it we do not act, because it is not an incentive of another's nature, but rather a disease of our own. Will we be free from this disease in peccatum? Ambulat also via Domini, quas non ambulant qui operatur; quia iam non ipse operatur illud, sed quod in eo habitat peccatum. Therefore, as we walk in the ways of the Lord, we do not obey the desires of sin; and since, on the other hand, we are not without sin, we possess the desires of sin. For the same reason, we do not do them by not obeying them, but sin, which dwells in us, moving us, since those who work iniquity, that is, those who obey the desires of sin, did not walk in the ways of the Lord. 2. But it must still be asked what things we ask to be forgiven when we say to God, Forgive us our debts: whether those that we commit when we obey the desires of sin, or whether we want Him to forgive us the desires themselves, which we do not do, but the sin that dwells in us. As far as I can get a glimpse, all the trace of that illness and weakness from which illicit desires proceed, which the Apostle calls sin, was destroyed together with everything that we had done, said and thought in obedience to it, by the sacrament of baptism, so that from now on this weakness or illness will not harm us, even if it resides in us, if we never obey any disordered movement of it, whether by thought, by word or deed, until it is completely healed when what we ask here is fulfilled saying: Your kingdom come; or also: Deliver us from evil. But since man's life on earth is a continuous temptation, although we are far from committing crimes, there is no lack, alienae, sed languor est nostrae: a quo languore omnimodo salvi erimus, cum et animo et corpore immortales facti fuerimus. Quapropter et quia in viis Domini ambulamus, non obedimus desideriis peccati; et quia non sumus sine peccato, habemus desideria peccati. Ac per hoc iam nos ea non operamur, non eis obediendo; sed quod in nobis habitat peccatum, eadem commovendo. Non enim qui operantur iniquitatem, id est, obediunt desideriis peccati, in viis Domini ambulaverunt. 2. Sed adhuc quaerendum est quae petamus dimitti nobis, quando dicimus Deo, Dimitte nobis debita nostra: utrum quae nos operamur, quando peccati desideriis obedimus; an ipsa desideria nobis dimitti volumus, quae nos non operamur, sed quod habitat in nobis peccatum. Quantum quidem ego sapere possum, languoris illius et infirmitatis, unde illicita desideria commoventur, quod peccatum appeliat Apostolus (ib.

7, 7-25), universus reatus sacramento Baptismatis est solutus, cum omnibus quae illi obedientes fecimus, diximus, cogitavimus; nec nobis deinceps languor iste obesset, quamvis inesset, si desideriis eius illicitis nullis unquam obedientiam praeberemus, sive operatione, sive locutione, sive tacita assensione; doñee etiam ipse sanaretur, cum id quod poscimus esset impletum, sive dicentes, Veniat regnum tuum; sive sayings, Deliver us evil (Mt 6,12.10.13): sed quoniam tempted est vita humano super terram (Iob 7,1); etiamsi a criminibus longe simus, non tamen deest ubi desideriis peccati, vel facto, vel dicto, vel cogitatu obedíamus;

However, there are occasions when we obey the desires of sin, whether by thought, by word or by deed, when, while guarding against the most serious sins, some small ones sneak in, because we are not prepared; that, if they all join forces against us, even if each one of them does not destroy us with their gravity, all together, however, they suffocate us with their multitude. By these also those who walk in the ways of the Lord say: Forgive us our debts; for, even though sins do not belong to the ways of the Lord, prayer and confession, nevertheless, refer to them. 3. Therefore, in the ways of the Lord, which are all included in the faith, by which one believes in Him who justifies the wicked and who also said: I am the way, no one commits sin; He only confesses. For when a man sins, he strays from the path; and, therefore, the sin committed, by which he abandoned the path, is not attributed to the path, and, for the same reason, those to whom the sin is not imputed are not counted as sinners on the path of faith. The apostle Saint Paul, recommending the righteousness of faith, showed that it was written about these in the Psalm: Blessed are those to whom their iniquities are remitted and whose sins are covered; blessed is the man to whom the Lord did not impute sin. This is what the ways of the Lord report, and since the righteous live by faith, they remove iniquity from these ways, which is infidelity. Anyone who walks in this way, that is, by pious faith, either does not commit sin, or, if he commits one by turning aside, it is not imputed to him, considering the way he walks, and he is considered as if he had not eaten it. Therefore, in this way it is understood quado adversus maiora vigilantibus, quaedam seizures minuta subrepunt quae si adversus nos colligantur, etsi non singula sui molibus conterunt, omnia tamen acervo nos obruunt. Et propter haec, etiam hi qui ambulant in viis Domini dicunt, Dimitte nobis debita nostra: quoniam ad vias Domini, et ipsa oratio pertinet, et ipsa confessio, quamvis non ad eas peccata pertineant. 3. Itaque in viis Domini, quas omnes lides una complectitur, qua in eum creditur qui iustificat impium (Rom 4,5), qui etiam dixit, Ego sum via (lo 14,6); nemo peccatum operatur, sed confitetur. Deviat ergo, cum peccat; et ideo peccatum viae non tribuitur, quod a deviante committiur: sed in via fidei pro non peccantibus habentur, quibus peccata non imputantur.

De quibus apostolus Paulus iustitiam fidei commendans, in psalmo scriptum esse monstravit, Beati quorum remissae sunt iniquitates, et quorum tecta sunt peccata: beatus vir cui non imputavit Dominus peccatum (Rom 4,7; et Ps 31,1 et 2). Hoc praestant viae Domini; ac per hoc, quoniam istus ex fide vivit (Rom 1:17), ab ista via Domini illa alienat iniquitas, quae est infidelitas. In hac atitem via, id est, in fide pia, quisquís ambulat, aut peccatum non operatur, aut si quid a deviante committitur, propter viam non imputatur, et tanquam non

Those who work iniquity did not walk rightly in the ways of the Lord, which in this indicated that iniquity that distances one from faith or does not bring one closer to it. In this sense the Lord of the Jews said: If I had not come, they would have no sin. And he did not say this because they had no sin before Christ came in the flesh and began to have it since he came, but he was referring to a certain sin, that of unfaithfulness, since they did not believe in Him. Therefore, those who work iniquity, not just any, but that of unfaithfulness, did not walk in the ways of the Lord, because all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth, and both are found in Christ, and apart from Him they are found nowhere. The apostle Saint Paul says: I say therefore that Christ was a minister of circumcision for the truth of God, in order to establish the promises of the Fathers; and that you Gentiles, through mercy, glorify God. Mercy lies in the fact that he redeemed us, and the truth lies in the fact that he fulfilled what was promised and will fulfill what has not yet been fulfilled and promises. Those who work iniquity, that is, unfaithfulness, did not walk in the ways, because they did not believe in Christ. Convert and believe piously in Him who justifies the wicked and in Him you will find mercy by forgiving you your sins, and truth by fulfilling your promises; that is, they will find the ways of the Lord. And walking in them, they will not work iniquity, because they will not possess infidelity, but faith, which works by love, and to which no sin is imputed. fuerit operatus accipitur. Et ideo bene etiam sic intelligitur, Non enim qui operantur iniquitatem, in viis eius ambulavemnt; ut hanc iniquitatem meansverit, quae recedit a fide, aut non accessit ad fidem. Quemadmodum enim ait Dominus de Iudaeis, Si non venissem, peccatum non haberent (lo 15,22); nec utique sine uUo peccato erant, antequam Christus vinoret in carne, et ex quo venit, coeperunt habere peccatum; sed peccatum quoddam certum, id est, infidelitatis, intelligi voluit, quoniam non crediderunt in eum: ita qui operantur iniquitatem, non quamlibet, sed hanc ipsam infidelitatis, non in viis eius ambulavemnt, quia uníversae viae Domini misericordia et veritas (Ps 24,10); utrumque autem in Christo est, et praeter Christum nusquam est. I say enim Christum, ait Apostolus, ministrum Fuisse circumcisionis propter veritatem Dei, ad confirmandas promissiones Patrum; Gentes autem super misericordiam glorificare Deum (Rom 15,8 et 9).

In hoc igitur misericordia, quia nos redemit; in hoc veritas, quia id quod promisit implevit, et impleturus est quod promittit. Qui ergo operantur iniquitatem, id est infidelitatem, non in viis eius ambulavemnt; quia in Christum non crediderunt. Ergo convertantur, et in eum qui iustificat impium, pie credant, atque in illo misericordiam peccatis dimissis, et veritatem completis promissis, hoc est, universas vias Domini inveniant: in quibus ambulantes non operabuntur iniquitatem; quia non tenebunt infidelitatem, sed fidem, quae per dilectionem operatur (Gal 5,6), et cui peccatum non imputatur. •
Excellencies of the law of God

SERMON 41 [v.4]. Who is this, dear ones, who says to the Lord: You commanded that your commandments be kept too much. May my paths be made straight to keep your justifications! Then I will not be confused by looking at all your commandments? Who says this except each of the members of Christ, or, rather, the entire Body of Christ? And what does it mean: You ordered to keep your commandments excessively? Does it mean that you commanded too much or that they should be guarded too much? Whichever of these two ways we understand, it seems contrary to that memorable and famous sentence: Nothing too much, which the Greeks attribute to their wise men and the Latins applaud. If it is true that nothing should be done in excess, how is it also true that what is said here: You commanded that your commandments be kept too much, whereas God would command something in excess; Or would you want it to be kept too much, if everything excessive were worthy of rebuke? Or will we say that the authority of the Greeks should not be taken into account at all, keeping in mind what he wrote? Has not God made the wisdom of the world foolish? And, therefore, do we rather believe that the sentence by which it was said: Nothing too much, is false than the divine word that we have read and sung: You commanded that your commandments should be kept too much, unless right reason, and not the haughtiness of the Greeks, prevents us from saying so? Anything that is more than what is appropriate is said to be too much. Little and too much are two words that are contrary to each other. A little is less than what is appropriate and too much is more s ERM o i v 1 [v.4]. Quis est, charissimi, qui Domino dicit, «Tu praecepisti mandata tua custodiri nimis. Utinam dirígantur viae meae ad custodiendas iustificationes tuas. Tune non confundar, dum inspicio in omnia mandata tua?» Quis est qui hoc dicit, nisi unumquodque membrum Christi, vel potius universum corpus Christi? Et quid est, Tu praecepisti mandata tua custodiri nimis? utrum, nimis praecepisti; an, nimis custodiri? Quodlibet horum intelligamus, contra illam memorabilem nobilemque sententiam hoc dictum videtur, quam Graeci laudant in sapientibus suis, et Latini laudando consentiunt: "Ne quid nimis" (TERENT., Andr. act. 1, se. 1).

Si enim hoc verum est, ut ne quid nimis fiat; quomodo verum est quod hic dicitur, Tu praecepisti mandata tua custodiri nimis? quando Deus aliquid vel nimis praeciperet, vel nimis custodiri vellet, si omne nimium reprehensione dignum esset? Diceremus ergo nos Milla graecorum sapientium auctoritate teneri, intuentes quod scríptum est, Nonne stultam fecit Deus sapientiam buius mundi? (1 Cor 1:20) et potius istam sententiam falsem esse crederemus, quam dictum est, «Ne
^narratives about the Psalms

of what is convenient; In the middle of these extremes there is a term, which is called enough or sufficient. Since, therefore, it is useful in life and customs that we do absolutely nothing more than what is appropriate, we should rather confess than deny that the sentence is true, nothing too much. Sometimes in the Latin language this word nimis is abused, so that nimis, too much, is used for valde, a lot, and in this sense we find it used in sacred books and in our conversations. For here, you commanded that your commandments be kept too much must be understood, if a good sense is to be given, by far. Also, when saying to a great friend: I love you too much, we do not mean to imply that we love him more than is appropriate, but rather a lot. In short, that Greek sentence does not use the word that is read here in the psalm; there in the sentence it is read agan, which means nimis, with excess; and here in the psalm we read esfodra, which means worth, much. But sometimes, as we said, the nimis is used too much, for good reason, a lot, in Scripture and in conversation. Hence, many even Latin codices do not write: You ordered that your commandments be kept "nimis", with too much, if not valid, a lot. 1 [v.9}. Let us consider, my brothers, the verses of this psalm and, as the Lord grants us, let us examine the sacred writings. How does the young man correct his path? Saving your words. He asks himself and answers. The question is this: How does the young man correct his path? the answer: Keeping your words. Here the keeping of God's words must be understood as the execution of his precepts, since they are kept in vain in memory if they are not kept in practical life. There are certain individuals who memorize the precepts of the Lord so that they do not forget them, but they do not put them into practice in life to correct themselves. Also: I still have many things to explain, but now you are not able to understand them. And even though he then promised to know the whole truth through the Holy Spirit, the apostle Saint Paul nevertheless exclaims: We know in part. For this reason we must understand that although the Holy Spirit, from whom we receive the pledge, leads us to the knowledge of all truth, it will be achieved when we have reached the other life, after having passed through this mirror and shadow and see face to face. How does this one say: With my lips I announced all the judgments of your mouth, whereas shortly before, that is, in the previous verse, he had said: Teach me your justifications? By virtue of what did he who still wants to learn his justifications announce all the judgments from the mouth of God? Did he already know all his judgments and already wanted to learn the justifications? But it is more to be admired that he already knew the inscrutable things and was ignorant of those that he ordered men to do. For justifications are not sayings, but acts of justice, that is, works of the righteous that God commands; and they are called God's even when we do them because we would not do them if He did not grant them. The judgments of God are those verdicts with which he judges the world now and will judge it at the end of the centuries. who said these things; Or whether it is said not of every man, which is more exempt from controversy, but of him who was promised the eternal homeland in heaven, the truth is that human life on earth is a continuous temptation and that the children of Adam have a heavy yoke upon them. It pleases me more to deal with this matter according to the ruling that understands that we call ourselves tenants or dwellers on the earth because we have found a superior homeland, from which we have received guarantee, and from which, upon arriving, we will never depart from it. For he who says in another psalm: I am a tenant before you, and a pilgrim, like all my fathers, does not say "like all men." Therefore, by saying like all my fathers, he undoubtedly wants to imply that these are the righteous who preceded him in time and sighed in this pilgrimage through the eternal homeland with a pious groan; of whom it was written in the epistle to the Hebrews: All these died in the heyday, without having received the promises, but, seeing them and greeting them from afar, they confessed that they are guests and pilgrims on the earth. Those who say such a thing declare that they are looking for their homeland, because, if they had remembered those they had abandoned, they would have had time to return; But now they desire a better one, that is, the heavenly one, and for this reason God is not ashamed to be and to be called their God, since he prepared a city for them. Also what we read: While we are living in the body, we are strangers to the Lord, it can be understood that it is not said about everyone, but about the faithful. Because faith is not for everyone. Furthermore, we observe what the Apostle adds to these words, since, having said: cui patria promissa est aeterna in caelis: hoc scio, quia tentatio est vita humano super terram (Job 7,1); et iugum grave est super filios Adam (Eccli 40,1). Verum me plus delectat secundum istam disputare sententiam, ut ideo nos in terra tenants vel Íncolas esse dicamus, quia supernam patriam, unde pignus accepimus, et quo pervenientes nunquam inde migremus, invenimus.

Nam et ille qui in alio psalmo dicit, Inquilinus ego sum apud te et peregrinus, sicut omnes patres mei (Ps 38,13); non ait, Sicut omnes homines; be saying, sicut omnes patres mei, iustus procul dubio vult intelligi, qui eum tempore praecesserunt, et in hac peregrinatione gemitu pió supernae patriae sighunt. De quibus scriptum est ad Hebraeos: «Secundum fidem mortui sunt hi omnes, cum non accepissent promissiones, sed longe eas videntes et salutantes, et confitentes quia hospites et peregrini sunt super terram. Qui enim talia dicunt, ostendunt quia patriam quaerunt. Et si quidem eius memores essent a qua discesserant, habuissent tempus revertendi; nunc autem meliorem appetunt, id est caelestem: ideo non confunditur de his Deus vocari Deus eorum; praeparavit enim eis civitatem” (Hebr 11:13-16). Et illud quod legimus, Quamdiu sumus in corpore, peregrinamur a Domino; potest intelligi hoc non esse omnium, sed fidelium: Non enim omnium est fides (2 Thes 3,2). Et videmus quid his verbis Apostolus iungat.

While we are living in the body, we are strangers to the Lord, he writes below: as if we walked by faith, not by vision, so that we would understand that this pilgrimage is for those who walk by faith. The infidels whom God neither foresaw nor predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son / cannot truly call themselves pilgrims on earth, / since, being there where they were born according to the flesh, they have no city elsewhere, and, therefore, they are not on earth as pilgrims, but as children of it. Hence the Scripture says about one of them: He made his house in death, and in hell his doors with the children of the earth. However, these are also the same pilgrims and tenants, but not with regard to this land, but to the people of God, to whom they are strangers. Hence the apostle Saint Paul says to believers and those who begin to participate in the holy city, which is not of this world: You are no longer pilgrims and tenants, but you are fellow citizens of the saints and householders of God. Therefore, those who are pilgrims of the people of God are citizens of the earth; but those who are citizens of God's people are pilgrims on earth, because all this people, while they are living in the body, are pilgrims towards God. Say, then: I am a pilgrim on earth; do not hide your commandments from me. 2. But who are those from whom God hides his commandments? Did God not want them to be preached everywhere? May they, being so evident to many, be equally loved by many! Well, what could be clearer than that you will love the Lord, your God, with all your heart, with all your

soul and with all your mind and love your neighbor as yourself, on whose two commandments the law and the prophets are based? To whom are these commandments unknown? All the faithful and many unbelievers know them. Why, then, does the faithful ask that what he sees is not hidden from the unbeliever not be hidden from him? Is it because it is difficult to know God, and therefore it is reasonable that it is also difficult to understand that you will love the Lord, your God, since one thing can be loved for another? Knowing one's neighbor is, without a doubt, easier, since every man is man's neighbor, and one should not think of any distant species where nature is common. Even though he who said to the Lord did not know his neighbor: Who is my neighbor, however, when it was proposed to a certain man who was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho and who fell among the thieves, the same man who had asked, seeing that only the one who performed mercy on him behaved like a neighbor, discovered that whoever loves his neighbor should consider no one a stranger to show mercy to him. But many do not even know themselves, since knowing oneself, as man should know himself, is not for all men; It is a matter of few. How then will he who does not know himself love his neighbor as himself? The younger son who went to a distant region, where he dissipated all his property by living licentiously, not in vain first turned to himself, saying: I will arise and go to my father, since he went so far away that he had turned away from himself. with which the spirit covets against the flesh, and you will find it where it is said: The covetousness of wisdom leads to the kingdom; and you will not find only this one, but many others that confirm the excellence of this good greed. But it is interesting to know that, when good covetousness is commemorated, what is coveted is expressed; But, when what is coveted is not indicated, but only the covetousness is recorded, then the evil is understood. If in the testimony adduced: The greed of wisdom leads to the kingdom, it had not been added of wisdom, in no way would it have said: Greed leads to the kingdom. On the contrary, when the Apostle wrote: I would not know covetousness if the law did not say do not covet, by not specifying the thing coveted or what you should not covet, he only understood evil covetousness by speaking in this way. Then what did his soul covet? Desire—he says—your justifications at all times. I think he didn't want them yet, since he coveted wanting them. Justifications are just acts, that is, works of justice. Therefore, if he who desires them does not yet possess them, how far away was he who still coveted to desire them! And how much more distant are those who do not even covet them! 4. man? So why do you want to have it, as if it came from outside? Or how can one covet him without having him, since he is nothing but covetousness? Well, to desire is undoubtedly to covet. What admirable and inexplicable disease is this? And yet it exists. The patient who suffers from boredom and wants to rid himself of this evil, covets or desires food when he desires not to have boredom; but this annoyance is a disease of the body. The greed by which we desire food is to lack boredom, and is found in the soul, not in the body; and it is possessed not by the delight of the throat and jaws, which is lessened by annoyance, but by the incentive of the recovery of health, with which it is provided to remove the annoyance of food. This is why it is not surprising that the spirit desires so that the body desires when the soul desires and the body does not desire. But when both appetites are found in the soul and both are covetous, why did the desire for the justifications of God covet? How do I have in one and the same soul the greed of this desire and I do not have the same desire? Or how these things are two and not one? Why did he covet desiring justifications and did he not covet justifications rather than the desire for them? Or why could he covet the desire for justifications and not covet the justifications themselves, since he coveted the desire for them, because he desired to have them? If this is so, you already coveted them. What need is there to covet their desire, when I already have it and perceive that I have it? For I could not covet the desire for justice if it were not by coveting justice. Could this perhaps be what I said before, that the love with which one loves what one should love must be loved, just as ha in homine esse concupiscentiam, in homine esse desiderium? Cur ergo concupiscitur ut habeatur, quasi forinsecus inferatur? Aut quomodo haberi eius concupiscentia sine ipso potest, cum non sit et ipsum quid aliud quam concupiscentia? Nam et desiderare procul dubio concupiscere est. Quis est iste mirabilis atque inexplicabilis languor? Et tamen est. Nam et aegrotus qui fastidio laborat, et vult evadete hoc malum, concupiscit utique desiderare cibum, dum concupiscit non habere fastidium: sed hoc fastidium morbus est corporis.

Concupiscentia vero qua concupiscit desiderare cibum, hoc est carere fastidio, in animo est, non in corpore: et habet eam non gutturis et faucium delectatio, quae fastidio restringitur; sed recuperandae ratio sanitatis, qua pellendum escae fastidium providetur. Et ideo non mirum est si appetit animus ut appetat corpus, quando appetit animus nec appetit corpus. Cum autem utrumque animi est, et utrumque concupiscentia est, cur concupisco desiderium iustificationum Dei? Quomodo in uno eodemque animo meo habeo concupiscentiam desiderii huius, et ipsum non habeo desiderium? aut quomodo ista duo sunt, et non unum? Utquid enim concupisco desiderare iustificationes, ac non ipsas iustificationes potius quam earum desiderium concupisco? aut quo pact possum iustificationum desiderium concupiscere, et ipsas iustificationes non concupiscere; cum ideo earum desiderium concupiscam,

to hate the love with which one loves what is not lawful to love? Indeed, we hate the greed with which the flesh lusts against the spirit; Well, what is this greed but bad love? However, we love the covetousness with which the spirit covets against the flesh, for what is this covetousness but good love? When it is said that it should be loved, what else is said but that it should be coveted? Therefore, as the justifications of God are rightly coveted, the covetousness of God's own justifications is also rightly coveted, the love of these justifications is rightly loved. Or is coveting something different from desiring? But not because desire is not coveting, but because not all greed is desire. For things that one has and those that one does not have are coveted, and by coveting, man enjoys the things he possesses; but, desiring, he covets those that he lacks. So what is desire? A greed for things that are missing. But when can God's justifications be missing or absent if not when they are ignored? Or should they also be considered absent when they are known and not practiced? Justifications are not words, but good works; Therefore, they may not be desired due to illness of the soul, and yet by the mind, in which it is seen how useful and healthy they are, the desire for them may be coveted. We often see what should be done and do not act, quia ipsas habere cupio? Quod si ita est, iam ipsas utique concupisco. Quid igitur opus est ut earum desiderium concupiscam, cum iam id habeam, et habere me sentiam? Non enim possem concupiscere desiderium iustitiae, nisi concupiscendo iustitiam. An hoc est quod superius dixi, quod diligenda sit etiam ipsa dilectio qua diligitur quod diligi oportet; sicut odio habenda est dilectio qua diligitur quod diligi non oportet? I hate quippe habemus concupiscentiam nostram qua caro concupiscit adversus spiritum: et quid est ista concupiscentia, nisi mala dilectio? Et diligimus concupiscentiam nostram qua spiritus concupiscit adversus carnem: et quid est ista concupiscentia, nisi bona dilectio? Cum autem dicitur, Diligenda est, quid aliud dicitur quam, concupiscenda est? Quocirca quoniam recte concupiscuntur iustificationes Dei, recte concupiscitur concupiscentia iustificationum Dei. Hoc enim alio moda sic potest dici: si recte diliguntur iustificationes Dei, recte diligitur dilectio iustificationum Dei. An aliud est concupiscere, aliud desiderare?

Non quod non sit concupiscentia desiderium, sed quia non omnis concupiscentia desiderium est. Concupiscuntur enim et quae habentur, et quae non habentur: nam concupiscendo, fruitur homo rebus quas habet; desiderando autem, absentia concupiscit. Desiderium ergo quid est, nisi rerum absentium concupiscentia? Sed Dei iustificationes absentes esse quomodo possunt, nisi quando nesciuntur? An et quando sciuntur et non fiunt, absentes habendae sunt? Nam quid sunt iustificationes, nisi opera iusta, non verba? Ac per hoc possunt infirmitate animae non desiderari; et ratione mentís, ubi videtur quam sint useful atque salubres, potest earum desiderium concupisci. Saepe enim quid agendum sit videmus, nec agimus; quia non delectat ut agamus, et cupimus ut delectet. Praevolat

It does not say "greed", but my soul coveted to desire your justifications. Perhaps this dweller on earth was such that he had already achieved what he had coveted, and, therefore, desired the justifications, the desire of which he once coveted, as he commemorates. But if he wanted them, why didn't he have them? For nothing, in truth, prevents us from having God's justifications if it is not not desiring them when His love shines and love towards them is lacking. But did he have them and did he fulfill them, since he says shortly after: Your servant exercised himself in your justifications, and, therefore, he only declares the degrees by which they are arrived at? First it is necessary to know how useful and decorous they are; then let his desire be coveted; and, finally, that, by increasing light and health, the exercise of those things of which the mere knowledge of them delights. time your justifications, both in prosperous and adverse events, because justice must also delight us in work and suffering, and we must not love it only in prosperity and abandon it in adversity, but it must be embraced at all times, then he adds: You rebuked the proud; Cursed are those who deviate from your commandments. The proud turn away from the commandments of God. It is one thing not to fulfill the commandments of God out of weakness or ignorance, and another to depart from them out of pride, as those who mortally generated us for these evils did. For they took delight in being like gods, and so through pride they deviated from the precept of God, which they were not unaware of having been placed upon them by the Lord, and which they could very easily have fulfilled without any dissuading, impeding or retarding weakness. Here is how all this heavy and unhappy misfortune of mortals becomes, in a certain way, a hereditary rebuke of the proud. When God said to Adam: Where are you?, he did not know where he was, but like a proud man he rebuked him; and he did not want to know where he was then, that is, what misery he had ended up in, but rather, by rebuking him with the question, he made him see it. Observe how, having said: You rebuked the proud, he did not add: Cursed are those who deviate from your precepts, as if he remembered only that single sin of the first men, but says: Cursed are those who depart. It was appropriate, therefore, that everyone should be frightened by that example so that they would not deviate from the fulfillment of the divine precepts, and thus, loving justice at all times, we would receive, in the midst of the mea desiderare iustificationes tuas in omni tempore; sive scilicet in rebus prosperis, sive in adversis, quia et in laboribus et doloribus debent delectare iustitia, nec ita est tempore diligenda tranquil, ut turbulento tempore deseratur, sed amplectenda est in omni tempore: continuo subiecit, Increpasti superbos; maledicti qui declinant a mandatis tuis. Superbi enim declinant a mandatis Dei. Aliud est quippe mandata Dei per infirmitatem vel ignorantiam non implere: aliud ab eis per superbiam declinare; sicut fecerunt qui nos mortaliter in haec mala genuerunt. Delectavit enim eos, Eritis sicut dii; ac sic a mandato Dei, quod sibi eum mandasse sciebant, et quod facillime, nulla infirmitate revocante impediente, tardante, implere poterant, per hanc superbiam declinarunt.

Et ecce tota ista dura et infelix aerumna motarlium, quodam moda haereditaria est increpatio superborum. Quando enim dixit Deus, Adam, ubi es? (Gen 3,5.9) non ubi esset ignorabat, sed superbum increpabat; et ubi tune esset, id est, ad quam miseriam pervenisset, non scire cupiebat, sed interrogando increpans admonebat. Vide autem quemadmodum cum dixisset, Increpasti superbos, non ait, Maledicti qui declinaverunt a mandatis tuis; ut illud tantum primorum hominum peccatum comeret inmentem: sed ait, Maledicti qui declinant. Oportebat enim ut omnes illo terrerentur exemplo a divinis non declinare mandatis, et diligendo

sufferings of this world, what we lost in the delights of paradise. 2 [y.22]. But since the proud do not bend their necks even with such great rebuke; Indeed, finding themselves brought down with the torment of suffering and death, they become puffed up with pride, imitating the arrogance of those who fall and mocking the humility of those who rise up, the body of Christ prays for them when he says: Remove shame and contempt from me, because I inquired about your testimonies. In Greek, testimonies are called martyrdoms. This word is already used in Latin. For this reason, those who were humiliated with various sufferings for the testimony of Christ and fought for the truth until death, are not called testes (witnesses), as we could do in Latin, but martyrs in the Greek language. Since you hear this Greek word more familiarly and with more pleasure, let us take the previous words as if it were said: Blame and contempt be apart from me, because I inquired about your martyrdoms. In saying this, will the Body of Christ consider it a shame to hear the opprobrium and contempt inflicted by the proud and impious, even though it is rather through them that it receives the crown? Why, then, does he ask that it be taken away from him as something serious and intolerable? Because, as I said, he prays for his enemies, for whom he sees that it is harmful to hold the name of Christ and his cross against Christians as a disgrace, which was despised by the Jews and which is the universal medicine of Christian humanity, by which only one is healed from that swelling, by which, arrogant, we fell, and, fallen, we eniustitiam in omni tempore, in huius mundi etiam labore recipere quod in paradisi amisimus voluptate. 2 [v.22]. Sed quoniam superbi nec in tanta deponunt increpatione cervicem, et cum sint deiecti laboris mortisque supplicio, extolluntur superbiae typho, imitantes elationem cadentium, irridentes humilitatem surgentium; pro eis orat Corpus Christi, cum dicit: Aufer a me opprobrium et contemptum, quoniam testimonia tua exquisivi. Testimonia graece martyria nuncupantur, quo verb iam utimur pro latino: unde illos qui propter testimonium Christi diversis passionibus humiliati sunt, et usque ad mortem pro veritate certarunt, non testes, quod latine utique possemus, sed graece martyres appellamus. Quoniam hoc ergo familiarius auditis et dulcius, sic accipiamus haec verba tanquam dictum sit, Aufer a me opprobrium et contemptum, quoniam martyria tua exquisivi.

Christi corpus ista cum dicit, numquid ab impiis et superbis audire opprobrium atque contemptum ullam deputat poenam, cum potius inde perveniat ad coronam? Cur ergo quasi grave aliquid et intolerabile a se poscit auferri, nisi quia, ut dixi, orat pro ipsis inimicis suis, quibus esse perspicit noxium, obiicere sanctum nomen Christi tanquam opprobrium Christianis, et eius a Iudaeis irrisam cruzem totamque humilitatis christianae medicinalm, qua sola tumor ille sanatur quo inflad cecidimus et iacentes amplius intumuimus, eadem superbia permanent et crescente
Excellencies of the law i.e. God

We fell even more, persisting and increasing the same arrogance that was taken for granted. Say, then, the Body of Christ, since you have already learned to love your enemies; Say to your Lord God: Remove reproach and contempt from me, because I inquired about your martyrdoms; That is to say, remove from me the reproach that I hear and the contempt with which I am reviled, because I sought your martyrdoms; for my enemies, whom you command me to love, who die and perish more and more every day despising and recriminating your martyrdoms in me, will undoubtedly revive and find the way if they venerate your martyrdoms in me. That's how it happened and we verified it. See that the martyrdom of Christ is not only no longer a disgrace among men in this world, but it is a great distinctive. See that not only before the Lord, but also before men, the death of his saints is precious. See that not only are their martyrs no longer despised, but they are venerated with great honors. See that young son, who for the swine he fed, that is, for the demons he worshiped, went, in pursuit of his previous little part of persecution, against the few Christians, how he revives after having died and is found after having perished, and is already preaching with great fervor in many large towns of Gentiles, extolling with the highest praise the martyrs to whom he once inflicted disgrace and contempt The Body of Christ, for this immense fruit of correction, conversion and redemption of its enemies, said to God: Remove reproach and contempt from me; and as if asked why the disgrace and contempt was imposed on him, he adds: because I sought your martyrdoms. will it contain? Dicat itaque corpus Christi; iam enim diligere didicit inimicos suos: dicat Domino Deo, suo, Aufer a me opprobrium et contemptum, quia martyria tua exquisivi: id est, opprobrium quod ideo audio, et contemptum quo ideo contemnor, quia martyria tua exquisivi, aufer a me. Inimici enim mei, quos a me praecipis diligi, qui magis magisque moriuntur et pereunt, cum martyria tua contemnunt et criminantur in me, profecto reviviscent et invenientur, si martyria tua venerentur in me. Ita factum est; hoc videmus.

Ecce martyrium Christi, et apud nomines et in hoc mundo, non solum non est opprobrium, sed magnum est ornamentum: ecce non solum in conspectu Domini, verum etiam in conspectu hominum iam pretiosa est mors sanctorum eius (Ps 115,15); ecce non solum non contemnuntur, verum etiam magnis honoribus praeferuntur martyres eius. Ecce filius ille iunior qui pro porcis quos pascebat, id est, pro immundis daemonibus quos colebat, particulam suam in paucissimis Christianis praecedentem persequebatur; iam nunc in tam multis et magnis populis gentium martyres, quibus ingerebat opprobrium, religiosissime praedicans, et maximis laudibus quos contemnebat exaltans, mortuus erat et revixit, perierat et inventus est (Lk 15,12-24). Hoc tam magno lucrative correctionis, conversionis et redemptionis inimicorum suorum corpus Christi Deo dixit, Aufer a me opprobrium et contemptum: et quasi quaereretur de qua re approbrium, de qua re contemptum, subiungit, Quoniam martyria tua exquisivi.

3 [v. 23-24]. Where is that disgrace now, where is that contempt? They went away and passed by; And because those who had perished were found, the shame and contempt also perished. But, when the Church made these prayers, I suffered them, because the princes—he says—sat down and spoke against me. Hence the persecution was serious, since the princes declared it seated, that is, endowed with eminent judicial power. Apply this to the Head, and you will see that the princes of the Jews sat around looking for a reason to lose Christ. Apply it to his Body, that is, to the Church, and you will find that the kings of the earth devised and decreed the way to put an end to the Christians. Indeed, the princes sat down and spoke against me; but your servant exercised your justifications. If you want to know what this exercise was, pay attention to what follows: Because my meditation is your testimonies, and my design is your justifications. Remember what I previously stated: that testimonies are martyrdoms. Remember also that, among the Lord's justifications, there is none more difficult and admirable than each man loving his own enemies. However, the Body of Christ exercised itself in this in such a way that it meditated on its martyrdoms and loved those who persecuted it with reproaches and contempt for its own martyrdoms. For he did not pray for himself, as I already remembered, but rather for them, saying: Take away from me reproach and contempt, for the princes spoke against me; but your servant exercised your justifications. How? My meditation being your testimonies, your martyrdoms, your justifications my 3 [v.23.24]. Ubi est mine illud opprobrium? ubi ille contemptus? Open atque transietunt; et quia inventi sunt qui perierant, illa perierunt. Sed quando Eeclesia talia precabatur, illa patiebatur. Etenim sederunt principes, inquit, et adversum me loquebantur. Inde persecutio gravis erat, quia eam sentes, hoc est iudiciariis sedibus eminentes, principes decernebant. Refer hoc ad ipsum caput; invenies sedisse principes Iudaeorum, consilium quaerentes quomodo Christum seguirent (Mt 26:3). Refer hoc ad corpus eius, id est Ecclesiam; invenies reges terrae excogitasse atque iussisse quomodo Christiani nusquam essent.

Etenim sederunt principes, et adversum me loquebantur: servus autem tuus exercebatur in tuis iustificationibus. Qualis exeteitatio haec fuerit, qui nosse desideras, quod adiunxit intellige: Nam et testimonia tua meditatio mea est, et consilium meum iustificationes tuae. I collected quod superius commendavi testimonia esse martyria. I collected in iustificationibus Domini nullam esse difficiliorem et mirabiliorem, quam ut suos quisque diligat inimicos. Sic ergo exercebatur corpus Christi, ut et martyria eius meditaretur, et diligeret eos a quibus opprobrantibus et contemnentibus propter ipsa martyria persecutions patiebatur. Non enim pro se, sicut iam commendavimus, sed pro ipsis potius orabat dices, Aufer a me opprobrium et contemptum. Sederunt ergo principes, et adversum me loquebantur: servus autem tuus exercebatur in iustificationibus tuis. Quonam mode? Nam et testi
Excellencies of the law of God

plan. Design that opposes another design. The design of the princes who sat down was to lose the found witnesses, the martyrs; The design of the patient martyrs was to win over their lost enemies. Those returned evils for good; these, goods for evils. Why do we marvel that those who killed ended up and those who died lived? Why do we marvel that the martyrs patiently received temporal death when the Gentiles became cruel, and the Gentiles, by praying the martyrs, were able to achieve eternal life, while the Body of Christ exercises itself by meditating on the martyrdoms and asking for goods for the perverse persecutors of the martyrs? SERMON

1 [v. 25]. We continue to consider, as the Lord grants us, what we must deal with in this great psalm. My soul stuck to the ground; quicken me according to your word. What does it mean my soul stuck to the ground? By adding and saying: quicken me according to your word, express why he asks that his soul be quickened: my soul stuck to the ground. Therefore, if he asks to be quickened because his soul stuck to the ground, it is not surprising that something bad is meant here. Indeed, this entire sentence says: I am dead; quicken me What is soil? If we consider the world as a great house, we will have the sky as its roof, and the earth as its floor. Thus, by what he said, he intended to separate himself from lo temonia tua meditatio mea est, et consilium meum iustificationes tuae. Consilium against consilium: consilium sedentium principum Fuit inventions martyres I will lose; consilium patientium martyrum Fuit imicos perditos invenire. Reddebant illi mala pro bonis; isti, bona pro malis. Quid ergo mirum si illi occidendo defecerunt, isti dying vicerunt? Quid, inquam, mirum si martyres saevientibus Gentibus temporalem mortem patientissime pertulerunt, et Gentes martyribus orantibus ad aeternam vitam pervenire potuerunt; dum corpus Christi sic exercetur, ut et martyria meditetur, et malis martyrum persecutoribus bona precetur? s ER M o

1 [v.25]. Sequitur in isto psalmo maiore, quodconsidere, et sicut Dominus dederit, pertractare debenmus, Adhaesit pavement anima mea; vivifica me secundum verbum tuum. What is it, Adhaesit pavement anima mea? Nam cum adiungit et dicit, Vivifica me secundum verbum tuum; quare are vivified poscat, utique causam praemisit, saying, Adhaesit pavement anima mea. Ergo quia propterea se vivifica petit, quia pavement adhaesit anima eius; mirum si boni aliquid hinc vult intelligi. Ita quippe se habet tota ista sententia, tanquam diceret: Mortuus sum; quicken me. Quid est ergo pavimentum? Si tanquam unam quamdam ilomum magnam universum mundum velimus accipere, videmus velut eius cameram caelum: terra erit igitur pavimentum. Vult itaque terrenis

reindeer and say with the Apostle: Our deal is in heaven. Therefore, being attached to earthly things is the death of the soul; and as an effective remedy for this evil, life is asked for when it is said: vivify me. 2. But it must be examined whether these words are appropriate to him who had previously said others by which it seems he attached himself more to God than to the ground, since his relationship was not on earth, but in heaven. For how can it be understood that he stuck to earthly things who just before said: Your servant exercised himself in your justifications, because your testimonies are my meditation, and your justifications my plan? These are, certainly, his antecedent words, which follow: My soul stuck to the ground. Should we perhaps understand from this that no matter how much someone advances in the justifications of the Lord, he still does not lack the inclination of mortal flesh towards earthly things, in the midst of which human life is a continual temptation on earth; and that, if it continually advances, it revives every day of this death, giving life to Him with whose grace our inner man is renewed day by day? When the Apostle said: While we are dwelling in the body, we are on a pilgrimage towards the Lord, and he desired to die and be with Christ, his soul was glued to the ground. Therefore, soil itself can rightly be understood as the body itself, since it comes from the earth; in which, because it is still corruptible and hinders the soul, one groans and says to God: My soul is stuck to the ground; quicken me according to your word. However, there must come a time when we will be with our bodies, et cum Apostólo dicere, Conversatio nostra in caelis est (Phil 3,20). Proinde terrenis adhaerere mors animae est; cui malocontrary poscitur vita, cum dicitur, Vivifica me. 2. Sed vívendum est utrum congruant huic verba ista, qui superius talia dixerat, quibus magis Deo videatur adhaesisse quam pavimento, ut conversatio eius non in terrenis, sed in caelestibus haberetur. Quomodo enim potest intelligi terrenis adhaesisse qui dicit: Servus autem tuus exercebatur in tais iustificationibus; nam et testimonia tua meditatio mea est, et consilium meum iustificationes tuae?

Haec sunt enim verba eius antecedentia, quorum antecedentium ista sunt consequentia, Adhaesit pavement anima mea. An ex hoc intelligere debenmus, quantumlibet quisque proficiat in iustificationibus Domini, habere eum mortalis carnis affectum circa ista terrena, in quibus vita humano tentatio est super terram (Iob 7,1); et ab hac morte si perseveranter proficit, quotidie reviviscere, vivificante illo, cuius gratia homo noster interior renovatur de die in diem? (2 Cor 4:16). Nam et illud Apostolus cum dicebat, Quamdiu sumus in corpore, peregrinamur a Domino (ib. 5,6), et concupiscebat dissolvi, et esse cum Christo (Phil 1,23); adhaeserat pavement anima eius. Unde et corpus ipsum, quia ex terra est, non absurde intelligitur pavimentum; quod adhuc quia corruptibile est et aggravat animam (Wis 9,15), recte in illo congemiscitur et dicitur Deo, Adhaesit pavi-
Excellencies of the law of God

always with God. But then, since they will no longer be corruptible, if we consider it diligently, they will not aggravate the soul, nor will we be attached to them, but rather they will be attached to us, and we to God. Hence it is said in another psalm: It is good for me to adhere to God. Thus, then, the bodies live for us, being united to us; and let us live for God, because it is good for us to be united to Him. It seems to me that this union, of which it is said my soul stuck to the ground, does not mean the union of the body and the soul, although some understood it that way; but rather the carnal affection of the soul, whereby the flesh lusts against the spirit. If this is so, without a doubt the one who says: My soul stuck to the ground; quicken me according to your word, not asking to be delivered from the body of this death by the death of the body, which will take place on the last day of this life, which, because it is brief, cannot be very distant, but let the lust that lusts against the spirit decrease as much as possible and the lust that lusts against the flesh increase more and more, until the former is annihilated in us and the latter is perfected by the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us. 3 [v. 26 j. He did not say, and rightly so: Give life to me according to my method, but according to your word. And what is this but "according to your promise"? He wants to be a son of the promise, not of pride, so that through grace the promise may be firm to all descendants. For this is the word of promise: In Isaac your lineage will be blessed. Mento animas mea, vivifica me secundum verbum tuum. Neque enim non cum corporibus nostris semper cum Domino erimus (1 Thess 4, 12-16); sed tune quia non erunt corruptibilia nec animas aggravabunt, si diligenterconsiderus, non eis nos, sed ipsa nobis potius adhaerebunt, nos autem Deo. Unde altetius psalmi verba illa sunt, Mihi autem adhaerere Deo bonum est (Ps 72,28): ut vivant corpora ex nobis, adhaerendo nobis; nos autem vivamus ex Deo, quia nobis adhaerere Deo bonum est. Adhaesio quippe ista de qua dictum est, Adhaesit pavimento anima mea, non coniunctionem carnis et animae, quamvis et ipsam quídam intellexerint; sed carnalem magis animae affectum, quo caro concupiscit adversus spiritum (Gal 5:17), will mean mihi videtur.

Quod si recte accipitur, profecto qui dicit, Adhaesit pavement anima mea, vivifica me secundum verbum tuum, non id orat, ut de corpore mortis huius, morte ipsius coiporís intervenente solvatur; quod dies ultimus vitae huius, qui propIcr eius brevitatem non potest esse diuturnus, quandoque facturus est: sed ut concupiscentia qua concupiscitur adversus spiritum, magis magisqne minuatur, et concupiscentia qua concupiscitur adversus carnem, magis ac magis augeatur; doñee is consummatur in nobis, et illa consummetur per Spiritum sanctum qui datus est nobis. 3 [v.26]. Bene autem non ait, Vivifica me secundum meritum meum; sed ait, secundum verbum tuum: quod quid est aliud, nisi, secundum ptomissum tuum? Filius promissionis vult esse, non filius elationis; ut secundum gratiam firma sit promissio omni semini. Hoc est enim verbum promissionis: In Isaac vocabitur tibi semen: hoc est, Non qui filii car-
