That is, the children of the flesh are not children of God, but the children of the promise are those numbered by seed. So, then, he confesses what he was by himself in what follows: I showed you "my" ways, and you heard me. Many codices write "your" ways; but many others, and mainly the Greeks, "my" ways, that is, the bad ones. It seems to me that it says: "I confessed my sins, and you heard me," that is, and you forgave them. Show me your justifications. I confessed my ways; you destroyed them; show me yours. Teach me so that I act, not only learn what I should do. Just as it was said of the Lord that he did not know sin, and it was understood that he had not committed it, so it must be said that he who practices it truly knows justice. This is the prayer of one who profits. Because, if he had certainly not practiced it in any way, he would certainly not have said the above: Your servant practiced your justifications. Therefore he does not want to learn from the Lord the justifications in which he exercised himself, but rather he desires, taking advantage and growing, to move from these to others. 4 [v.27-28}. Then he adds and says: Insinuate to me the way of your righteousness; or as many codices write: Instruct me; which, translated from the Greek, is more accurately said: Make me understand. And I will exercise myself in your wonders. He calls wonders of God the greatest justifications that he longs to learn by taking advantage of. There are justifications from God so wonderful that those who do not experience them think that human weakness cannot reach them. Hence the latter, laboring and somewhat fatigued by this difficulty, adds: My soul fell asleep nis, hi filü Dei, sed filii promissionis deputantur in semine (Rom 9,7.8). Nam quid erat ipse per seipsum, in eo quod sequitur, confitetur: Vias meas enuntiavi, et exaudisti me. Nonnulli quidem codices habent, vias tuas; sed plures, et máxime graecis, vias meas, hoc est, malas. Nam hoc mihi videtur dicere, Peccata mea confessus sum, et exaudisti me, hoc est, ut dimitieres ea. Twelve me iustijicationes tuas. Confessus sum vias meas, delesti eas; twelve me yours. Sic twelve me, ut agam; non ut tantummodo sciam quid agere debenam. Sicut enim dictum est de Domino quod non noverat peccatum (2 Cor 5:21), et intelligitur, non fecerat; sic et iustitiam ille veré dicedus est nosse, qui facit. Proficientis haec oratio est.

Nam utique si omnino non faceret, proferto illa superiora non diceret: Servus autem tuus exercebatur in tuis iustificationibus. Non ergo in quibus exercebatur, has vult a Domino discerne; sed ab istis ad alias uttering, velut crescendo, desiderat pervenire. 4 [v.27.28]. Denique adiungit et dicit, Viam iustificationum tuarum hints mihi; vel, sicut nonnulli codices habent, instrue me: quod expressius de graeco dicitur, fac me intelligere. Et exercebor in mirabilibus tuis. Ipsas iustificationes amplores, quas uttering cupit apprehendere, mirabilia Dei vocat. Sunt ergo quaedam Dei iustificationes ita mirabiles, ut humano infirmitas ab eis qui experti non sunt, non ad eas posse pervenire credatur. Unde laborans iste, et earum difficultate quodam moda fatiguetus, adiungit: Dormitavit anima mea prae taedio; with.

for boredom; strengthen me with your words. What does it mean he fell asleep? He grew warm with the hope, for which he believed he would achieve them. But strengthen me—he says—with your words so that I do not lose, by falling asleep, those that I perceive I have acquired. Strengthen me with your words in those that I already have and practice so that I can, taking advantage, move from these to others. 5 [v.29] And what is it that hinders progress in the path of God's justifications, so that man can achieve other wonders? What can it be but what he asks in the next verse to be removed from him, saying: Remove the way of iniquity from me? And since the law of facts was introduced, so that crime abounded, he continues and says: By your law have mercy on me. By what law? By the law of faith. Listen to the Apostle: Where then is boasting? Excluded has been. By what law? Because of the works? Not by truth, but by faith. The law of faith is that by which we ask and believe that it must be given to us by grace that we do what we cannot perform for ourselves; Let it not happen that, not knowing the justice of God, wanting to establish our own, we do not submit to the justice of God. In this way, in the law of facts is found the justice of God, who commands; and in the law of faith, the mercy of God, which helps. 6 [v.30-32]. After having said: And by your law have pity on me, he determines or points out in a certain way, if we may say so, the benefits that he has already achieved, in order to seek others that he has not yet achieved, for he says: I have chosen the path of truth. sign me in verbis tuis. Quid est, dormitavit, nisi ab spe friguit qua eas se apprehensuram esse crediderat? Sed, confirm me, inquit, in verbis tuis, ne ab eis quoque ad quae pervenisse me iam sentio, decidam dozing: confirm itaque me in eis verbis tuis quae iam teneo, quae iam fació, ut ex eis ad alia possim uttering pertendere. 5 [v.29]. Et quid impedit in via iustificationum Dei sic ambulare, ut homo facile possit ad illa etiam mirabilia pervenire? Quid putamus, nisi quod a se amoveri in consequentibus rogat say: Viam iniquitatis amove a me? Et quia lex factorum subintravit, ut abundaret delictum (Rom 5:20); sequitur, et dicit, Et lege tua miserere mei. Qua lege, nisi lege fidei? Audi Apostolum: Ubi est ergo gloriatio tua? Exclusive est. Per quam legem? factorum? Non; sed per legem fidei (ib. 3,27).

Haec est lex fidei, qua credimus et oramus per gratiam nobis donari, ut faciamus quod per nosmetipsos implere non possumus; ne ignorantes Dei iustitiam, et nostram volentes constituere, iustitiae Dei non simus subiecti (ib. 10,3). In lege itaque factorum est Dei iubentis iustitia; in lege autem fidei, subvenientis misericordia. 6 [v.30.32]. Cum autem dixisset, Et lege tua miserere mei; de beneficiis eius quae iam consecutus est, quodammodo, si dici potest, praescribit, ut impetret caetera quae nondum est consecutus. Ait enim: Viam veritatis chose: iudicia tua non sum oblitus. Adhaesi testimoniis tuis;

No? I have not forgotten your judgments. I joined your testimonies, Lord; Don't confuse me. That is to say, I chose the path of truth to run on; I did not forget your judgments to run; I joined your testimonies so that I can continue where I run and reach where I intend, because this does not depend on the one who wants or the one who runs but on God, who has compassion. Then he continues, saying: I ran the path of your commandments as you enlarged my heart. I wouldn't have run if you hadn't dilated my heart. Without a doubt, in this verse he explains the reason for having said: I chose the path of truth; I have not forgotten your judgments; I joined your testimonies. This path is that of God's commandments. But as he rather exposes to the Lord his benefits than his own merits, as if he were asked: "How did you run the path? Choosing, not forgetting the judgments of God, and uniting yourself to his testimonies? Could you perhaps do these things for yourself? Answer: "No." Your help, but I performed it when you enlarged my heart. The enlargement of the heart is the delight of justice; and this is a gift that God grants us so that we may not shrink in his precepts for fear of punishment, but may be enlarged with the love and pleasure of justice. where God walks! In this breadth charity is spread in our hearts by the Holy Spirit, which has been given to us. Et in illo magis quam sub sole vivunt qui non inaniter audiunt quod Apostolus said: «Quae sursum sunt quaerite, ubi Christus est in dextera Dei sedens; quae sursum sunt sapite, non quae super terram. Mortui enim estis, et vita vestra abscondita est eum Christo in Deo” (Col 3:1-3). Ac per hoc si vita nostra ibi est ubi veritas, non est vita nostra sub sole ubi vanitas.

Sed hoc tam magnum bonum magis habemus in spe, non tenemus in re: et secundum spem nostram beatus Apostolus ista locutus est; quia et illud eum dixisset, Vanitati creatura subiecta est, adiecit atque ait, Non sponte, sed propter eum qui subiecit in spe. Ergo in spe, qua speramus nos adhaesuros contemplandae veritati, subiecti sumus interim vanitati. Creatura quippe ist spiritualis, animalis, corporalisque omnis in homine est; imo homo est. Sponte peccavit, et inimica facta est veritati: sed ut merit puniretur, non sponte subiecta est vanitati. Denique post pauca. Non solum autem, inquit, sed et nos ipsi primitias spiritus habentes, id est, qui nondum quidem ex toto quod sumus, sed

Seeing is not hope, since what one sees, what do you expect? If we wait for what we do not see, we wait patiently. Therefore, while we are here, according to the flesh, we wait for its adoption through the patience of hope; Therefore, we are also subject to vanity regarding being under the sun. So, while we live here in this way, how can we not see the vanity, to which we are subject in hope? Then what does this man express when he says: Avert my eyes so that they do not see vanity? Does he ask that what he endures in hope not be fulfilled in this life, but that it be of such a kind or condition, that it may be fulfilled in him at some time, as to spirit, soul, and body, that he may not see vanity, being delivered from the bondage of corruption, and brought (as to spirit, soul, and body) into the freedom of the glory of the children of God? 2. These words can certainly be understood in this way without departing from the norm of faith. But they have another meaning, which I like more. The Lord says in the Gospel: If your eye is pure, your whole body will be resplendent; But if your eye is evil, your whole body will be dark. So that, if the light that is in you is darkness, the darkness itself, how great it will not be! Therefore, it is extremely important that, when doing something good, we see with what intention we do it, since the action is not weighed by the work, but by the purpose for which it is done. Therefore, we must not only think if the work is good, but mainly if it is ex ea parte qua pecoribus meliores sumus, Deo, non vanitati subditi sumus, hoc est, per primmitias spiritus: «et ipsi in nobismetipsis ingemiscimus, adoptionem exspectantes redemptionem corporis nostri. Spe enim salvi facti sumus. Spes autem quae videtur, non est spes: quod enim videt quis, quid sperat? Si autem quod non videmus speramus, per patientiam exspectamus.» Quamdiu itaque hic secundum carnem sumus, cuius adoptionem et redemptionem per patientiam spei adhuc exspectamus; tamdiu secundum id per quod sub sole sumus, vanitati subiecti sumus. Quandiu igitur ita sumus, unde possumus non videre vanitatem, cui etiam subiecti sumus in spe? Quid est ergo quod iste dicit, Averte oculos meos, ne videant vanitatem?

An hoc petit, ut non quidem in hac vita quod in spe gerimus impleatur, sed ut in ea sorte sit, quae in illo quandoque possit impleri, cum liberabitur a servitute corruptionis, et spiritu et anima et corpore, in libertatem gloriae filiorum Dei (Rom 8, 20-25), ubi iam non videat vanitatem? 2. Possunt quidem verba ist sic intelligi, non praeter regulam fidei; sed est hic alius sensus quem mihi fateor plus pleasureré. Dominus in Gospel says: «Si fuerit oculus tuus simplex, totum corpus tuum lucidum erit. Si autem oculus tuus fuerit nequam, totum corpus tuum tenebrosum erit. "Si ergo lumen quod in te est tenebrae sunt, ipsae tenebrae quantae erunt?" Proinde magni interest, cum aliquid boni facimus, cuius rei contemplatione faciamus. Officium quippe nostrum, non officio, sed fine pensandum est; ut scilicet non tantum si bonum est quod faci-

well the purpose for which we execute it. These eyes with which we contemplate why we do what we do, are the ones that ask us to turn away so that they do not see vanity and act carried away by it when doing good. The desire for human praise occupies the first place in this vanity; Therefore, many great things were done by those who were called great in the world, who, seeking glory before men, not before God, greatly praised in the cities of the Gentiles and living for it as just, prudent, strong and temperate, these vain people received their reward in vain. The Lord, wanting to divert the eyes of his people from this vanity, says: Take heed that you do not do your good works before men, so that they may see you, for in this way you will have no reward from your Father, who is in heaven. Next, dealing with some divisions of good work and precepting about alms, fasting and prayer, he orders at all times that none of these works be done for human glory, and continually says that those who work for it have already received their reward; that is, not the eternal, which for the saints is kept together with the Father, but the temporal, which those who act seek, looking at the vanity of their actions; Not because human praise is bad, for what thing should be desired more earnestly by men than for them to please the things they should imitate, but because to do well solely to be praised by men is to pay attention only to the vanity of their works? Therefore, no matter how great the praise that a just man receives from his works, he must not put the end of his good actions in them, but refer them to the glory of God, by whom mus, sed praecipue si bonum est propter quod facimus, cogitemus. Hos oculos quibus contemplamur quare faciamus quod facimus, averti poscit ne videant vanitatem; id est, ne hanc attendat, propter quam faciat, cum boni aliquid facit. In qua vanitate praecipuum locum obtinet amor laudis humanoe, propter quam plana magna fecerunt qui magni in hoc saeculo nominati sunt, multumque laudati in civitatibus gentium, quaerentes non apud Deum, sed apud homines gloriam, et propter hanc velut prudenter, fortiter, temperanter, íusteque vivoste; ad quam pervenientes perceperunt mercedem suam, vani vanam.

Ab bac vanitate volens Dominus avertere oculos suorum: «Attendite», inquit «ne iustitiam vestram faciatis coram hominibus, ut videamini ab eis; alioquin mercedem non habebitis apud Patrem vestrum, qui in caelis est. Deinde cum ipsius iustitiae quasdam parts exsequeretur, praecipiens de eleemosynis, de oratione, de ieiunio, ubique id admonuit, ne aliquid eorum propter gloriam hominum fiat, et ubique dicit eos qui ptopterea faciunt, percepisse mercedem suam (Mt 6,1-23), id est non aeternam quae sanctis reposita est apud Patrem, sed temporalem quam quaerunt qui contemplamur in suis operibus vanitatem: non quia ipsa laus humano culpanda est (nam quid tam optandum est hominibus, quam ut eis placeant quae debenant imitari?), sed propter ipsam laudem

Good people work well, since they do not work for themselves, but for Him. Finally, in the same Sermon on the Mount the Lord had already said: Let your light shine before men so that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father, who is in heaven. Therefore, if we want our eyes to be turned away from vanity, we must look, when we do any good work, to that in which it ended, that is, to the glory of God. Let not the praises of men be the end of works, but let us direct these praises and order all things to the praise of God, through whom, without the error of the one who praises, everything that is praised in us is given to us. If it is vain to do good for the praise of men, how much more vain will it be to do good to obtain money, or increase it, or retain it; or for any other temporary comfort that comes to us from outside, since all things are vanity! And what other wealth is that of the man who works with all his effort under the sun? In short, we should not do good works for this temporary health, but rather for the eternal one that we hope for, in which we will enjoy the immutable good that will come to us from God. What do I say? What must be God? If the saints of God had carried out their good works for this temporary health, the martyrs of Christ would never have carried out the good work of confession with the loss of this temporary health. But, not paying attention to vanity, because the health of men is vain, they received help in tribulation; nor did they covet the day (the life) of the bene operari, hoc est vanitatem in suis operibus intueri. Quandoquidem et ipsa ab hominibus laus hominí iusto quantacumque provenerit, non ibi esse debent eius finis boni, sed etiam ipsa referenda est ad laudem Dei, propter quem bona faciunt veré boni; quoniam non a seipsis, sed ab illo fiunt boni. Denique in eodem sermone Dominus iam dixerat eis: Luceat lumen vestrum coram hominibus, ut videant vestra opera hona, et glorificent Patrem vestrum, qui in caelis est (ib. 5,16). Ubi finem posit, hoc est in gloria Dei, hoc debenmus quando aliquid boni facimus intueri, si avertuntur a vanitate oculi nostri. Non ergo sit finis boni operis in laudibus hominum, sed ipsas laudes hominum corrigamus, et ad Dei laudes omnia referamus, a quo nobis datur quidquid in nobis sine laudantis errore laudatur.

Porro si vanum est propter hominum laudes bona faceré, quanto vanius propter adipiscendam pecuniam, vel augendam, sive retinendam, et si quid huiusmodi est commodi temporalis, quod nobis accessit extrinsecus? Quia omnia vanitas: quae abundantia hominis in omni labore suo, quo ipse laborat sub sole? Propter ipsam i denique temporalem salutem non debenmus faceré bona opera nostra, 1 sed potius propter illam quam speramus aeternam, ubi bono immutabili perfruamur, quod nobis erit ex Deo, imo quod nobis est ipse Deus. Si enim sancti Dei propter hanc temporalem salutem bona opera facerent, nunquam martyres Christi bonum opus confessíonís in eiusdem salutis amissione perficerent. Sed acceperunt auxilium de tribulatione, non intuentes vanitatem, quia vana salus hominis (Ps 59,13); et diem

men, because man became like vanity and his days pass like a shadow. 3 [v.38}. When we ask God to grant us what seems to be in our power, that is, to turn our eyes away from seeing vanity, what else is done but appreciating his grace? Some, being men who flattered themselves too much and boasted of the powers of their own will, did not take their eyes off that vanity, because they thought that they would become just and good by themselves, and so they loved the glory of men more than that of God. But this is vanity and presumption of spirit. Therefore, after having said: Turn my eyes away from seeing vanity; quicken me in your way, and this way is truth, not vanity, he added next: Establish your word in your servant through your fear. And what else is it but giving me to do what you say? The word of God is not established in those who, acting contrary to it, stir it up in themselves, but in those in whom it remains immobile. So God established his word through his fear in those to whom he gives the spirit of his fear; but not of that fear of which the Apostle says: You did not receive the spirit of bondage a second time in fear, for this fear is cast out by perfect charity, but of that fear which the prophet calls the spirit of the fear of God; of truly chaste fear, which remains forever and ever; of the fear by which one fears offending the loved one. For in a way the adulterous woman fears her hominum non concupierunt (Ier 17,16), quia homo vanitati similatus est, dies eius sicut umbra praetereunt (Ps 143,4). 3 [v.38]. Cum autem Deus rogatur, ut ea quae videntur esse in nostra potestate, id est, oculorum aversio a videnda vanitate ab illo nobis concedatur, quid nisi eius gratia commendatur? Nonnulli enim ab ea vanitate non averterunt oculos suos, quia putaverunt a seipsis se fieri iustos et bonds, et dilexerunt gloriam hominum magis quam Dei (lo 12,43); quia et ipsi homines sunt, qui sibi nimium placuerunt, et de sui arbitrii viribus praesumpserunt: sed etiam haec vanitas et praesumptio spiritus est (Eccl 6,9): Cum ergo dixisset, Averie oculos meos, ne videant vanitatem; in via tua vivifica me; quae via non vanitas, sed veritas est: deinde subiunxit, Statué servo tuo eloquium tuum in timorem tuum. Quod quid est aliud quam, Da mihi ut faciam quod eloqueris?

Ñeque enim statutum est eloquium Dei his qui in se movent illud contra fazando; eis autem statutum est in quibus immobile est. Statuit itaque Deus eloquium suum in timorem suum eis quibus dat spiritum timoris sui: timoris autem non illius de quo dicit Apostolus. Non enim accepistis spiritum servitutis iterum in timore (Rom 8:15); hunc enim consummata charitas foras mittit timorem (1 lo 4,18): sed illius timoris quem dicit propheta spiritum timoris Dei (Is 11,3); timoris utique casti, permanentis in saeculum saeculi (Ps 18:10), timoris quo timetur offendi

husband, and from another the caste; The adulteress fears that she will show up at home, the caste that she will abandon her. 4 [v.39J. Amputate my reproach that I suspected, because your judgments are pleasant. Who is there that has mere suspicions of his disgrace, and does not rather each one know his own before that of any other stranger? Man may rather be suspicious of others, but not of his own, because what is suspected is unknown. Where conscience speaks there is no conjecture of its own shame, but science. What, then, does my suspected disgrace mean? Without a doubt, the meaning of this phrase must be deduced from the previous meaning, because as long as man does not avert his eyes so as not to see vanity, he suspects others of what he performs within himself, and believes that others serve and act for the same reason for which he serves God or does good. Men can see what we do, but the purpose of our actions is hidden from them; This gives rise to suspicion, and thus man dares to judge the hidden things of men, and many times falsely; and if some do it truthfully, yet it is done without sufficient reason. For this reason, the Lord, when speaking of the end for which we must do good to remove our eyes from the contemplation of vanity, warned us that we should not do good works for the praise of men, saying to us: Take heed that you do not do your good works before men, to be seen by them. He also charged us not to do it for money, telling us: Do not store up treasures on earth; and likewise: qui amatur. Aliter quippe timet adultera virum suum, aliter casta: adultera, ne veniat; caste, ne deserat. 4 [v.39]. Amputa, inquit, opprobrium meum quod suspicatus sum, quia indicia tua suavia. Quis est qui suum opprobrium suspicatur, et non magis novit suum quisque opprobrium, quam cuiuslibet alienum? Suspicari enim potius alienum potest homo, non suum; quoniam quod suspicatur, ignorat: in suo autem opprobrio non est cuiusque suspicio, sed scientia, ubi loquitur conscientia. Quid est ergo quod ait, Opprobrium meum quod suspicatus sum? Nimirum de superiore sensu etiam iste ducendus est: quoniam quamdiu non averti homo oculos suos ne videant vanitatem, quod in seipso agitur, hoc de alus suspicatur; ut propter quod ipse colit Deum, vel propter quod bona opera facit, propter hoc credat et alterum faceré.

Possunt quippe homines videre quod agimus; cuius autem rei contemplatione agamus occultum est: et ideo datur suspicionibus locus, ut audeat homo iudicare de occultis hominum, et false plerumque, et, si vera, tamen incognita fearé suspicari. Propterea Dominus cum de ipso fine loqueretur propter quem iustitiam faceré deben, ut oculos nostros a contemplatione averteret vanitatis, monuit ne propter laudes hominum bona opera faciamus, dicen: Attendite ne faciatis iustitiam vestram coram hominibus, ut videamini ab eis. You cannot serve God and riches. He advised us not to do them for the clothing and food we need, saying: Do not worry about your life, thinking about what you will eat; nor for your body, wondering what you should wear. After having advised us on all these things, as we can suspect that those whom we see living well, and of whom we do not see the motive of their actions, acted for some of them, he added next: Do not judge so that you will not be judged. Hence, when he said here: Take away my reproach which I suspected, he added: because your judgments are pleasing, that is, they are true. The lover of truth calls what is true pleasant. But the judgments of men about the hidden things of other men, because they are rash, are not pleasant. For this reason he called what he had suspected of others his disgrace. The Apostle also says that those who compare themselves with themselves do not understand. And man is very inclined to suspect another of what he experiences in himself. This reproach of his, having suspected in others what he perceived in himself, asked that it be taken away from him so as not to be like the devil, who suspected the interior of the holy Job that he did not serve God freely, for which reason he asked to tempt him to discover in him the crime that he blamed on him. 5 [v.40]. But since emulation or greed is what suspects with pleasure the opprobrium of others, not being able to censure the good work, because what is visible defends or justifies itself, it reproaches the purpose for which it is done, because what is hidden, ne propter pecuniam, you say: nolite vobis thesaurizare in terra; et, Non potestis Deo serve et mammonae. Monuit, ne propter ipsum necessarium victum atque vestitum, they say: Ne solliciti sitis animae vestrae quid manducetis, ñeque corpori vestro quid induamini (Mt 6,1.19. 24.25). Et cum haec omnia monuisset, quia possumus suspicari eos quos iuste vivere videmus, et quo fine faciant non videmus, propter aliquid huiusmodi benefacere; continuous subiecit: Nolite iudicare, ne iudicemini (ib. 7,1). Unde et hic cum dixisset, Amputa opprobrium meum quod suspicatus sum; addidit, quia iudicia tua suavia, id est, iudicia tua vera. Veritatis enim amator suave clamat esse quod verum est. Hominum autem iudicia de occultis hominum, non suavia, quia reckless.

Et ideo suum dixit opprobrium quod de alus est suspicatus; quia et hoc quod Apostolus ait, Comparantes semetipsos sibimetipsis (2 Cor 10:12), non intelligunt: hoc enim proclivius homo suspicatur in alio, quod sentit in seipso. Hoc itaque opprobrium suum petebat auferri, quod in se senserat, et in alus fuet suspicatus; ut non esset diabolo similis, qui de occultis sancti Iob suspicatus est quod non gratis Deum coleret, quem poposcit tentandum, ut crime quod obiieeret inveniret (Iob 1,9-11). 5 [v.40]. Sed cum libenter alterius opprobrium nonnisi aemulatio suspicetur, dum bonum opus reprehendí non potest, quia se asserit quod

to does not manifest itself; and thus, not seeing what is hidden and envying what is visible, he suspects evil as he pleases when he pleases. Against this perversity, by which man willingly suspects an evil that he did not see, charity must be exercised, which is not envious, and which the Lord especially recommends, saying: I give you a new commandment: that you love one another; By this everyone will know that you are my disciples: that you love one another. And, speaking of the love of God and neighbor, he says: The entire law and projects are based on these two precepts. Hence this man also says against the disgrace of his suspicion, which he longs to be cut off: See that I covet your commandments; quicken me with your justice. I wanted to love you with all my heart, with all my soul and with all my mind, and my neighbor as myself; quicken me with your righteousness, not with mine; that is, fill me with that charity that I desired. Help me to do what you command and give me what you command. Quicken me with your justice. Dying was in me, but I cannot find living except in you. Your righteousness is Christ, who was made by God Wisdom for us, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption; so that, as it is written, "he who glories may glory in the Lord." In Him I find the commandments that I longed for, so that in your righteousness, that is, in Him, you may give me life. He is the Word of God, and the Word who became flesh to also be my neighbor. apertum est; et quo fine fiat they reprehended-, quia non se exserit quod occultum est; atque ita male suspicari eum libet cui líbet, non vídendo quod latet, et invidendo quod eminet: proferto contra hoc malura, quo quisque libenter de nomine malum quod non perspicit suspicatur, chantas habenda est, quae non aemulatur (1 Cor 13,4); quam Dominus praecipue commendat, they say, Mandatum novum do vobis, ut vos invicem diligatis; et, In hoc scient otnnes quia discipuli mei estis, si dilectionem habueritis in invicem (lo 13,34.35): et de dilectíone Dei et proxími loquens, In bis, inquit, duobus mandatis tota Lex pendet et Prophetae (Mt 22,40). Unde et iste contra suae suspícionis opprobrium quod desiderat amputan, Ecce, inquit, concupivi manda tua; in tua iustitia vivifica me. Ecce concupivi ex todo corde, ex tota anima, ex tota mente diligere te, et proximum sicut me: non in mea, sed in tua iustitia vivifica me, hoc est, ista charitate quam concupivi, imple me. Adiuva ut faciam quon commendas, dona ipse quod mandas.

In tua iustitia vivifica me: quia in me unde morerer habui; unde autem vivam non invenio nisi in te. Iustitia tua Christus est, «qui factus est nobis sapientia a Deo, et iustitia, et sanctificatio, et redemptio; ut, quemadmodum scriptum est, Qui gloriatur, in Domino glorietur» (1 Cor 1,30.31). Et in illo invenio mandata tua quae concupivi, ut in tua iustitia, hoc est in illo, vivifices me. Ipse est enim Verbum Deus; et Verbum caro factum est, ut esset et proximus meus (lo 1,14).

SERMON 13 1 [v.41]. Today's sermon must join the one we had yesterday on the longest psalm of all the others. The verse we are going to talk about begins like this: And your mercy be upon me, O Lord! This little verse seems to be united with the antecedent, since it did not say; "Come upon me," but: And come upon me. The previous one is: See that I covet your commandments; quicken me with your justice; and then he continues: And come upon me, O Lord! your mercy. Then what does he ask but to fulfill the commandments he longed for through the mercy of Him who commanded? When he adds: And let your mercy come upon me, Lord; your health, according to your words, that is, according to your promise, declares in a certain way what he had said. Quicken me with your justice. Hence the Apostle wants us to understand that we are children of the promise, so that we do not believe that what we are is ours, but that we attribute everything to the grace of God, since Christ was made wisdom by God for us, and righteousness and sanctification, and redemption, so that, as it is written, "he who glories may glory in the Lord." When he says quicken me with your righteousness, he certainly desires to be quickened by Christ, and this is mercy who asks to come upon him. Christ himself is the salvation of God. With this word he declared what mercy he spoke of when he said: And let your mercy come upon me. If we wish to know what mercy this is, let us hear the SESMO.

1 [v.41]. Pristine sermoni, quem de psalmo qui est omnium prolixissimus, nuper habuimus, de verbis eius quae sequuntur iste iungendus est. Haec verba sunt: Et veniat super me mercy tua, Domine. Quae sententia superiori videtur annexa: non enim ait, Veniat super me; sed ait, Et veniat. Est autem illa superior, Ecce concupivi mandata tua; in tua iustitia vivifica me; deinde sequitur, Et veniat super me mercy tua, Domine. Quid hic ergo poscit, nisi ut mandata quae concupivit, per eius misericordiam faciat, qui mandavit? Exponit enim quodammodo quid dixerit, In tua iustitia vivifica me; cum subiungit, Et veniat super me mercy tua, Domine, salutare tuum secundum eloquium tuum: hoc est secundum promissionem tuam. Unde nos vult Apostolus filios promissionis intelligi (Rom 9,8); ne arbitremur nostrum esse quod sumus, sed totum Dei gratiae retribuamus. Factus est enim nobis Christus sapientia a Deo, et iustitia, et sanctificatio, et redemptio; ut, quemadmodum scriptum est, Qui gloriatur, in Domino glorietur (1 Cor 1,30 et 31). Quod ergo ait, In tua iustitia vivifica me; in Christo utique vivifican cupit, et ipsa est mercy quam super se poscit comere. Ipse Christus est et salutare Dei; quo verb exposuit quam misericordiam diceret ubi ait, Et veniat super me mercy tua, Domine. Si ergo quaerimus quae sit ista misericordia, audiamus quod sequitur:

Salutare tuum secundum eloquium tuum. Ab eo quippe hoc promissum est, qui vocat ea quae non sunt, tamquam sint (Rom 4:17). Nondum enim werent quibus promitteretur, ne quisquam de meritis gloriaretur. This comforted me in my depression, because your word gave me life. Does forgetfulness occur in God, as in men? Why is it called remember} Although in other places in the Holy Scripture the same word is used, for example: Why have you forgotten me?, and even God himself says through the prophet: I will forget all his iniquities, and the word forget is frequently read in many other passages, it must be taken into account that this is not understood of God in the same way that it takes place in men. Because in the same way that it is said of God that he repents when, without having been expected by men, he changes things without changing his counsel, because the counsel of God remains eternally, in the same way it is said that he forgets when it seems that he delays the help or the promise or does not give what they deserve to sinners, or any other similar thing, then believing that he forgot what was expected or feared and did not happen. All these things are said according to a usual locution by which human affection acts or is moved, although God does them by an invariable disposition, without memory failing, nor intelligence being obscured, nor will being changed. Quamvis in alus sanctae Scripturae locis ipsum verbum omnino ponatur, ut est, Quare mei oblitus es (Ps 41,10); et Oblivisceris inopiam nostram (Ps 43,24); et ipse Deus per Prophetam, Omnes, inquit, iniquitatis eius obliviscar (Ez 18:22): et alibi atque alibi saepius hoc legitur. Dicuntur ista locutione morali, qua humanus movetur affectus; quamvis haec Deus faciat certa dispositione, non defective memoria, nec obscurata intelligentia, nec volúntate mutata. I would have forgotten. Remember, he says, your word (given) to your servant, that is, fulfill the promise to your servant. With which you gave me hope, that is, with whose word you gave me hope, because you promised me. 2 [v.50]. This consoled me in my despondency. Namely, this hope is what was given to the humble, the Scripture saying: God resists the proud and gives grace to the humble. Hence the Lord himself says through his own mouth: He who exalts himself will be humbled and he who humbles himself will be exalted. Here we understand, with reason, that it deals not with that humility with which each one humiliates himself by confessing his sins and not attributing justice to himself, but with that with which he is humiliated with some tribulation or despondency that his pride deserves; or with which your patience is exercised or tested; so shortly after this psalm says: Before being humiliated I commit a crime; and also the book of Wisdom: Support yourself in pain and be patient in humiliation, because gold and silver are purified by fire, and acceptable men, in the furnace of tribulation. By saying acceptable, he gave hope that it would comfort in humility. Also our Lord Jesus Christ, when predicting to the disciples that they would be humiliated by their persecutors, did not leave them without hope, but gave it to them for their comfort, saying to them: With your patience you will win your souls. And about the body, which could be killed by his enemies, and which could be almost completely destroyed, he says: Not a hair of your heads will perish. This hope was given to the Body of Christ, which is the Church, so that id exciderit, admonetur. Memento, inquit, verbi tui servo tuo: hoc est, imple promissum servo tuo. In quo spem dedisti mihi: hoc est, in quo verbo, quoniam promisisti, me sperare fecisti. 2 [v.50]. Haec console me est in humilitate mea. Haec scilicet spes quae data est humüibus, dicente Scriptura, Deus superbis resistit, humilibus autem dat gratiam (Iac 4,6; et 1 Petr 5,5). Unde ore proprio etiam ipse Dominus ait: Quoniam qui se exaltat, humiliabitur; et qui se humiliat, exaltabitur (Luke 14:11; et 18:14). Bene hic intelligimus etiam illam humilitatem, non qua se quisque humiliat confitendo peccata, nec sibi arrogando iustitiam; sed qua quisque humiliatur aliqua tribulatione vel deiectione, quam meruit eius superbia, aut exercetur probaturque patientia: unde paulo post dicit hic psalmus, Priusquam humiliarer, ego deliqui.

Et illud in libro Sapientiae: In dolore sustine, et in humilitate tua patientiam habe; quoniam in igne probatur aurum et argentum, homines vero acceptabiles in camino humiliationis (Eccl 2,4.5). Quod ait acceptabiles, ibi spem dedit quae consolaretur in humilitate. Et Dominus Iesus hac humilitatem cum discipulis praediceret a persecutoribus esse venturam, non eos sine spe reliquit; sed hanc etiam, qua consolarentur, dedit dices, In vestra patientia possidebitis animas vestras: de ipso quoque corpore quod ab inimicis posset occidi, et quasi penitus interire, Capillus, inquit, capitis vestri non peribit (Luke 21,19.18). There is another hope that greatly consoles the humility of tribulation, which was given to the saints by the word of God, which promises the help of grace so that no one will faint. The Apostle also says of it: God is faithful, and does not allow you to be tempted beyond your strength, but with the temptation he provides a way out so that you can endure it. The Savior also gave this hope through his mouth when he said: Satan asked tonight to sift you like wheat, but I prayed for you, O Peter, so that your faith would not fail. Likewise, he also gave this hope in the prayer that he taught when he admonished us to say. Do not let us fall into temptation, because in a way he promised that he would give his people who were in danger what they asked for when they prayed. Therefore, it must be understood that this psalm speaks rather of this hope when it says: This comforted me in my depression, because your word gave me life. This was recorded more precisely by those who translated not word, but saying, since the Greek writes loguion, which means saying, and not logos, which is translated by word. 3 [v.51j. Or is it that perhaps by saying: This comforted me in my humility, does he point out the humility that comes from that sin that was unfortunately committed in the happiness of paradise, for which man was dejected and condemned to death? In this humility indeed, by which man was made like vanity and his days passed away as a shadow, all are children of wrath, unless those predestined for the eternal life before the foundation of the world are reconciled to God through the Mediator. The ancient fathers also had their hope in this Mediator, knowing through a prophetic spirit that he would come in the flesh. Therefore the word that was inspired to them about this Mediator can be understood very well by the one recorded here, if we take as their voice what was said about it: Remember your word (given) to your servant, with which you gave me hope. This consoled me in my humility. That is, in my mortality, because your word gave me life so that I would have hope of life in my condemnation to death. The proud acted wickedly to the extreme, since the humiliation of mortality did not subdue them.

He continues and says: I remembered your name in the night, O Lord, and I kept your law. Night is the despondency, in which the penalty of mortality is found, for there is night in the proud who act iniquitously to the extreme; There is night in the sorrow caused by sinners who abandoned the law of God; In short, there is night in the place of this pilgrimage until the Lord comes and illuminates the hidden darkness and reveals the thoughts of the heart, God then giving each one the praise he deserves. On this night man must remember the name of God, so that whoever glories may glory in the Lord; Therefore it was also written: Not to us, Lord, not to us, but give glory to your name. In this way, he who does not act for his glory, but for that of God, since he does not act for his righteousness, but for that of God, that is, God giving it to him, keeps the law, as this one says: I remembered in the night, Lord, and I kept your law. If, trusting in his own power, he had not remembered the name of God, he would not have kept it, since our help is found in the name of the Lord. 8 [v.56]. For this reason he added: This was done for me, because I inquired of your righteousness. Justices certainly yours, with which you justify the wicked, not mine, which never make me pious, but proud. These justices by which those who cannot be righteous by themselves are justified freely by the grace of God were called by others, or rather, justifications, because, in truth, in the Greek text it is not written dicaiosinas, that is, justices, but dicaiomata, justifications. But what does it mean when it says: This happened to me; or: Was this made for you? What does this mean? Perhaps the law, since, having said: And I kept the law, he added to these words: This was made for me, as if he said: "This law was made for me." But let us not stop explaining how the law was given to him, since the Greek phrase from which this Latin was transferred sufficiently indicates that it is not about the law when it is said: This was made for me, because the Greek word law (nomos) is of the masculine gender, and there it was written with the feminine article: This was made for me. It is asked, therefore, in the first place: What thing was made?; and then, whatever it was: In what way was it? This, he says, was made for me; but not this law, because the Greek text, as I said, rejects this sense. Perhaps it will be tonight, since the entire preceding sentence reads like this: I remembered your name in the night, O Lord, and I kept your law, and it continues: this was made for me. Therefore, not being the law, it was undoubtedly the night that was made for him. But how was the night made for me, because I sought your justifications, since in seeking the justifications of God, light becomes rather than night? If night is correctly understood as what is recorded: it was made for me, it must be understood as if it were said: "It was made for me", that is, it came to be useful to me. Illusion or despondency of mortality is not absurdly understood to be like the night, in which the affections of mortals are sometimes hidden, so that innumerable and serious temptations originate from such darkness, to the point that in the same night beasts of the forest also pass through, and roaring cubs of lions, who ask the Lord for food for themselves, for which reason the Lord said of that roaring lion that he seeks someone who can devour what he previously I commemorated: Satan asked to sift you like wheat this night; That is to say, that on this night, in which the beasts of the jungle have free passage, that roaring lion asked God for you to be his food; then certainly this same dejection in the place of this pilgrimage, which is rightly considered night, benefits those who exercise themselves healthily in it to learn not to become arrogant, for whose sin man was thrown into this night, since the beginning of pride in man is apostasy from God. for me, in such a way that neither the night nor the law is understood, but that the pronoun this is taken in the sense in which it is taken in another psalm, which reads: One thing I asked of the Lord, "this" I will seek. Here it does not indicate what or what this is, one of which it is said that I will look for, recording in the feminine gender what was indicated by the neuter. Without a doubt, it was said unexpectedly: One thing I asked for, this I will seek, because it is not clear what that thing is; and, according to the common way of speaking, he had to say, in the neuter gender in Latin, unum; "One thing I asked of the Lord: Hoc, this, and not able, this one, I will seek: to dwell in the house of the Lord." In Latin, in the ending of some neuters it is not usually required that what is implied be neuter; for example, unum bonum, a good; unum donum, a gift, or something similar, but whatever it is, even if it expresses masculine or feminine gender in itself or refers to words that do not carry gender with them, all of this is understood, according to the common way of speaking, as referred to under the neuter gender. Thus, in this place it could be said: "Haec", this was made for me, as if saying: "Hoc, this, was made for me." If we inquire what this is, what he said above comes to light: I remembered your name in the night, O Lord, and I kept your law. This was made for me; That is to say, I did not do it for myself to have kept your law, but it was certainly done to me for your sake: For I sought your justifications, not my own. God is, then, says the Apostle, the one who works in us to will and to act for his benevolence. God also says this through the prophet: And I will make you walk in my justifications and keep my gere, ut nec lex, nec nox subaudiatur, sed hoc pronomen quod est Haec, non accipiatur aliter quam se habet ille in alio psalmo locus ubi legitur, Unam petii a Domino, hanc requiram (Ps 26:4). Nec dicit quid unam, vel quam unam, de qua dixerit, Hanc requiram; sed femininum genus quasi pro neutral positum est. Unusitate quippe dictum est, Unam petii, hanc requiram; ubi non subauditur quae illa una sit: quod usitatius diceretur, Unum petii a Domino, hoc requiram, ut inhabitem in domo Domini. In his enim neutris non solet exigi neutrum quod subaudiendum sit, ut puta, unum bonum, aut unum donum, vel si quid huiusmodi; sed quidquid illud est, etiamsi masculine vel feminino genere nuncupetur, vel sine ullo nomine ullius generis quibuslibet verbis insinuetur, sólita omnino locutione sub genere neutral intelligitur.

Ita ergo et hic eo modo dici potuit, Haec facta est mihi, tanquam dictum esset, Hoc factum est mihi. Si autem quaeramus quid illud sit, occurrit quod supra dixerat: Memor Fui in nocte nominis tui, Domine, et custodivi legem tuam. Hoc factum est mihi; Id est, hoc quod custodivi legem tuam, non per meipsum feci, sed factum est mihi, utique abs te: quia iustificationes, non meas, sed tuas exquisivi. Deus est enim, inquit Apostolus, qui operatur in vobis et velle et operani, pro bona volúntate (Phil 2,13). Hoc etiam per prophetam Deus dicit: Et faciam ut in iustificationibus meis ambuletis, et iudicia mea observatis, et faciatis (Ez 36,27). Quapropter Deo dicente, Ego faciam

1 [v.57]. Now, with the good pleasure of God, we undertake the exposition of the following verses of this great psalm: My portion is the Lord, or what other codices record: My portion, O Lord!... It can be recorded in both ways, since each man participates in God by uniting himself with Him, as it is written. For me it is a good thing to unite with God, since men are not gods by nature, but are made by the participation of Him who alone is true God. Therefore, it must be understood either that men choose for themselves the parts in this world, or that they have in their lot parts or daughters by which each one lives, some in one way and others in another, God being, in a certain way, the part or portion of the righteous by which they always live. Both senses can be accepted. But let's hear what follows:... I said, it is keeping your law. Thus, to sweetness Discipline is healthily added to goodness. But it should not be asked for and desired for a small sweetness and goodness, that is, for a small holy love, but for one that is so great that it cannot be extinguished by any oppression, as happens to a great flame, which, under the force of the wind, the more it is whipped, the more violently it ignites. For this reason it was little to say: You used gentleness with your servant, if he did not also ask that you teach him the sweetness of goodness and that he could patiently endure such great discipline. Since he does not say "give me", but teach me, I ask: How is sweetness taught, if it is not given? Certainly, many know what does not delight them, and of these things that they have knowledge they do not perceive sweetness or softness; for softness cannot be known unless it delights. Likewise, discipline, which is reduced to the punishment ordered for amendment, is learned by receiving it, that is, it is not learned by hearing, or reading, or thinking, but by experiencing it. But science, which he mentioned in the third term among the things he said teach me about, is given by teaching. For what else is teaching but giving science? In such a way these two things intertwine, that one cannot be found without the other. No one is taught without learning and no one learns without being taught. Therefore, if the disciple is incapable of learning the things that are taught to him by the Master, the Master cannot say: "I taught him, but he did not." learned." He will be able, however, to say: "I told him what I should tell him, but he did not learn, because he did not perceive, he did not understand, he did not understand"; because, if he had taught, without a doubt the other would have learned. Therefore, God, when he wants to teach, first gives intelligence, without which man cannot learn the things that belong to the divine teaching. Hence this one also says shortly after: Give me intelligence.

Sweet are you, Lord; or as many other codices write: Sweet are you, oh Lord!; and some also: Sweet are you, or: Good are you, in the sense that we previously gave to this word. And in your sweetness (or goodness) teach me your justifications, mandatis tuis credidi, nisi, credidi quod tu illa mandaveris, non aliquis homo, quamvis per nomines hominibus ministrata sint? Twelve ergo me suavitatem inspiring charitatem, twelve me disciplinem donating patientiam, twelve me scientiam illuminating intelligentiam: Quoniam mandatis tuis credidi. Quod ad illam humiliationem melius refertur, quae facta est in Adam, in quo omnis creature humano tanquam in radice vitiata, quoniam veritati subiecta esse non voluit, subiecta est vanitati (Rom 8:20). Quod vasis misericordiae profuit experiri, ut deiecta superbia diligatur obedientia, et pereat non reditura miseria. 6 [v.68]. clones. He truly wants to practice the justifications of God, since he wants to learn them with the sweetness of Her who said: Sweet are you, O Lord! 1 [v. 69]. He says this as one who learns God's justifications with his sweetness. His heart curdled like milk. Whose? Of the proud, whose iniquity he said was multiplied upon him. By this word, curdled, he wanted it to be understood in this place that his heart was hardened, because it is also used in a good sense, as in Psalm 67, where it is said: Monte achesado, monte pingüe, and it is understood as full of grace; which some also translated curdled mountain. But he takes care that on his part he opposes their hardness of heart, and thus he says: Vero I meditated on your law. What law? Which is certainly most just and most merciful; hence it is said to him: And by your law have mercy on me. By this law he resists the proud, so that they may be obstinate, and gives grace to the humble, so that they may love obedience and receive exaltation. Tanquam ille hoc dicit, qui in eius suavitate iustificationes Dei discit. Quanto magis enim suavia sunt quae iubet qui iuvat, tanta magis ea scrutatur amans, ut cognita faciat et fazando cognoscat; quia perfectius cognoscuntur, cum fiunt. 8 [v.70]. Coagulatum est ut lac cor eorum.

Quorum, nisi superborum quorum super se multiplicatam dixit iniquitatem? Obduruisse autem cor eorum vult intelligi hoc verbo et hoc loco. Sed vide quid a se opponat duritiae cordis illorum: Ego vero, inquit, legem tuam meditatus sum. What legem? Utique iustissimam et misericordissimam: unde illi dicitur, Et lege tua miserere mei. humility in order to free oneself from penal humility, of which he now speaks. 9 [v. 71]. It is good for me to have humbled myself, so that I may learn your justifications. I had already said above, and not long ago: Before being humiliated, I committed a crime; That's why I kept your saying. This is related to the present, since by the fruit itself it shows that it was good for him to be humiliated; but there he also indicated the reason, namely, that the crime preceded the criminal humiliation. From what it says there: Therefore I kept your saying, and from what it says here: so that I may learn your justifications, it seems to me that it sufficiently demonstrates that knowing these justifications is the same as keeping them, and keeping them is the same as knowing them. For Christ knew what He rebuked, and yet He rebuked sin, even though it was said of Him that He did not know sin. I knew it with a certain knowledge and I ignored it with a certain ignorance. Thus, many also learn God's justifications and do not learn them. They know them with a certain knowledge and they ignore them with a certain ignorance, because they do not practice them. Then he said: so that he may learn your justifications, understanding that he knows them to execute them. 10 [v. 72]. But since this is only done for love, the next verse, which says: The law of your mouth is better for me than thousands of gold and silver, shows where the delight is of the one who works, and therefore it was said: Teach me your justifications with your sweetness. Charity loves more the law of God, who loves covetousness thousands of gold and silver. Meditatione quippe legis huius, voluntary servatur humilitas, ut poenalis humilitas evadatur, de qua mox dicit. 9 [v.71]. Bonum mihi quoniam bumiliasti me, ut discam iustificationes tuas. Quod vero ibi ait, Propterea eloquium tuum custodivi; hic autem, Ut discam iustificationes tuas: satis significasse mihi videtur hoc esse ista nosse quod custodire, hoc custodire quod nosse. Eo moda hic ergo intelligendus est dixisse, Ut discam iustificationes tuas; ea news qua fiunt. 10 [v.72]. SERMON 18 1 [v.73]. When God made man from dust and breathed life into him, it was not commemorated there that he had formed him with his hands. Therefore, I do not understand why some believed that God made the remaining beings with his words, and that man, as being more excellent, was formed with his hands, unless perhaps, because it is read that the body of man was formed from dust, they think that it could not be made except with the hands, not realizing that what was written in the Gospel of the divine Word: All things were made by Him, it cannot be verified if the human body was not also made by the Word or Word of God. But they plead the testimony of this psalm, and say: "Behold, man cries clearly: Thy hands made me and formed me." But they say it as if it had not also been said very clearly: I will see the heavens, the work of your fingers; and, likewise, no less clear: And the heavens are the work of your hands; and even much more clearly: And his hands formed the arid earth. The hand of God is the power of God. If you are concerned about the plural number, since he did not say "your hand", but your hands, take the power and wisdom of God through the hands of God, since both were called Christ; which is also understood to be the arm of God, as it is read in Isaiah: And the arm of the Lord, to whom has it been revealed? Or take the Son and the Holy Spirit at the hands of God, because the Holy Spirit works with the Father and the Son, and for this reason the Apostle says: All these things are done by one and the same Spirit. There were also those who distinguished these two verbs: fecerunt me and finxerunt me, they made me and formed me, in such a way that they affirmed that God made the soul and formed the body, since he said of the soul: Omnem flatum ego feci, I made every spirit; and of the body it is read: et finxit... and God formed man, dust of the earth. As if everything that is formed is made and everything that is made is not formed; and, therefore, they say that the soul is rather made than formed, since it is not a body, but a spirit; as if it had not been written: He who forms the spirit of man in man. However, when these two verbs are in the same place speaking of man and it is not denied that both parts of man, that is, that the soul and the body, have been created by God, he will elegantly assign to the soul the verb to make, and to the body the verb to form, saying that the soul was made, and the body formed, shaped or configured. Aut accipiant manus Dei, Filium et Spiritum sanctum; quia et Spiritus sanctus cooperator est Patris et Filii: unde ait Apostolus, Omnia haec operatur unus atque idem Spiritus (1 Cor 12:11). Propterea quippe dixit, Unus atque idem; ne tot spiritus quod opera putarentur, non quod sine Patre et Filio Spiritus operetur. Liberum est igitur quomodo intelligantur manus Dei: dum tamen nec ea quae facit manibus, Verb faceré negetur; nec ea quae facit Verb, manibus faceré non putetur; nec propter manus forma corporis, aut alia manus sinistra, alia dextra, nec propter Verbum sonus oris, vel motus animi transitorius operanti Deo inesse credatur.

Et ideo animam factam potius dicunt esse quam fictam, quia non est corpus, sed spiritus; quasi non scriptum sit, Qui finxit spiritum hominis in ipso (Zach 12:1). But was this said by Adam, of whom, since all men came from him, being made, it cannot also be said that each of the men was made by reason of origin and descent? Or can it be rightly said: Your hands made me and shaped me, because each one is made by his parents, without lacking the work of God, begetting them and creating Him, because, if the operative power of God were removed from things, they would perish? Nothing at all originates, whether from the elements of the world or from the parents or the seeds, if God does not work in beings. This is why he says to the prophet Jeremiah: Before I formed you in the womb I knew you. But did God make man, whether the first or each of those who are born later, without understanding so that now it is said to him: Your hands made me and shaped me; give me understanding? Was not human nature endowed with understanding so that by it it could be distinguished from beasts? Or is it that by sinning she degraded herself to such a point, that she must be restored in this also. The Apostle says to all who belong to regeneration: Be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and understanding is in the mind. And it also says: Be transformed with the renewal of your knowledge. And of those who did not participate in this regeneration he says: I command you and testify in the Lord that you no longer walk as the Gentiles walk in the vanity of their mind, darkened in understanding and separated from the way of God because of the ignorance that is in them causa re, finxerunt me; sed, plasmaverunt me: magis diligentes minus latine declinare de graeco, quam dicere finxerunt, quod aliquando etiam de simulatione dici solet. 3. An etiam secundum hoc recte dici potuit, Manus tuae fecerunt me, et plasmaverunt me, quoniam unusquisque non sine opere Dei etiam de parentibus fit, ipso creante, illis generatibus? Quoniam si operatoria Dei potentia rebus subtrahatur, intereunt; nec aliquid omnino sive de mundi elementis, sive de genitoribus, sive de seminibus nascitur, si ea non operetur Deus.

of the blindness of his heart. In order for these inner eyes, whose blindness is not to understand, to open and become clearer more and more, hearts are purified by faith. For, although no one can believe in God unless he understands something, yet the same faith, by which he understands, is healed so that he understands more excellent things. There are some things that, if we do not understand them, we do not believe them, and there are others that we do not understand if we do not believe them, because if faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of Christ, how can he who preaches the faith believe who, while keeping other things to himself, does not understand the language spoken to him? But, if there were not other things that we cannot understand unless we first believe them, the prophet would not say: If you do not believe, you will not understand. Therefore our understanding serves to understand what it has to believe, and faith to believe what it has to understand; and so that these same things may be understood more and more, the mind serves in the same understanding. But this is not done by our own and natural forces, but by God helping us and giving it to us, just as medicine, not nature, is what makes the damaged eye recover the ability to see. Therefore he who says to the Lord: Give me understanding that I may learn your precepts, does not completely lack it, like the beasts; nor, even if he be a man, should he be counted among the number of those who walk in the vanity of the mind, darkened in intelligence and separated from the path autem qui huius regenerationis consortes non erat, "Hoc" inquit, "dico et testificor in Domino, ut non iam ambuletis sicut et Gentes ambulant in vanitate mentis suae, obscurati intelligentia, alienati a via Dei per ignorantiam, quae est in illis propter caecitatem cordis eorum” (Eph 4, 17.18.23). Propter hos igitur interior oculos, quorum caecitas est non intelligere, ut aperiantur, et magis magisque serenentur, fide corda mundantur (Act 15,9). Quamvis enim, nisi aliquid intelligat, nemo possit credere in Deum; tamen ipsa fide qua credit, sanatur, ut intelligat amplificara. Alia sunt enim quae nisi intelligamus, non credimus, et alia sunt quae nisi credamus, non intelligimus. Nam cum fides sit ex auditu, auditus autem per verbum Christi (Rom 10:17); quomodo credit praedicanti fidem, qui, ut alia taceam, linguam ipsam quam loquitur non intelligit? Sed nisi essent rursus aliqua quae intelligere non possumus, nisi ante credamus, propheta non diceret, Nisi credideritis, non intelligetis (Is 7:9, sec. LXX).

Proficit ergo noster intellectus ad intelligenda quae credat, et fides proficit ad credenda quae intelligat; et eadem ipsa ut magis magisque intelligantur, in ipso intellectu proficit mens. What the Latins said, translating the Greek text, da mihi intellectum, give me understanding, the Greek text says more concisely: sinetison me. The Greek summarizes it in a verb, synetison, the da mihi intellectum. Latin cannot do it. Just as, if one could not say in Latin sana me, heal me, one would say da mihi sanitatem, as here, da mihi intellectum, or one would say sanum me fac, as here one can also say intelligentem me fac, make me intelligent. This certainly could have been done by an angel, for he said to Daniel: I came to give you understanding; and there, in the Greek text, the same verb is found as here: sinetisai se, as if the Latin said sanitatem daré tibi, I came to give you health, to which the Greek said "I came to heal you." He stood among the Ubal, and called and said, "Make me understand the vision." In that passage the same Greek verb is recorded as here, namely, synetison. Thus, God, who is light, illuminates pious minds by himself so that they may understand the divine things that are said or shown. But if he uses the ministry of an angel to do so, the angel can also do something in the mind of man so that he perceives the light of God, and through it understands. But it is said that it gives understanding to man and, so to speak, that it intellectualizes him, in the same way that it is said that someone gives light to the house or illuminates it by opening a window, without him penetrating and illuminating it with his light, but rather opening the passage through which the light penetrates and the house is illuminated. But the sun that enters through the window and illuminates the house did not create the house, or the man, who made the window; or he ordered someone to do it, or helped the one who did it, or did something to open the way for his light to enter; but God also made the rational and intellectual mind of man, through which he could perceive his light; and he also made the angel, in such a way that he could work something that would help the human mind to receive the light of God; and also helps the mind to receive the angelic operation; and he illuminates it by himself, so that he sees not only the things that are shown by the truth, but the truth itself. Sed nec sol qui per fenestram illustrat domum, ipse creavit eamdem domum, aut hominem qui fenestram fecit in domo, aut ipse illi iussit ut faceret, aud adiuvit ipse facientem, aut aliquid egit ut aperiretur qua suum lumen infunderet: Deus autem et hominis mentem rationalem atque intellectualem fecit, qua posset capere lumen eius; et angelum talem fecit, qui operani posset aliquid unde ad capiendum lumen Dei mens adiuvaretur humano; et eamdem sic adiuvat mentem, ut angelicam recipiat operationem; et eam sic illuminat de seipso, ut non solum illa quae a veritate monstrantur, sed ipsam quoque proficing perspiciat veritatem. SERMON 19 1 [v.73]. Our Lord Jesus Christ asks in this psalm through the prophet, as for himself, that God give understanding to his Body, which is the Church, so that it may know the commandments of God. For, since the life of his Body, that is, of his people, is found hidden with Him in God and He suffers need in this Body, He asks for what His members need, and thus He says: Your hands made me and formed me; Give me understanding so that I may learn your commandments. "Since you formed me," he says, "reform me so that what the Apostle says may be done in the Body of Christ: Be transformed with the renewal of your knowledge." 2 [v.74]. Those who fear, he says, will see me and rejoice; or as other codices write: They will rejoice, because I hoped in your words, that is, in the things you promised, so that the children of the promise may be descendants of Abraham, in whom all nations are blessed. But who are those who fear God and who will they see and rejoice, because they waited on the words of God? If this voice uttered by Christ is from the Body of Christ, that is, from the Church; or if it is proper to Christ uttered in or by the Church, are they not among those who fear God? Was it said this way because fear takes place in the present time, that is, while human life is a continuous temptation on earth, and the joy that he meant here will take place when the righteous shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father? all, since by the flesh, which lusts against the spirit, even the regenerate are forced to groan under its oppression, says considering all this: I know, Lord, that your judgments are righteousness; and with the truth you have humiliated me. May your mercy be fulfilled and comfort me, according to your word given to your servant. Mercy and truth are so recommended in the Holy Scripture that, being found in many places in it, they are recorded in a special way in the psalms, and in one of them it is said: All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth. Here also the truth was first recorded, with which we are humbled to death by the design of Him whose judgments are justice itself; then mercy, by which we are restored to life by promise of Him whose benefit is grace. Hence it says: According to your word given to your servant; that is, according to what you promised your servant. But by this we understand regeneration, by which we are adopted here as children of God; or faith, hope and charity, three things that are built in us although they come from the mercy of God, however, in this calamitous and troubled life they are only the consolation of the unfortunate, not the joy of the blessed; That is why it is said: Let your mercy be fulfilled to comfort me. 4 [v.77}. But since after these things and through them the others must also come, he continues and says: Let your commiserations come to me, and I will live. I will certainly live when I will in no way be able to fear dying, since only eternal life is called life, and nothing other than the sempiterna matris eorum sic in omnibus pertenditur usque in diem sepulturae in matrem omnium should be understood as such (Eccli 40,1), ut propter carnem concupiscentem adversus spiritum (Gal 5,17), etiam regenerati gemere sub eius gravitate cogantur: hoc ergo consideras, “Cognovi”, inquit, “Domine, quia iustitia iudicia tua, et veritate humiliasti me. taking advantage and failing, when it is not indicated or understood what is being taken advantage of or failing, progress is commonly taken in a good sense, and failure in a bad sense. But, when indicated, taking advantage can also be understood in a bad sense, and failing in a good sense. Thus, the Apostle clearly says: Avoid profane novelties of words, because they profit greatly for evil; and he also says of some: They take advantage for the worse. Likewise, the defect of good is bad for evil, and the defect of evil is good for good. Of the good defect it was said: My soul desires and faints for the courts of the Lord. Here it does not say: My soul fainted "for your" health, but: It fainted "for your" health; that is, he fainted longing for your health. Therefore this defect is good, since it indicates a desire for good that has not yet been achieved, but longs for it very avidly and vehemently. And who says this? The chosen lineage, the royal priesthood, the holy people, the people of acquisition; and he says it from the origin of the human race to the end of this century, in those who in their respective time lived, live and will live here desiring Christ. Witness to this is the holy old man Simeon, who, having taken the Lord in his hands as a child, said: Now, Lord, send away your servant in peace, according to your word, because my eyes have seen your salvation. God had predicted that he would not die before seeing the Christ of the Lord. The same desire that this old man had must be believed that all the saints of past times had. Hence it is that the Lord himself said to his disciples: Many prophets and kings desired to see what you see, and they did not see it; and hear what you hear, and did not hear; so that this voice is also theirs: My optabilis. Nam cum sint inter se duo ista contraria, proficere et deficere; usitatius profectus in bono accipitur, defectus in malo, quando non additur vel subintelligitur in quid proficiatur vel deficiatur: cum vero additur, potest et malum esse proficere, bonumque deficere. Aperte quippe dixit Apostolus, Profanas autem verborum novitates Evita: multum enim proficient ad impietatem (2 Tim 2,16): ait et de quibusdam, Proficient in peius (ib. 3,13). Ita et defectus a bonus in malum malus est, a malo in bonum bonus est. Bono quippe defectu dictum est, Desiderat et deficit anima mea in atria Domini (Ps 83.3). Sic et hic non ait, Defecit a salutari tuo; sed, Defecit in salutare tuum, hoc est, ad salutare tuum, anima mea.

Bonus est ergo iste defectus: indicat enim desiderium boni, nondum quidem adepti, sed avidissime ac vehementissime concupiti. Sed quis hoc dicit nisi genus electum, regale sacerdotium, gens sancta, populus acquisitionis (1 Ptr 2,9), ab origine generis humani usque ad huius saeculi finem, in eis qui suo quique tempore hic vixerunt, vivunt, victuri sunt, desiderans Christum? See here again that laudable and blessed defect of the eyes, but of the interior eyes, which does not come from the weakness of the soul, but from the constancy of the desire for the promise of God, since this promise is contained in the words in eloquium tuum, in your saying. How do these eyes say: When will you comfort me? By praying and groaning with the intention and hope of this. The tongue is what speaks; the eyes do not usually speak; However, in a certain way, the desire of prayer is the voice of the eyes. In what he says: When will you comfort me?, he suggests that he is suffering from some delay. Hence also that of another psalm: And you, O Lord, how long? This happens either to make the delayed joy sweeter, or because it is a feeling of those who desire, which seems prolonged to the one who loves even though it is brief to the giver. The Lord, who orders everything by number, weight and measure, knows when to do what he does. 3 [v. 83]. No doubt, due to ardent spiritual desires, carnal desires are tempered; This is why the psalmist continues: For I became like a wineskin with the frost; I didn't forget your justifications. No doubt he wants the flesh of this death to be understood by stone, and by frost the benefit of heaven, whereby, as if held back by the cold, the appetites of the flesh are dulled;

And this is why it happens that God's justifications are not removed from memory by not thinking about anything else, because what happens is what the Apostle says: Pay no attention to the flesh in its appetites. Hence, having said: Because I became like a skin with the frost, he adds: I have not forgotten your justifications; That is, I did not forget why I became such. For the boiling of appetite was dulled so that the memory of charity could boil. 4 [v.84}. How many are the days of your servant? When will you give me justice against my persecutors? In the Apocalypse the martyrs say this and are required to be patient until the number of brothers is completed. The Body of Christ asks about the days he will remain in this world. And so that no one thinks that the Church will disappear from here before the end of the world comes, and, therefore, that there will be some time in this century in which there will be no Church on earth, when the Lord is asked about its days, he mentions the judgment, undoubtedly to demonstrate that it too must be on the earth until the judgment, in which revenge will be taken on the persecutors. If anyone is concerned why, the psalmist asks what the disciples asked the Master When he answered them: It is not for you to know the times that the Father put in his power, why not tell him that in this passage in the Psalm it was prophesied that they would ask him this same thing and that the voice of the Church, which he announced here so far in advance, was fulfilled in his question 5 [v.85].

It was in God's hands or in his, offering it to God to give it life. 7 [v. l l l ]. I inherited your testimonies forever. Some Latins, wanting to express with a single word what is recorded in Greek with one, translated haereditavi by haereditate acquisivi, although certainly this Latin word should rather mean or indicate the one who gives the inheritance than the one who receives it. So haereditavi would have the meaning of ditavi, I enriched (someone). Therefore, it is better to declare the meaning in its entirety by saying with two words, whether it is said haereditate possedi, possessed in inheritance, or haereditate acquisivi; non haereditatem, sed haereditate, I acquired by inheritance; not the inheritance, but in inheritance. If you wonder what you inherited, answer: Your testimonies. And what did he mean? That he became a witness of God, that he confessed his testimonies; That is to say, that he became a martyr and that he confessed as martyrs confess, that this was granted to him by the Father, of whom he is heir. Many certainly wanted to and could not; However, none could without having wanted to; because they would not have been able to if they had wanted to deny the testimonies of God. But it is also true that his will was helped by God. That is why he affirms that he acquired these testimonies as an inheritance and forever, because in them is not found the temporal glory of men who seek vain things, but the eternal glory of those who suffer for a short time and reign without end. Hence he continues: because they are the joy of my heart. Even though they are affliction of the body, yet they are joy of the heart. datis^ tuis non erravi. 8 [v.112]. Then he adds: I inclined my heart to eternally execute your justifications for retribution. He who says: I incline my heart, had already said: Incline my heart toward your testimonies, so that we may understand that this is the joint work of the divine gift and our own will. But are we to make God's justifications eternally? The works we do in relation to the needs of others cannot be eternal, any more than the needs themselves are eternal. The psalm continues: I reputed, judged or counted as transgressors all the sinners of the earth, since the Latins translated the Greek word eloguisamen in many ways. The sentence is profound, and with the help of God we have to fathom it, putting more effort into another dissertation. And what is added: That is why I always loved your testimonies, makes it even deeper, since the Apostle says: The law works wrath; and, giving the reason for this saying, he adds: because where there is no law, there is no prevarication either, implying by this that not all are prevaricators, since not all have law. great psalm: I reputed transgressors; or, rather, prevaricant, because the Greek text says parabainontas and not parabatas. We try to find out, I repeat, how it is to be understood: I considered all sinners on earth to be transgressors, taking into account that the Apostle says: Where there is no law, there is no prevarication. But he says this to distinguish the law from the promises. So that the meaning is better understood, let us record what it says above: The promise made to Abraham and his lineage that he would be the heir of the world was not by the law, but by the righteousness of faith. For if they are heirs by the law, faith is vain, and the promise worthless, because the law works wrath; and where there is no law, there is no prevarication. Then by faith, so that, according to grace, the promise may be established for the entire race; not only for the one of the law, but also for the one of the faith of Abraham, who is the father of us all. Why does the Apostle say this except to demonstrate that the law, without the grace of the promise, not only does not remove sin, but increases it? Hence it was also written: The law was introduced so that crime would abound. But since all crimes are forgiven by grace, not only those committed without law, but also those committed with it, he adds: Where crime abounded, grace abounded all the more. Therefore, the Apostle does not consider all sinners to be transgressors, but only those who transgress the law, for he says: Where there is no law, there is no prevarication. For this reason, according to the Apostle, every prevaricator is a sinner, because he sins while having the law; But not every sinner is prevaricating, because some sin without the law, and where there is no law, there is no prevarication. Sed quia omnia per gratiam dimittuntur, non solum quae sine lege, verum etiam quae in lege commissa sunt; ideo ibi secutus adiunxit: Ubi autem abundavit delictum, superabundavit gratia (ib. 5,20).
