no one sinned unless he had the law, would not the Apostle himself have said: All those who sinned without the law will perish without the law. But if, according to this psalm, all sinners on earth are prevaricators, there is no sin without prevarication; and as there is no prevarication without law, there will be no sin without law. Then he who says: I called all sinners on earth transgressors, wants it to be understood that there are no sinners at all apart from those who transgress the law; and for this reason the psalm seems to be opposed to Him who said: All who have sinned without the law will perish without the law. According to the Apostle, there are some sinners who are not prevaricating, because they sin without law, and where there is no law, there is no prevarication. According to the psalmist, there is no sinner without prevarication, because he considers all sinners on earth to be prevaricating. Therefore, according to this, no one sins without law: because where there is no law, there is no prevarication. Should we say that it is true that where there is no law there is no prevarication, but that it is not true that some sinned without law; o that it is true that some sinned without law, but that it is not true that where there is no law there cannot be prevarication? Both sentences were recorded by the Apostle; Therefore, both are true, because both were spoken by the Truth through the mouth of the Apostle. But in what way will it be true what, without a doubt, the Truth said in this psalm: I counted all the sinners of the earth as transgressors? We are asked: Who are those who, according to the Apostle, sinned without law, since none of them should peccat in lege, sed non omnis peccator praevarkator est, quia peccant iiI qui sine lege; Ubi autem non est lex, nec praevaricatio. Porro, si nemo sine lege peccaret, non idem ipse apostolus diceret, Quicumque sine lege peccaverunt, sine lege peribunt. Secundum istum vero psalmum, si praevaricantes sunt omnes peccatores terrae, nullum est utique sine praevaricatione peccatum: nulla est autem praevaricatio sine lege; nullum est igitur nisi in lege peccatum. Qui ergo dicit: Praevaricantes deputavi omnes peccatores terrae, nullos esse omnino, nisi qui legem transgressi sunt, vult intelligi peccatores; et ob hoc adversatur illi qui tlixit: Quicumque sine lege peccaverunt, sine lege peribunt.

Secundum illum quippe sunt aliqui peccatores, quamvis non sint praevaricantes, id est, qui sine lege peccaverunt: Ubi enim non est lex, nec praevaricatio: secundum istum autem nullus est sine praevaricatione peccator; quia praevaricantes deputat omnes peccatores terrae. Nullus ergo secundum istum sine lege peccavit; quia ubi non est lex, nec praevaricatio. An íorte dicturi sumus, verum quidem esse quod nec praevaricatio sit ubi non est lex, sed verum non esse quod aliqui sine lege peccaverint; aut verum quidem esse aliquos sine lege peccasse, sed verum non esse, ubi lex non est, praevaricationem esse non posse? At utrumque Apostolus dixit: verum est ergo utrumque, quia utrumque per Apostolum Veritas tlixit. Quomodo ergo erit verum quod in psalmo isto eadem procul dubio Veritas dixit, Praevaricantes deputavi omnes peccatores terrae? Respondetur enim nobis: Qui sunt ergo illi qui secundum Apostolum sine lege

be considered prevaricating, whereas, according to the same Apostle, there is no prevarication where there is no law? 2. Without a doubt, when the Apostle said: All who have sinned without the law will perish without the law, he was referring to the law that God gave, through his servant Moses, to his people Israel. This is demonstrated by the very words that accompany this sentence. He spoke of the Jews and the Greeks, that is, of the Gentiles, who did not belong to the circumcision, but to the foreskin; and therefore he said of these that they were without law, because they had not received the law, which the Jews boasted of having received. Hence he says to them: If you call yourself a Jew and rest in the law and glory in God..., etc. But it must be seen from what this sentence came: All who have sinned without the law will perish without the law. Wrath—he says—, indignation, tribulation and anguish (there will be) for every soul of man who does evil from the foreskin and from the Greek; but (there will be) glory, and honor, and peace to everyone who does good; for the Jew first and for the Greek, since there is no acceptance of persons in God. To this he adds the words remain reason for this question, and says as follows: All those who sinned without the law will perish without the law, and all those who sinned in the law will be judged by the law, wanting to make the Jews understand by the latter and the Greeks by the former, because it dealt with them and demonstrated that both were subject to sin, so that both would confess that they needed grace. Hence it says: For there is no distinction, since all have sinned, and need the glory of God, since they were justified freely by his grace through the

redemption, which is found in Christ Jesus. Of whom did he say that all sinned but of the Jews and the Greeks, of whom he had said: There is no distinction? He had also said of them shortly before: We accuse the Jews and the Greeks of being all under sin. Therefore, all who sinned without the law, that is, without that in which the Jews boasted, will perish without the law, and all who sinned in the law, that is, the Jews themselves, will be judged by the law. And they will not cease to perish, unless they believe in Him who came to seek what had perished. 3. Some Catholic expositors, paying little attention to these words of the Apostle, understood them differently from how they pray, and thus said that sinners perished without law; and those who sinned in the law will only be judged, but will not perish, believing that they must be purified by temporal punishments, as was the one of whom it was said: He, however, will be saved through the fire. But this is very well understood to be due to the foundation, which the Apostle was talking about when he spoke these words, since he had previously said: Like a wise architect, I laid the foundation, and another builds on it. Let each one see how he builds on it, because no one can lay another foundation outside the foundation, which is Christ Jesus, and the rest that he said until the place where it is recorded that he who builds on this foundation will be saved by fire, not gold, silver or precious stones, but wood, hay and straw, if he does not refuse to receive the foundation, he abandons it once received, that is, if he prefers it to all his carnal pleasures, which imprison him and make him sucum-

peccaverunt? Non enim et eorum quisquam praevaricans deputandus est, cum secundum eumdem apostolum, praevaricatio non sit ubi lex non est. 2. Sed nimirum cum diceret Apostolus, Quicumque sine lege peccaverunt, sine lege peribunt, de illa lege agebat quam Deus dedit per Moysen famulum suum populo suo Israel. Hoc ipsa quae circumstant, verba eius ostendunt. Disputabat enim de Iudaeis et Graecis, id est Gentibus, non ad circumcisionem, sed ad praeputium pertinentibus; ideo sine lege eos dices, quia non acceperant legem quam se accepisse gloriabantur Iudaei: unde illis ait, Si autem tu ludaeus cognominaris, et requiescis in lege, et gloriaris in Deo. Denique unde ad hanc sententiam venerit, intuendum est, ut diceret, Quicumque sine lege peccaverunt, sine lege peribunt. Ira, inquit, et indignatio, tribulatio et anguish in omnem animam hominis operantis malum, Iudaei primum et Graeci; gloria autem et honor et pax omni opera ti bonum, Iudaeo primum et Graeco: Non est enim personarum acceptio apud Deum. Ad haec addidit unde nunc quaestio est, et ait, Quicumque enim sine lege peccaverunt, sine lege peribunt; et quicumque in lege peccaverunt, per legem iudicabuntur (Rom 2,8.17). Hos utique Iudaeos, illos autem Graecos volens intelligi, quoniam de his agebat; utrosque sub peccato esse demonstrans, ut egere se gratia utrique fateantur: propter quod dicit, Non enim est distinctio: omnes enim peccaverunt, et egent gloria Dei; iustificati gratis per gra-

tiam ipsius, per redemptionem quae est in Christo Iesu. Quos ¡taque dicit omnes peccasse, nisi Iudaeos et Graecos, de quibus dixerat, Non enim est distinctio? Nam de his et paulo ante: Causati enim sumus, inquit, Iudaeos et Graecos omnes sub peccato esse (ib. 3,22.23.24.9). Ac per hoc quicumque sine lege peccaverunt, illa scilicet de qua Iudaei gloriabantur, sine lege peribunt; et quicumque in lege peccaverunt, id est ipsi Iudaei, per legem iudicabuntur. Nec ideo non peribunt, nisi credant in eum qui venit quaerere quod perierat (Luke 19:10). 3. Nonnulli quippe etiam catholici tractatores, in his Apostoli verbis aliter quam se res habet parum attendendo sapuerunt, ut dicerent illos perire qui sine lege peccaverunt; Hos autem qui in lege peccaverunt, iudicari tantummodo, non perire: tanquam per poenas transitorias credantur esse purgandi, sicut ille de quo dictum est, Ipse autem salvus erit, sic tamen quasi per ignem. Sed hoc merit fundamentali bene intelligitur, de quo agebat Apostolus, ut hoc diceret. You surpass quippe dixerat, Ut sapiens architectus fundamentum posui; alius superaedificat: unusquisque autem videat quomodo superaedificat. Fundamentum enim aliud memo potest will put praeter id quod positum est, quod est Christus Iesus: et caetera usque ad eumdem locum, ubi eum dixit per ignem salvari, qui super hoc fundamentum, non aurum, argentum, lapides pretiosos, sed ligna, fenum, stipulam aedificat (1 Cor 3,10.15); no tamen

I think that those who believed that they would not perish, those of whom it was said: They will be judged by the law, believed it only because they judged that they had Christ as their foundation. But they paid little attention to these words of the Apostle, as I have shown, since the same Scripture says that the Apostle recorded this of the Jews, who did not have Christ as their foundation. What Christian will say that the Jew will not perish, even if he does not believe in Christ, but will only be judged, whereas Christ himself testifies that he was sent to the Jewish nation for its sheep that had perished, and adds that on the day of judgment the Sodomites, who certainly perished without law, are to be tolerated more than the city of Judea, which did not believe in Him who worked miracles with such extraordinary power? 4. Then if the Apostle, considering the law, which the Lord gave, through Moses, to the people of Israel and not to the other nations, said that they did not have this law, what are we to understand that was said in this psalm when he recorded: I counted all the sinners of the earth as transgressors, if we do not understand that there is another law, not given by Moses, according to which all the sinners of the remaining nations are transgressors? Where there is no law, there is no prevarication. What law is this but that of which the Apostle himself says: The Gentiles, who have no law, naturally respuit ne recipiat, nec receptum deserit fundamentum; idque omnibus carnalibus suis, quibus capitur atque succumbit, delectationibus anteponit, cum ad hunc articulum ventum fuerit, ut aut illae deserantur, aut Christus; ubi si non anteponitur Christus, non illi est fundamentum. Omnibus quippe structurae posterioribus partibus anteponitur fundamentum. Nec cogitasse existimo eos qui senserunt non perire de quibus dictum est, Per legem iudicabuntur, nisi quia fundamentum habent Chtistum. Parum ergo attenderunt quod demonstravimus; atque ipsa Scriptura clamat, de Iudaeis hoc Apostolum dicete, qui sine fundament sunt Christo.

Quis autem Christianus dixerit non perire Iudaeum, si non credat in Christum, sed tantummodo iudicari: cum Christus ipse ad eamdem gentem, propter oves quae inde perierant, se missum esse testetur (Mt 15,24); et tolerabilius dicat futurum Sodomitis in die iudicii, qui utique sine lege perierunt, quam civitati Iudaeae quae in eum non credidit tanta virtute mirabilia facientem? (ib. 11,23.24). 4. Si ergo Apostolus secundum legem quam Deus per Moysen populo Israel dedit, caeteris autem gentibus non dedit, sine lege dixit esse caeteras gentes; quid intellecturi sumus in isto psalmo dictum esse, Praevaricantes aestitnavi omnes peccatores terrae, nisi intelligamus aliquam legem non per Moysen datam, secundum quam sunt praevaricantes caeterarum gentium peccatores? Ubi enim lex non est, nec praevaricatio.

they comply with the precepts of the law; Are these who have no law law to themselves? Then in the sense that says they have no law, so they also sinned without the law and perished without it. Then the grace of the Savior found everyone prevaricating; some more and others less. Knowing, then, the grace of God, which is the only

who frees from prevarication, which is committed by the knowledge of the law, praying, says: Confige clavis...: Pierce my flesh with the nails of your fear. Thus the Latins translated, with more precision, what could be said in Greek with a single word; thus: cazeloson. Some preferred to translate this word as confige, pierces, without adding clavis, with nails; and thus, by wanting to express the only Greek word with a Latin word, they did not give the perfect meaning to the word, because, saying only confige, pierces, the nails cannot be heard; and cazeloson cannot be perceived without the sound of nails, nor can it be expressed in Latin except with two words, as it was said: Confige clavis. And what does this mean here except what the Apostle says: It behooves me alone to glory in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by which the world is crucified for me, and I for the world; and also: I am crucified with Christ; and it is no longer I who live, but Christ is the one who lives in me. And what else is it but that my righteousness, which comes from the law, by which I became a transgressor, is no longer in me, but the righteousness of God, that is, that which for me comes from God, not from me? Thus lives in me, not I, but Christ, who was made by God wisdom for us, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption, so that, as it is written, he who boasts may glory in the Lord. It also says: Those who belong to Jesus Christ crucified the flesh with the passions and lusts. Having said here that they crucified their flesh, in this psalm God is asked to do so by saying: Pierce my flesh with the nails of your fear;

manifestior praevaricatio. Restabat ergo, ut omnibus non sua, sed Dei, id est a Deo donata, iustitia subveniret. Unde ait Apostolus;: Per legem cognitio peccati. Non ergo ablatio, sed cognitio. Lex enim ad hoc prodest, ut mittat ad gratiam. Quod quid est aliud, nisi, Non est in me iustitia mea, quae ex lege est, in qua praevaricator effectus sum; sed iustitia Dei, id est, quae mihi ex Deo est (Phil 3:9), non ex me? Sic quippe in me vivit, non ego, sed Christus, "qui factus est nobis sapientia a Deo, et iustitia, et sanctificatio, et redemptio: ut, quemadmodum scriptum est, Qui gloriatur, in Domino glorietur" (1 Cor 1,30.31). item dicit, "Qui autem sunt lesu Christi, carnem crucifixerunt cum passionibus et concupiscentiis" (Gal 5,24). patent is the prevarication. It only remains, then, that everyone should be helped by justice, not by each one's own, but by God's, that is, that given by God. For this reason the Apostle says: The knowledge of sin by the law. Sin is not erased by the law, but is known by the law. But now, he says, without the law, the righteousness of God was manifested, witnessed by the law and the prophets. Therefore the psalmist also added: This is why I loved your testimonies. Which is as if he said: "Since the law, whether given in paradise, or printed in nature, or promulgated in writing, makes transgressors of all sinners on earth, therefore I loved your testimonies, which by your grace are found in your law, so that not my own righteousness but yours may be found in me." The law certainly serves to lead to grace. Not only insofar as it testifies to the justice of God, which is without the law, but also in so far as it constitutes prevarications; to such a degree that the letter kills, and forces one to resort through fear to the life-giving spirit, by which all sins are erased and the master of good works is inspired. That's why he says: I loved your testimonies. Some codices always add, others do not. If it is found in them, always must be taken in such a way as to mean "while we live in the world," since here the testimonies of the law and the prophets are necessary to attest to the justice of God, by which we are justified freely. Our testimonies are also necessary here, for which the martyrs gave the same life that is spent here. 6 [v.120].

and it is said so that we understand that the good we do must be attributed to the grace of God, who works in us to will and to act out of benevolence. 7. But why, after having said: Pierce my flesh with the nails of your fear, did he add: because I feared your judgments? What does it mean: Move over your fear, because I feared? If he had already feared or was afraid, why did he still ask that God crucify his flesh with his fear? Did he want his fear to be increased, in order to fear so much as would be sufficient to crucify his flesh, that is, the lusts and carnal affections, as if to say: "Perfect your fear in me, for I feared your judgments"? Here is another deeper meaning, which, with the help of the Lord, I must bring to light by examining the abyss of this text of Scripture: Pierce, he says, my flesh with the nails of your fear, because I feared your judgments; But perfect charity, which constitutes freedom not from the fear of punishment, but from the love of justice, casts away this fear with which one fears punishment (which is not chaste). Because this fear with which one does not love justice, but rather fears punishment, is servile, because it is carnal, and, for the same reason, it does not crucify the flesh, since it lives the will to sin, which is manifested in works when impunity is expected. And, therefore, when it is believed that punishment will follow, it lives latently, but it lives. I would prefer that you pee; ut intelligamus etiam id quod recte facimus, gratiae Dei esse tribuendum, qui in nobis operatur et velle et operari, pro bona volúntate (Phil 2,13). 7. Sed quid sibi vult, quod cum dixisset, Confige clavis a timore tuo carnes meas; addidit, a iudiciis enim tuis timui? Quid est, Confige a timore tuo; timui enim? Si iam timuerat, vel timebat, cur adhuc, ut a timore suo Deus crucifigeret carnes eius, orabat? An addi sibi volebat timorem, ut tantum timeret, quantum sufficeret crucifigendis suis carnibus, id est concupiscentiis affectibusque carnalibus; tanquam say, Perfice in me timorem tuum; timui enim a iudiciis tuis? Sed est hic alius altior sensus, quantum Deus donat, scrutato sinu Scripturae huius eruendus.

Confige, inquit, clavis a timore tuo carnes meas; a iudiciis enim tuis timui: hoc est, a timore tuo casto, qui permanet in saeculum saeculi (Ps 18,10), carnalia mea desideria comprimantur; a iudiciis enim tuis timui, cum mihi lex minaretur poenam, quae mihi non poterat daré iustitiam. Sed hunc timorem, quo poena metuitur, consummata charitas foras mittit (1 lo 4,18); quae non timore poenae, sed delectatione iustitiae liberos reddit. Timor namque iste, quo non amatur iustitia, sed timetur poena, servilis est, quia carnalis est; et ideo non crucifigit carnem. Vivit enim peccandi voluntas, quae tune apparet in opere, quando speratur impunitas, Cum vero poena creditur secutara, latenter vivit: yivjt
Excellencies of the law of God

What the law prohibits is permitted, and he feels that it is not; for he does not spiritually delight in good, but carnally fears the evil with which it threatens. On the contrary, with chaste fear, the same charity, which casts out unchaste fear, fears sinning even if no punishment comes, since it believes that (this punishment) is not lacking, since for the love of justice it counts the same sin as punishment. With such fear the flesh is crucified, because carnal delights, which are rather prohibited by the letter of the law than avoided, are conquered by the love of spiritual goods and by the same they are destroyed until a perfect and complete victory is achieved. Pierce—he says—with the nails of your fear my flesh, because I feared your judgments, that is, give me chaste fear, since, as a pedagogue, it leads me to ask for the fear of the law, with which I feared your judgments, SERMON 26 1 [v.121]. I now undertake the examination and exposition of the following verses of this great psalm: I wrought judgment and righteousness; Do not hand me over to those who mistreat me. It is not surprising that judgment and justice were carried out by what he had previously asked for out of fear of God, but chaste, his flesh pierced with nails, that is, his carnal lusts, which usually prevent our judgment from being right. Even though in our usual conversation both the upright and the perverse are called judgment, for which reason it is said to men in the Gospel: Do not judge by appearance. Mallet enim licere, et dolet non licere quod lex vetat; quia non spiritualiter delectatur eius bono, sed carnaliter malum metuit quod minatur. Timore autem casto ipsa, quae hunc timorem foras mittit, peccare timet charitas, etiamsi sequatur impunitas; quia nec impunitatem íudicat secuturam, quando amore iustitiae peccatum ipsum deputat poenam. Tali timore meats crucifiguntur; quoniam carnales delectationes, quae legis littera vetantur potius quam vitantur, spiritualium bonorum delectatione vincuntur, et eadem usque ad perfectionem crescente victoria primuntur. Confige ergo clavis, inquit, a timore tuo carnes meas; a iudiciis enim tuis timui: hoc est, Da mihi castum timorem, ad quem petendum me tanquam paedagogus timor legis ille perduxit, quo timore a iudiciis tuis timui. What can only be accomplished with your grace, so that, since men have not been able to accomplish it with their own strength, every mouth remains silent and no one believes himself to be great. Let everyone be small and everyone will be held guilty before you, because no man will be justified by the law before you, since only sin is known by the law. But now the righteousness of God has been revealed without the law, the law and the prophets testifying to it. These are your wonderful testimonies that search the soul of this little one; and he found them, because he was humbled and made small. For who fulfills your commandments as they should be fulfilled, that is, by faith, which works through love, if the same love is not spread in his heart through the Holy Spirit? 4 [v.131]. This little boy also declares the following: I opened my mouth and inhaled, because I desired your commandments. What did you want? Fulfill divine commandments. But, since the weak man could not do strong things, nor the small one great things, he opened his mouth, confessing that he would not do them by himself, and he aspired to do them. He opened his mouth asking, seeking, calling, and, thirsty, bedigus et egenus ad gratiam confugeres, et clamares: Miserere mei, Domine, quoniam infirmus sum (Ps 6,3). Hoc ergo scrutando intellexit hic parvulus, quod minimus Apostolorum Paulus, id est parvulus, ostendit, ideo datam legem quae vivificare non posset, quia conclusit Scriptura omnia sub peccato, ut promissio ex fide Iesu Christi daretur credentibus (Gal 3,21,22). Ita, Domine, ita fac, misericors Domine; impera quod non possit impleri, imo impera quod nonnisi per tuam gratiam possit impleri: ut cum nomines per suas vires id implere nequiverint, omne os obstruatur, et nemo sibi magnus videatur. Sint omnes parvuli, et reus fiat omnis mundus tibi: quia «non iustificabitur ex lege omnis caro coram te; per legem enim cognitio peccati. Nunc autem sine lege iustitia tua manifestata est, testimonium habens a Lege et Prophetis” (Rom 3:19-21). Haec sunt mirabilia testimonia tua, quae scrutata est anima parvuli huius; et ideo invenit, quia humiliatus est, et parvulus factus est.

Quis enim facit mandata tua sicut facienda sunt, id est, ex fide quae per dilectionem operatur (Gal 5,6), nisi eius in corde per Spiritum sanctum ipsa dilectio diffundatur? (Rom 5:5). 4 [v.131]. Hoc etiam iste parvulus confitetur: Os meum, inquit, aperui, et attraxi spiritum, quoniam mandata tua desiderabam. Quid desiderabat, nor will I do a divine mandate? Sed non erat unde faceret infirmus fortia, parvulus magna: aperuits os, confitens quod per se ipse non faceret; et attraxit unde faceret: aperuit os petendo, quaerendo, pulsando; et sitiens hausit Spiritum bonum, unde faceret, quod per

The good Spirit came to fulfill the holy, just and good commandment, which he could not fulfill by himself. If we, being evil, give good things to our children, how much more will our Father, who is in heaven, give the good spirit to those who ask him? For those who act by their own spirit are not children of God, but all those who act by the Spirit of God. And this is not because they do not act, but because, not doing anything good of their own, they are moved by the good Spirit to do it, since each one becomes a good son the more the more abundantly the good Spirit is given to him by the Father. 5 [v. 132]. This one still asks. He certainly opened his mouth and inhaled, that is, he attracted the spirit; but still calls the Father; and seek, and drink; and the more he perceives the sweetness, the more ardently he feels the thirst. Hear the words of the thirsty: Look at me, he says, and have mercy on me according to the judgment of those who love your name, that is, according to the judgment you made to those who love your name; because in order for them to love you, you first loved them. For thus says the apostle Saint John: We love God; and, as if asked why we loved Him, He added: "because He first loved us." 6 [v. 133]. Also observe what he says very clearly: Direct my steps according to your saying and let no iniquity dominate me. What does this express except: "Make me upright and free, according to your promise"? The more charity reigns in each person, the less iniquity dominates him. Then what does he ask but that, seipsum non poterat, mandatum sanctum et iustum et bonum (ib. 7,12). If enim nos cum simus malí, novimus bona data I will give filiis nostris; quanto magis Pater noster de cáelo dat Spiritum bonum petentibus eum? (Le 11,10.13). Non enim qui spiritu suo agunt, sed quotquot Spiritu Dei aguntur, hi filii sunt Dei (Rom 8,14): non quia ipsi nihil agunt; sed ne nihil boni agant, a bono aguntur ut agant. Nam tanta magis efficitur quisque filius bonus, quanto largius ei datur a Patre Spiritus bonus. 5 [v.132]. Denique iste adhuc petit. Os quidem aperuit, et attraxit spiritum; sed adhuc ad Patrem pulsat, et quaerit: bibit, sed quanto suavius ​​sensit, mucho ardentius adhuc sitit.

Audi verba sitientis: Réspice, inquit, in me, et miserere mei secundum iudicium diligentium nomen tuum: id est, secundum iudicium quod in eos fecisti, qui diligunt nomen tuum; quoniam ut diligerent te, prius dilexisti eos. Sic enim Ioannes apostolus ait, Nos diligimus, inquit, Deum: et velut causa quaereretur, quae nos diligere fecit; adiunxit, Quoniam ipse prior dílexit nos (1 lo 14,19).. 6 [v.133]. Vide et iste quid apertissime dicat: Gressus mos direct secundum eloquium tuum, et non dominetur mei omnis iniquitas. Ubi quid aliud dicit quam, Rectum et liberum me fac secundum promissum tuum? Quanto autem magis regnat in quocumque Dei charitas, both minus ei dominatur iniquitas. Quid ergo aliud petit, quam ut donor
Excellencies of the law of God

God granting it to him, love God? For, by loving God, he loves himself, and thus he can profitably love his neighbor as himself, in whose two precepts are contained the law and the prophets. Then what do you ask but that the precepts that God imposes by commanding be fulfilled by helping? 7 [v. 134]. But what does this mean: Deliver me from the slanders of men, and I will keep your commandments? If men blame him for true crimes, they do not slander him; If false, how is it that you want to be freed from slander, that is, from false crimes, which cannot harm you in any way? The false crime, such as slander, does not constitute a man guilty; at most, only before the male judge; But, when God is the judge, no false crime harms, because it is not imputed to the accused, but rather to the accuser. Or is it that here the prayer of the Church and of all the Christian people is prefigured, who was redeemed from the slanders of men, with which Christians were persecuted everywhere? But does he keep the commandments of God for this reason? Did not the holy people more gloriously keep the commandments of God in the midst of slander and tribulation when they raged everywhere, without yielding to the insinuating impieties of the persecutors? Without a doubt, deliver me from the slanders of men, and I will keep your commandments, is: "Do you, having infused your Spirit, do not overcome me with terror the slanders of men and do not lead me from your commandments to their evil deeds, since, if you do this with me, that is, if, by giving me patience, you free me from the slanders of enemies, so that I do not fear Deo diligat Deum? [v.134].

Crimen quippe falsum, quod est calumnia, reum non facit hominem, nisi apud iudicem hominem: ubi autem Deus iudex est, nullus false crimine laeditur; quia non cui obiicitur, sed obiicienti potius imputatur. An hic Ecclesiae praesignatur oratio, et universi populi christiani, qui redemptus est a calumniis hominum, quibus exagitabantur usquequaque Christiani? Sed numquid propterea Dei mandata custodit? Nonne Inter ipsas calumnias, quando fervebant, multo gloriosius populus sanctus in tribulationibus Dei mandata servabat, cum ad perpetrandas impietates persequentibus non cedebat? Sed nimirum hoc est, Redime me a calumniis hominum, et custodiam mandata tua: Tu age infuso Spiritu tuo, ne me calumniae hominum terroribus vincant, et a tuis mandatis ad sua mala facta traducant. Si enim hoc mecum egeris, id est, hoc modo me ab

false accusations that are brought against me, I will keep your commandments among the same slanders." 8. [v.135]. Illuminate your face upon your servant, that is, manifest your presence by helping and favoring. And teach me your justifications: Teach me to execute them. This is read more clearly in another place, where it is said: Teach me to do your will. Those who hear, even if they retain in memory what Hear, it is in no way to be judged that they learned if they do not practice it, for the word of Truth says: everyone who has heard from the Father and learned, comes to me. Then he who does not work, that is, he who does not come, did not learn. codices it is read: Because I did not keep your law. Then streams of water flowed, that is, torrents of tears. And it is said in Latin: Descenderunt exitus aquarum, because of the way of speaking that can be said: Montes descenderunt pedes mei, through the mountains my feet descended, although it is not said in; pilam, I went down to the pool. Therefore, descenderunt very well says, they ran or descended, paying attention to the humility of penitence, since they ascended when they became conceited and exalted with stubborn pride. They seemed to be on high when, not knowing the justice of God, they wanted to establish their own; patientia donata redemeris; inter ipsas calumnias custodiam mandata tua. faciam voluntatem tuam (Ps 142,10). Qui enim audiunt, licet memoria teneant quod audiunt, nequáquam didicisse putandi sunt, si non faciunt. didicit. 9 [v.136].

Descenderunt ergo exitus aquarum, id est effusions lacrymarum. Et ea locutione qua dicere potuit, Montes descenderunt pedes mei; etsi non diceret, per montes, vel, in montes: ea locutione dicitur, Scalas descendit, etsi non dicatur, per scalas; aut, Piscinam descendit, etsi non dicatur, in Piscinam. Et bene ait, descenderunt, humble yourself scilicet poenitendi. Ascenderunt enim, quando per superbiam contumacem erecti fuerant et elati. Sursum enim sibi esse videbantur, quando ignorantes Dei iustitiam, constituere volebant suam (Rom 10:3): in qua fatigueti et legis praevari-

the law, they came down from that height weeping, so that, by repenting, they might rather obtain the justice of God. There are some codices that do not write descenderunt, but transierunt, they passed beyond, as if he had said, exaggerating, that crying he crossed the sources of the waters, so that we can understand exitus aquarum; That is to say, he cried more than waters flow from springs. And why does he cry this way for not having kept the law? In order to obtain grace, which erases the iniquity of the penitent and helps the will of the believer. SERMON

1 [v. 137-138]. Previously he who sings this psalm had said: Streams of water flowed or descended from my eyes, because they did not keep your law. In which he testified that he cried a lot for his prevarication. Therefore, now, giving the reason why he must have cried a lot and grieved greatly for his sin, he says: You are righteous, Lord, and your judgment is right. You commanded (to guard) your justice, and your testimonies, and your truth beyond measure. Without a doubt, every sinner must fear this justice of God, right judgment and truth, because by it God condemns all those whom he condemns, and they cannot in any way justly complain of their condemnation against a just God. This is why the cry of the penitent is just or reasonable, since, if an impenitent heart is condemned, it is condemned justly. He calls the testimonies of God justice, because catione confusi, ab illa elatione descenderunt flendo, ut iustitiam Dei potius impetrarent poenitendo. Sunt codices qui non habent descenderunt, sed transierunt, tanquam exaggeranter diceret transisse se flendo fontes aquarum; ut hoc intelligamus exitus aquarum: id est, plus flevisse, quam manant aquae de suis exítibus. Cur autem non custodita lege sic fletur, nisi ut impetretur gratia, quae poenitentis delet iniquitatem, et ctedentis adiuvat voluntatem? SERMO

1 [v.137-138]. Dixetat superius qui cantat hunc psalmum, Exitus aquarum descenderunt oculi mei quoniam non custodierunt legem tuam: ubi se multum flevisse testatus est praevaricationem suam. Proinde, velut rationem reddens cur multum flere debuerit et suum graviter doleré peccatum, Iustus es, inquit, Domine, et rectum iudicium tuum. Mandasti iustitiam testimonia tua, et veritatem tuam valde. Haec utique iustitia Dei rectumque iudicium et veritas, omni est metuenda peccanti: hac enim damnantur divinítus quicumque danmantur; nec est omnino qui de sua damnatione contra Deum iustum recte conqueri possit. Inde fletus rectus est poenitentis; quoniam si cor eius impoenitens damnaretur, iustissime utique damnaretur. Sane iustitiam dicit testimonia Dei:

shows that he is just by ordering justice; and this is also true, because God makes himself known by such testimonies. 2 [v.139]. But what does what follows mean: My zeal repudiated me, or as some codices write: your zeal?; They also add some: from your house, and they do not write "he disowned me", but he devoured me. It seems to me that this was amended by considering another psalm in which it is written: Zelus domus tuae comedit me, zeal for your house devoured me, which we know was also commemorated in the Gospel. However, tabefecit, repudiated me, is somewhat similar to what is said there, comedit. Regarding zelus meus, my zeal, which many codices recorded, does not imply any question, since it is not surprising that someone is repudiated by his zeal. What some codices say: zelus tuus, your zeal, indicates the man who has zeal for God, not for himself; but he does not object to this zeal also being called mine. Well, what else does the Apostle say when he writes. Why am I zealous for God with a zeal for God? By saying I am jealous, he shows that the zeal is his. But as he said for God, that is, not for himself, but for God, he added: with zeal for God; and certainly God, through his Spirit, is the one who inspires this zeal in his faithful; zeal of love, not hate. And, if not, let us see what care the Apostle took over this zeal to force him to say: I fitted you with a man to present you, as a chaste virgin, to Christ; However, I fear lest as the serpent deceived Eve with his cunning, so your minds will also be corrupted, failing from simplicity and chastity towards Christ. He was devoured by zeal for the house of God, which he was jealous for iustum quippe, proving himself by commanding iustitiam. Est etiam haec veritas, ut Deus testimoniis talibus innotescat. 2 [v.139]. Sed quid est quod sequitur: Tabefecit me zelus meus; vel, sicut alii codices habent, zelus tuus? Habent nonnulli etiam, domus tuae: et non, tabefecit me; sed comment me. Quod ex alio psalmo, quantum mihí videtur, putatum est emendandum, ubi scriptum est, Zelus domus tuae comedit me: quod commemoratum etiam in Gospel novimus (Ps 68,10; lo 2,17). Simile tamen aliquid est, tabefecit, ei quod ibi est, comedit. Zelus autem meus, quod plures codices habent, nullam ingerit quaestionem: quid enim mirum est si zelo suo quisque tabescit? Quod vero habent aliqui, zelus tuus, significat hominem Deo zelantem, non sibi; sed non repugnat si ipse dicatur et meus. Nam quid aliud dicit Apostolus, Aemulor enim vos Deo, aemulatione Dei?

Nam saying, Aemulor vos, quid, nisi aemulationem demonstrat suam? Sed quia dixit, Deo, id est, non sibi, sed Deo; ideo addidit, aemulatione Dei. Hanc quippe suo Spiritu fidelibus suis inspirat Deus: amoris enim est, non livoris. Nam quae fuet cura ut hoc Apostolus diceret? «Aptavi enim vos», inquit, «uni viro virginem castam exhibite Christo: timeo autem ne sicut serpens Evam seduxit versutia sua, sic et vestrae minds corruptantur a simplicitate et castítate quae est in Christo» (2 Cor 11,2.3). Comedebat eum zelus domus Dei, quam tamen zelabat Christo, non
Excellencies of the law of God

Christ, not for himself. The husband is jealous of his wife, but the husband's friend should not be jealous of her for himself, but for the husband. This man's zeal must be taken in a good sense, since he gives his reason, saying: Because my enemies have forgotten your words. Then, according to this, they repaid him evil for good, because he was zealous for God with so much affection and love that he said he was repudiated by this zeal; But they tormented him as an enemy, because he wanted those whom he was jealous of in loving God. But he, not being ungrateful to the grace of God, by which he was reconciled to God, being an enemy of Him, loved his enemies and was jealous of them for God, grieving and repudiating himself because they forgot his words. 3 [v.140}. Then, considering the flame of the love of God with which he was burned in the words of God, he says: Your word is exceedingly burning, and your servant loved it. The impenitent heart of his enemies, who had forgotten the words of God, was rightly jealous, and for this reason he was inflamed with desire to lead them to what he most ardently loved. 4 [v.141]. “I am young,” he says, “and despicable; I didn't forget your justifications. I did not behave like my enemies, who forgot your words. It seems that the younger one, who did not forget God's justifications, grieves for his older enemies, because they forgot them. Well, what does it mean: I, young man, have not forgotten? That the adults forgot. In the Greek text it is written neoteros, the young man or the youngest. This word is also recorded in the passage where it was said. From sibi. Sponsus enim sibi zelat sponsam suam: amicus autem sponsi non eam sibi zelare debent, sed sponso. Bonus ergo et huius intelligendus est zelus: causam namque subiungit et dicit, Quia obliti sunt verborum tuorum inimici mei. Retribuebant ergo mala pro bonis; quoniam zelabat illos Deo tam vehementer et ardenter, ut eo zelo tabefactum se diceret; illi autem ob hoc in ipsum inimicitias exercebant: quia utique ut Deum amarent volebat, quos amando zelabat. Non ingratus enim gratiae Dei, per quam fuet ex inimico reconciliatus Deo, etiam ipse suos diligebat inimicos, et eos zelabat Deo, dolens et tabescens quod essent verborum eius obliti. 3 [v.140]. Deinde considers ipse, in verbis Dei qua flamma dilectionis arderet: Ignitum, inquit, eloquium tuum valde, et servus tuus dilexit illud.

Merito zelabat in suis inimicis cor impoenitens, qui fuerant obliti verborum Dei: ad hoc enim flagrabat eos adducere, quod ipse flagrantissime diligebat. 4 [v.141]. Iunior ego sum, inquit, et contemptus; iustificationes tuas non sum oblitus: non sicut inimici mei, qui obliti sunt verborum tuorum. Videtur autem minor aetate non oblitus iustificationes Dei doleré pro inimicis suis aetate maioribus qui obliti sunt. Nam quid est, Iunior ergo non sum oblitus, nisi, lili maiores obliti sunt? NetÓTepo? est enim graece, quod est etiam in illo loco ubi dictum est, In quo corrigit iunior viam suam? Hoc autem nomen comparativum est, et

How does the young man correct his path? This word is in a comparative degree, and therefore compares this young man with the elder. Let us recognize here the two peoples who fought in the womb of Rebekah, when, by virtue of the one who calls, not of the works, she was told: "The older will serve the younger." But the younger here calls himself contemptible, and for this reason he was made greater, because God chose the ignoble and contemptible roses of the world, and those that are not as if they were so that those that are might disappear. See that the last are first, and the first are last. 5 [v.142}. It is not without reason that those who sought to establish their justice while ignoring God's justice forgot the words of God. However, this young man did not forget her, because he did not want to have his own, but rather God's, of which he now also says: Your justice is eternal and your law is truth. How can the law not be true, by which sin is known and at the same time bears witness to the justice of God? Well, that's what the Apostle says. The justice of God was manifested, witnessed by the law and the prophets. 6 [v.143]. Because of her, the younger suffered such persecution from the older, that he said the following: Tribulation and need caught up with me; Your commandments are my meditation. Be taught, persecute, provided that the commandments of God are not abandoned, and by these commandments those who persecute are also loved. ideo bene intelligitur in comparatione maioris. Duos ergo populos hic agnoscamus, qui etiam in Rebeccae uterus luctabantur; quando non ex operibus, sed ex vocante dictum esí ei, Maior serviet minori (Gen 25, 22.23; Rom 9,12.13). Sed contemptum se dicit hic minor; ideo factus est maior: quia ignobilia et contemptibilia mundi elegit Deus, et ea quae non sunt, tanquam sint, ut quae sunt evacuentur (1 Cor 1,28); et ecce sunt novissimi qui weret primi, et primi qui weret novissimi (Mt 20:16). 5 [v.142]. Nec immerito obliti sunt verborum Dei, qui suam iustitiam constituere voluerunt, ignorantes iustitiam Dei (Rom 10:3): iste autem iunior non est oblitus, qui non suam voluit habere iustitiam, sed Dei, de qua etiam nunc dicit, lustitia tua iustitia in aeternum, et lex tua experts. Quomodo enim non veritas lex, per quam cognitío peccati, et quae testimonium perhibet iustitiae Dei? Sic enim dicit Apostolus: lustitia Dei manijestata est, testijicata per Legem et Propbetas (ib. 3,20.21). 6 [v.143].

Propter hanc passus est persecutionem iunior a maiore, ut diceret iunior quod sequitur: Tribulatio et necessitas invenerunt me, mandata tua meditatio mea est. Saeviant, persequantur; dum tamen mandata Dei non relinquantur, et ex ipsis mandatis etiam qui saeviunt dilígantur.

7 [v.144]. Justice are your testimonies eternally; Give me understanding, and I will live. This young man asks for understanding, since, if he did not have it, he would not understand any more than the elderly. But he asks him in tribulation and in need to understand to what extent everything that can be taken from him by the enemies who persecute him, by whom he says he is despised, must be despised. He said I will live because, if tribulation and destitution reached such an extreme that this life is taken from him by the hands of enemy persecutors, yet he will live eternally, because he put justice before temporal things, which endures eternally. This justice is the martyrdoms of God in tribulation and destitution; That is, they are the testimonies by which the martyrs were crowned. SERMON 29 1 [v.145]. No one will doubt that the cry raised to God by those who pray is in vain if it is carried out by the sound of the bodily voice without the heart being raised to God. If it takes place in the heart, even if the bodily voice remains silent, it may be hidden from men, not from God. When we pray to God, whether with our mouths, when necessary, or in silence, we must always cry out with our hearts. The cry of the heart is a vehement thought that, when it occurs in prayer, expresses the great affection of the one who prays and asks, so that he does not distrust of getting what he asks for. You cry out with all your heart when you are not distracted by something else. These prayers are rare to many and frequent 7 [v.144]. lustitia testimonia tua in aeternum, intellectum da mibi, et vivam. Intellectum poscit iste iunior; quem si non haberet; non super seniores intelligeret: sed eum poscit in tribulatione et necessitate, quo intelligat quam sit contemnendum quod ei possunt auferre persequentes inimici, a quibus se dicit esse contemptum. Ideo dixit, et vivam: quia si eo usque tribulatio necessitasque pervenerit, ut per inimicorum persequentium manus vita ista finiatur; Vivet in aeternum, qui temporalibus praeponit iustitiam, quae manet in aeternum. Quae iustitia in tribulatione et necessitate martyria sunt Dei, hoc est testimonia, pro quibus sunt mattyres coronati. SERMO

1 [v.145]. Clamor ad Dominum, qui fit ab orantibus, si sonitu corporalis vocis fiat, non intention in Deum corde; quis dubitet inaniter fieri? Si autem fiat corde, etiam silente corporis voce; alium quemlibet hominem potest latere, non Deum. Sive ergo cum voce carnis, quando id opus est, sive cum silentio, ad Deum, cum oramus, corde clamandum est. Est autem clamor cordis magna cogitationis intentio; quae cum est in oratione, magnum exprimit desiderantis et petentis affectum, ut non desperet effectum. Tune joint in toto corde clama tur, quando aliunde non cogitatur. Such prayers are rare sunt multis. crebrae autem

few, but I don't know that anyone can always have them. Tal tells us that it was his prayer who sings this psalm, saying: I cried out with all my heart; Hear me, Lord. And, declaring why he took advantage of his cry, he adds: I will look for your justifications. He cried out to God with all his heart and desired that He would hear him in his search for his justifications. Therefore, we pray to seek or investigate what we are commanded to do. How far he who seeks is still from doing so! It is not necessary for the one who seeks to find, or for the one who finds to act, although one cannot act without finding, nor can one find without searching. But the Lord gave great hope, saying: Seek, and you will find. Wisdom also says, which is nothing else apart from Him: The wicked will seek me, and will not find me. Then it was not said to the evil, but to the good: Seek, and you will find. What do I say? It was said to those who shortly afterwards in the same place it was announced: If you, being evil, know how to give good things to your children..., etc. Then how is it that it is said to the evil ones: Seek and you will find, if, on the other hand, it is said: The evil ones will search for me and will not find me? Or did the Lord want them to search for something other than wisdom when He promised that they would find if they searched? Certainly in it are found all the things that should be sought by those who wish to be happy. Then in it are found the justifications of God. Therefore, it remains to be understood that not all evil people fail to find wisdom if they want, but only those who are evil insofar as they hate it, for he also said this: The evil ones will seek me, and paucis; omnes vero utrum cuiquam, nescio. Talern suam commemorat orationem, qui cantat hunc psalmum, says: Clamavi in ​​toto corde meo; exaudi me, Domine. Cui autem rei suus clamor proficiat, adiunxit: lustificationes tuas exquiram. Ad hoc ergo clamavit in toto corde suo, et hoc sibi desideravit a Domino exaudiente praestari, ut iustificationes eius exquirat. Proinde quod ut faciamus iubetur, ut exquiramus oratur. They will not find me, because they hated wisdom. Then they didn't find it, because they hated it. But if they hate her, why do they look for her? Because they did not seek it for itself, but for some evil that they love, and they think that through it they will achieve it more easily. Certainly there are many who seek with great effort the sentences of wisdom and want it to form the arsenal of their science, but not that of their life, to arrive, not by the customs that wisdom orders, but by the voices that it contains, to the praise of men, which is vain glory. Therefore when they seek wisdom, they do not really seek it, because, if they sought it, they would see according to it. Therefore, they seek to puff themselves up with their words; and the more they swell, the further they move away from it. This one who asks the Lord for the same thing that the Lord commands him to do, so that God may work in him what he commands him to execute, since God is the one who works in us to will and to act due to his good will, says: I cried out with all my heart; Hear me, Lord, and I will seek your justifications, to make them, not only to know them, lest he become like that undocile servant, who, even if he has understood, does not obey. 2 [v. 146]. What follows is dark and requires a little slower explanation. I came forward in the middle of the night and cried out. Many codices do not say at midnight (intempesta nocte), but at dawn (immaturitate); I barely found one that had the preposition duplicated: in immaturitate. Immaturity or early morning in this place means the premature time of the night, that is, it is not opportune for something to be done while awake; which is also commonly said "untimely hour." The midnight in which one must rest was called intempesta, untimely. No doubt, it was so called because it is inopportune to the actions of those who are awake. The ancients called what is opportune tempestuous, and what is untimely untimely, deriving the word from tempus, time, not from tempestas, tempest, which by the use of the Latin language is thus called the disturbance of the sky. Although historians use this word without any concern, saying ea tempestate when they mean "at that time." For this is how the eminent Latinist Virgil uses it when he says: Vnde haec tam clear suddenly tempestas, since he did not imply by this name that it was a sky disturbed with winds and clouds, but rather a sky that appeared bright due to a sudden and radiant serenity. What was said in Greek in Aoria, not with a single word, but with two, that is, with the preposition and the citur, et usque ad mortem corporis, si hoc flagitat extreme tentatio, pro testimonyrum divinorum veritate certetur: ubi autem non est salus, succumbit infirmitas, et deseritur veritas. 3 [v.147]. Sed quod sequitur habet aliquid obscuritatis, quod aliquanto diutius exponendum est. Praeveni intempesta night, et clamavi. Plures codices non habent, intempesta night; sed, immaturitate: vix autem unus inventus est quí haberet geminatam praepositionem, id est, in immaturitate. Immaturitas itaque hoc loco nocturnum tempus est, quod non est maturum, id est, opportunum ut agatur aliquid vigilando: quod etiam vulgo dici solet, inopportune hour. Nox quoque intempesta, id est media, quando quiescendum est, hinc procul dubio nuncupata est, quia inopportuna est actioníbus vigilantium.

Tempestivum enim dixerunt veteres opportunum; et intempestivum, inopportunum: a tempore ducto vocabulo, non ab illa tempestate, quae consuetudine latinae linguae caeli disturbed iam vocatur. Quanquam isto verbo libenter utuntur historicí, ut dicant, Ea tempestate, quod volunt Eo tempore intelligi: et quod aít locutor egregius, Unde haec tam clear suddenly Tempestas? (VIRG. Ipsa et quod sequitur dicit, Praevenerunt oculi mei ad matutinum, ut meditarer eloquia tua. Ponamus enim matutinum, quando qui sedebant in umbra mortis, lux orta est eis (Is 9,2); nonne in sanctis qui prius werent in terra, ad hoc matutinum oculi Ecclesiae praevenerunt, quia hoc futurum antea praeviderunt, ut meditarentur eloquia Dei, quae tune erant, et in Lege ac Prophetis haec fuga nuntiabant? 6 [v.149]. However, there is a judgment without mercy, but for those placed on the left, because they did not show mercy. 7 [v.150]. Those who persecuted me with iniquity approached, he says, or as other codices write: iniquitously. The persecutors approach when they come to torment the flesh and destroy it. Hence Psalm 21, in which the passion of the Lord was prophesied, says: Do not depart from me, for the tribulation is near, since these things are said not threatening, but already enduring the passion. It calls, therefore, close to the tribulation, which took place in the flesh, since there is nothing closer to the soul than the flesh it carries. Then the pursuers approached as they tormented the flesh of those they pursued. But pay attention to what follows: They turned away from your law. The closer they came in persecuting the righteous, the further they went from justice. But how did they harm those who came in pursuit of them, since the proximity of the Lord was more intimate to them, since He will never depart from them? 8 [v.151]. Then he continues: You are near, O Lord, and all your ways are true. It is the custom of saints to attribute truth to God even in the midst of tribulations, confessing that they suffer them with reason. This is what Esther did, this is what holy Daniel did, this is what the three young men in the oven did, this is what others confessed erit eis qui non credunt Domini Gospel (1 Petr 4:17). Et ultimum tempus iudicii non erit sine mercy, quia coronal te, ait psalmus, in miseratione et misericordia (Ps 102,4). Iudicium autem sine Misericordia, sed sinitris qui non fecetunt Misericordiam (Iacobi 2,13). 7 [v.150]. Appropinquaverunt, inquit, persequentes me iniquitate; vel, sicut nonnulli codices habent, inique. Tune appropinquant qui persequuntur, quando usque ad carnem cruciandam perimendamque perveniunt. Unde psalmus vicesimus primus, ubi passio Domini prophetata est, Ne discedas, inquit, a me, quoniam tribulatio proxima est (Ps 21,12); cum ea dicantur quae non imminente, sed iam praesente ipsa passione perpessus est. Sed proximam dixit tribulationem, quae fiebat in carne; nihil est quippe animae propius carne quam gestat. Propinquaverunt ergo persequentes, affligendo eorum carnem, quos persequebantur. Sed attende quod sequitur: A lege autem tua longe facti sunt.

Quanto magis propinquaverunt persequendis iustis, mucho magis longe facti sunt a iustitia. Sed quid nocuerunt eis, quibus persequendo propinquaverunt; When interior is propinquatio Domini eorum, a quo nullatenus deseruntur? 8 [v.151]. What the Greek text says catarjas, some Latins translated ab initio; others, by initio, and others, by in initiis. Those who preferred to translate it in plural followed the way of speaking of the Greeks. But in Latin it is more common to say ab initio or initio (from the beginning) what is recorded in Greek, in the plural, catarjas, but in an adverbial sense, as happens when we Latins say alias hoc jacio, which seems to be recorded in the feminine plural, but is an adverb that means in another time. Then what does it mean ab initio cognovi, or better, if we say it by an adverb: "Initio" cognovi de testimoniis tuis, quia in aeternum fundasti ea: Firstly, or from the beginning, I knew of your testimonies that you established them eternally? He says that the testimonies of the Lord were established eternally by Him, and he assures that He knew this from the beginning; and that he did not know it by anything else but by the same tesQuaeri autem potest quomodo hic dictum sit, Omnes viae tuae veritas; cum in alio psalmo legatur, Universae viae Domini misericordia et veritas (Ps 24:10). timoniums What testimonies are these but those with which God testified that he would give an eternal kingdom to his children? But since he affirmed that he would give it in his only begotten Son, of whom he said: And his kingdom will have no end, he stated that he established the same testimonies eternally, because what God promised for them is eternal. When the same reality is seen, the testimonies that are needed now to believe it will no longer be necessary by themselves. And since they take place in Christ, that is why it is very clear to have said you established them, since no one can establish another foundation apart from the established one, which is Christ Jesus. How did he come to know these things from the beginning if it were not because the Church speaks, which was not lacking on earth from the beginning of the human race, whose first fruits are the holy Abel, who also was sacrificed in testimony of the blood of the future Mediator, which was to be shed for the impious brother? For from the beginning it was said: There shall be two in one flesh. When the Apostle explains this, he says that it is a great sacrament, but I say—he adds—in order to Christ and his Church. in this despondency, he says. Look at my despondency and deliver me, because I have not forgotten your law. Thus the proud is cornered by evils to be humiliated and the humble is freed from them to be exalted. 2 [v.154]. Judge—he says—my judgment and redeem me. In a way he repeated the previous sentence, because what he says: Look at my despondency, is the same thing that judges my judgment; and deliver me is the same as and redeem me. What he said before: Because I have not forgotten your law, agrees with what he now says: Quicken me by your saying, for the saying of God is his law, which he did not forget, humbling himself to be exalted. The same exaltation belongs to what says: Give life to me, because the exaltation of the saints is eternal life. 3 [v.155]. Far from sinners—he says—is health, because they did not seek your justifications. But who separates you, O you, who said: Health is far from sinners? Who separates you from sinners so that health is not far from you, but with you? What certainly separates you is that you did what they did not do, that is, you sought God's justifications. But what do you have that you haven't received? Are you not the one who just before said: I cried out with all my heart, O Lord, I will seek your justifications? maste to search for them. He, then, separates you from those from whom health is far away, because they did not seek God's justifications. 4 [v.156]. He already saw this himself. But I would not see it if I did not see it in him and if it were not in him, because these words are from the Body of Christ, of which we are members. I also knew that your judgment would not be made on me without your mercy. 5 [v.157]. Many persecute and trouble me, but I have not separated myself from your testimonies. (This) happened, we know it, we remember it, we see it. The whole earth was red with the blood of the martyrs; The sky is full of flowers with their crowns; the churches were adorned with their monuments; The times are marked with their festivals; health is restored by its merits. And where does all this come from if it is not that what was predicted of this man spread throughout the entire globe of the earth was fulfilled: Many persecute me and trouble me, but I have not separated myself from your testimonies? We see it and we thank the Lord, our God. You indeed, man; you in another psalm, you yourself said. Had it not been for the Lord being in us, we might have been swallowed alive. This is why you did not depart from their testimonies and reached the palm of the supreme vocation among the hands of many who persecuted and troubled you. 6 [v.158]. We know the persecutions that the Body of Christ, that is, the holy Church, endured from the kings of the earth. Then let us also recognize his words here, which sound like this: Princes persecuted me without cause, and my heart feared your words. How did Christians harm the kingdoms of earth, when their King had promised them the kingdom of heaven? In what way, I will repeat, had they harmed the kingdoms of the earth? Did the King of the Christians forbid his soldiers to pay and deliver what was owed to earthly kings? Did he not, when the Jews came to slander him about this, say: Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's? Did He not also pay the tribute, taking it out of the fish's mouth? Did his predecessor, perhaps, to the soldiers who asked what they should do to achieve eternal health, say: "Detach yourself from your commitment, throw away your weapons, abandon your king, so that you can place yourself at the command of God"? He who, so as not to be defeated in combat, fears the words of the Lord, rejoices in them victoriously. 3 [v.163]. So that we would not think that hatred of the words of God could arise from that fear, even though he had already said I rejoiced, in which he would not have burst out if he hated them, yet he further adds: I hated injustice and abominated it, but I loved your law. That is to say, that fear of the words of God did not engender hatred of them, but rather preserved charity intact, since, since the law of God is his words and his sayings, there is no danger of love perishing through fear when fear is chaste. Thus, good children fear and love their parents; Thus, the chaste woman fears that her man will abandon her and loves to enjoy him. Therefore, if the father, man, and the husband, man, should be feared and loved, our Father, who is in heaven, should be many more; and that Husband, who is more beautiful, not because of the beauty of the flesh, but because of virtue, than all the sons of men. But who loves the law of God? Those who love God. And what is so sad about the father's law for good children? Perhaps correcting the one he loves and scourging everyone whom he accepts as a son? Keep in mind that whoever refuses these judgments does not get the promises. Then praise the paternal judgments regarding punishment if the promises regarding the reward are loved. 4 [v.164}. So do this man who says: I praised you seven times a day for the judgments of your righteousness. Seven times a day means always, since this number usually symbolizes universality. For this reason, to the six days of the works of God the sepmoliti was added, ab illo sunt insuper acquisiti. Quisquís ergo a verbis Dei, ne in certamine vincatur formidat, super eadem verba victor exsultat. 3 [v.163]. Nam ne putaremus ex illa formidine odium verborum Dei potuisse subrepere; quamvis iam dixerit, Exultavi super eloquia tua, quod utique non diceret, si odisset ea; tamen adhuc addidit, et dicit: Iniustitiam odio habuit, et abominatus sum; legem autem tuam dilexi. Nempe a verbis eius illa formed non fecit eorumdem verborum odium, sed integram tenuit charitatem. Ñeque enim lex Dei non sunt verba et eloquia Dei. Absit ergo ut timore pereat amor, ubi castus est timor. Sic patres a filiis piis et timen tur et amantur; sic púdica coniux virum et timet, ne ab illo diseratur, et amat, ut fruatur.

Si ergo et pater homo, coniux homo, et timeri et amari debent; multo magis Pater noster qui in coelis est (Mt 6,9), et ille sponsus, non carne prae filiis hominum, sed virtute formosus (Ps 44,3). A quibus enim diligitur lex Dei, nisi a quibus diligitur Deus? Et quid habet bonis filiis triste lex patris? An quoniam quem diligit corripit, et flagellat omnem filium quem recipit? (Hebr 12,6). At qui haec iudicia respuit, promissa non recipit. Paterna ergo iudicia laudentur et in flagello, si promissa diligantur in praemio. 4 [v.164]. Ita plane facit iste, qui dicit, Septies in die laudavi te, super iudicia iustitiae tuae. Septies in die quod ait, significat Semper. In the same sense of universality it was also said: The righteous man will fall seven times and will rise again. That is, the just man who does not transgress, otherwise he would no longer be just; In whatever way he is humiliated, he does not perish. It was said that he will fall seven times in response to all kinds of tribulations with which he is brought down in the sight of men; and it was added he will rise considering that he benefits from the same tribulations. This sentence is sufficiently clarified by the one that follows in the same book: But the wicked will perish in evil. Therefore, for the righteous to fall and rise seven times is not to rush into evil. No wonder the Church praised God seven times a day for the judgments of his justice, because, when the time had come to begin the judgment for the house of God, it did not perish in all its tribulations, but was glorified with the triumphs of the martyrs. 5 [v.165]. Much peace, he says, to those who love your law, and there is no stumbling block for them. Does this mean that the law is not a stumbling block for them or that those who stumble in any way love it? Both things can be understood correctly, since he who loves the law of God also exalts what he does not understand in it; and, when something seems wrong to him, he rather judges that he does not understand it and that some great mystery is hidden there. This is why the law of God does not serve as a stumbling block. But so that he does not stumble in any way, he should not regard men of any profession, no matter how holy, so that his faith hangs on their customs, no diebus divinae operationis, septimus adiectus est quietis (Gen 2,2); et per septem dies cutrentes et recurres, tempora universala volvuntur. Nec ob aliud dictum est, Septies cadet iustus, et resurget: id est, non perit iustus, modis ómnibus humiliatus, sed non praevaricatus, alioquin non erit iustus. Nam pro omni genere tribulationis, qua in conspectu hominum deiicitur, positum est, septies cadit; et pro eo quod ex ipsis omnibus tribulationibus proficit, positum est, resurget. Satis illustrat in eo libro consequens sententia praecedentem: ibi enim sequitur, Impii autem infirmabuntur in malis (Prov 24,16). Hoc est itaque iusto septies cadere et resurgere, in omnibus malis non infirman.

Merit igitur septies in die laudavit Ecclesia Deum super iudicia iustitiae ipsius; quia cum tempus esset ut iudicium inciperet a domo Domini (1 Petr 4:17), in omnibus tribulationibus suis non infirmata, sed coronis martyrum glorificata est. 5 [v.165]. Fax fine, inquit, diligentibus legem tuam, et non est scandalum. Utrum ipsa lex diligentibus se scandalum non est, an diligentibus eam nullum est undecumque scandalum? Be utrumque recte intelligitur. Who enim diligit Dei legem, etiam quod in ea non intelligit honorat; et quod ei sonare videtur absurde, se potius non intelligere, et aliquid magnum latere ibi iudicat: ideo lex Dei non est ei scandalum. Ut autem nullum scandalum omnino patiatur, non sic homines sanctae cuiusque proíessionis attendat, ut fides eius ex eorum moribus pendeat;

It may happen that, as some of those whom he held in high esteem fall, he perishes by stumbling; but love the same law of God, and he will have much peace and there will be no stumbling block for him. Love the law with certainty, which does not know how to induce sin even though many sin with it. 6 [v.166}. I hoped, he says, for your health, O Lord, and I loved your commandments. What would it have profited the righteous of old to have loved the precepts of God if Christ, with whose spirit given to them they were able to love the commandments of God, and which is the salvation of God, had not delivered them? Therefore, if those who loved his commandments expected the salvation of God, how much more necessary was Jesus, that is, the salvation of God, to save those who did not love them? This prophecy can also conveniently be applied to the saints of these times, counted from the time when grace was revealed and the Gospel was preached, since those who love the commandments of God await Christ, so that when Christ, our life, appears, then we too may appear with Him in glory. 7 [v.167-168}. My soul kept—he says—your testimonies and loved them ardently, or as some codices simply write: and he loved them, my soul understanding. Your commandments are kept when they are not denied. This is the exercise of martyrs, since testimonies in Greek are called martyrdoms. But since it is of no use to be burned in the flames for the testimonies of God in the absence of charity, that is why he adds: And I loved them greatly. In the previous verse (166) he had said: I loved your testimonies; In this one (167) it says: I kept and loved your testimonies; ne aliquibus cadentibus quos pro magno habebat, ipse scandalo pereat: sed ipsam Dei legem diligat, et erit ei pax Fine, nullumque scandalum. Securus enim diligit eam, in qua etiamsi multi peccant, peccare ipsa non movit. 6 [v.166]. Exspectabam, inquit, salutare tuum, Domine, et mandata tua dilexi. Quid enim iustis profuisset antiquis Dei dilexisse mandata, nisi eos Christus qui est Dei salutare, liberasset; cuius etiam spiritu impertito mandata Dei diligere potuerunt? Si ergo exspectabant salutare Dei, qui mandata eius dilexerunt; quanto magis necessarius erat Iesus, hoc est salutare Dei, salvis faciendis eis qui mandata eius non dilexerunt?

Potest ista etiam sanctis istorum temporum, ex quo gratia revelata Evangelium praedicatur, congruere prophetia: exspectant enim Christum qui mandata Dei diligunt, ut cum Christus apparuerit vita nostra, tune et nos appareamus cum illo in gloria (Col 3,4). 7 [v.167-168]. Custodivit, inquit, anima mea testimonia tua, et dilexi ea valde: vel, sicut nonnulli codices habent, dilexit, ut subaudiatur, anima mea. Custodiuntur testimonia Dei, dum non negantur. Hoc est martyrum officium, quia testimonia graece martyria nuncupantur. Sed quia pro testimoniis Dei etiam flammis concremari sine chántate nihil prodest (1 Cor 13,3), ideo addidit, Et dilexi ea valde. Supra autem dixe-

and in the following (168): I kept your commandments and your testimonies, for it says like this: I kept your commandments and your testimonies. And he says this because he who truly loves them, keeps them willingly. But since it often happens that, in keeping the commandments of God, we make ourselves enemies of those against whose will we keep them, therefore the testimonies must also be kept with all strength, lest they be denied due to the persecution of the enemies. 8. Then, having said that he did both things, he attributes to God the accomplishment of them, adding and saying: For all my ways are before you, O Lord! It says, I kept your commandments and your testimonies, for all my ways are before you, as if to say, "If you had turned your face away from me, I would have been troubled and would not have kept your commandments and testimonies. I kept them because all my ways are before you." He certainly wanted to imply that God saw his ways with favorable and favorable eyes, as requested by the one who said: Do not turn your face away from me. Also, the face of God is on those who do evil, but to erase their memory from the face of the earth. But he did not say, of course, that God saw his ways like that, but rather how God knows the way of the righteous and the way he said to Moses: I know you better than all. Because, if having his ways before God did not help him walk, he would not say that he kept his commandments and testimonies, because all his ways were in the presence of the Lord. So he knew how to hear: Serve the Lord with fear

and rejoice in Him with trembling; Perceive the teaching, lest the Lord be angry and you depart from the right path, for if he had not remained in the presence of the Lord, he would not have remained in the path of righteousness. The apostle Saint Paul also orders this fear to those who says: Work out your salvation with. fear and trembling; and, stating why he says this, he adds: God: it is he who works in you to will and to act according to his benevolence. Then God has before his presence the ways of the; righteous to direct your steps, because these are the paths that were written about in Proverbs: God knows the paths, which are on the right. And those who are on the left are perverse, he adds, in which he gives us to understand that the Lord will not know these last ways; and, for the same reason, he will say to the wicked: I do not know you. To demonstrate the fruit that follows from God knowing the paths that are on the right, that is, those of the righteous, he adds next: He will make your steps straight, he will extend your paths in peace. This is why this one also says: I kept your commandments and your testimonies; Well, as if we asked him: "What was the reason for being able to keep them?", he continues and says: For all my ways are before the Lord.

rat, Mandala tua dilexi; deinde sequenti versu, Testimonia tua, et custodivi, et dilexi: postea, Et maniata tua, et testimonia tua custodivi; ait enim, Custodivi maniata tua et testimonia tua. Who enim diligit, ipsa veraciter libenterque custodit. Cum ergo se iste utrumque fecisse dixisset, Deo tribuit unde fecit, adiungendo atque saying: Quia omnes viae meae in conspectu tuo, Domine. Ideo, inquit, custodivi mandata tua et testimonia tua; quia omnes viae meae in conspectu tuo. Tanquam diceret: Si avertisses a me faciem tuam, ferem conturbatus, nec tua mandata et testimonia custodirem. Custodivi ergo, quia omnes viae meae in conspectu tuo. Propitio quippe et adiuvante conspectu, voluit intelligi Deum videre vias suas; sicut oravit qui dixit, Ne averías faciem tuam a me (Ps 26,9). Nam utique facies Domini est et super facientes mala, sed ut perdat de terra memoriam eorum (Ps 23,17). Non sic proferto iste dixit vias suas ab illo videri; sed sicut novit Dominus vias iustorum (Ps 1,6), et sicut ait Moysi, Scio te prae omnibus (Ex 23,17). Nam si hoc eum non adiuvaret gradientem, quod eius viae sunt in conspectu Dei, non diceret ideo se custodisse mandata et testimonia eius, quia omnes viae suae sunt in conspectu Domini. Novit enim audire, Servite Domino in timore, et exsultate ei cum

tremore: apprehendite disciplinam, nequando irascatur Dominus, et pereatis de via iusta (Ps 2,11 et 12); quia nisi in conspectu Domini esset, via iusta non esset. Nam hunc timorem et tremorem apostolus etiam Paulus imponit eis quibus dicit, Cum timore et tremore vestram ipsorum salutem operamini: et cur hoc dixerit aperiens, Deus est enim, inquit, qui operatur in vobis et velle et operani, pro bona volúntate (Phil 2,12.13). Ad hoc sunt ergo in conspectu Domini viae iustorum, ut dirigat gressus eorum, quoniam ipsae sunt viae de quibus scriptum est in Proverbiis, Vias autem quae a dextris sunt, novit Dominus: perversae autem sunt, inquit, quae a sinistris: ut intelligeremus quod eas non noverit Dominus, propter quos perversis dicturus est, Non novi vos (Mt 7,23). Porro ut ostenderet quo fructu vias quae a dextris sunt, id est iustorum, noverit Dominus, continuo subiecit: Ipse enim rectos faciet gressus tuos, et itinera tua in pace producet (Prov 4,27). Ecce quare ait etiam iste, Custodivi mandata tua et testimonia tua. Et velut quaereremus hoc unde potuerit: Quia omnes, inquit, viae meae in conspectu tuo, Domine.

oh Lord! That is to say, let the prayer that I pray before you come to you because the Lord is close to those whose hearts are troubled. Give me understanding, according to your word. He asks for what he promised, because he says: according to your word, as if leaving: "according to your promise." The Lord promised this when he said: I will give you understanding. 2 [v. 170]. Let my prayer penetrate your presence, Lord; Deliver me, according to your word. It repeats, in a way, the request. Because what he had first said: Let my prayer come into your presence, Lord, is similar to what he said later: Let my prayer come into your presence, Lord; and what he previously added to the previous verse: Give me understanding, according to your word, also agrees with what was added to the present verse: Deliver me, according to your word; since, by receiving understanding, he is freed who by himself, not understanding, is deceived. 3 [v. 171]. My lips, he says, will utter a hymn when you have taught me your justifications. We know how Goddess teaches the submissive to God. Everyone who has heard from the Father and learned comes to Him who justifies the wicked to keep the justifications of God, not only retaining them in memory, but also acting. Therefore he who glories glories not in himself, but in the Lord, and utters a hymn of praise. 4 [v.172}. But since he has already learned and praised God, his Teacher, next he wants to teach. As he already foresees the dangers that would follow from contradictors and persecutors when the word of God was preached, he adds: Let your hand be made to save me, because I have chosen your commandments. To avoid not even completely enclosing your words in my heart, but also having them preached by the tongue, I chose your commandments and with love I repressed fear. May your hand be ready to save me from the hand of another, for in this way God saved the martyrs by not allowing them to kill them regarding the soul, since the health of man is vain regarding the body. It can also be taken let your hand be done, that is, or let your hand be ready, so that it is understood that Christ is the hand of God, according to that of Isaiah: And the arm of the Lord, to whom was it revealed? For certainly the Only Begotten was not made, since all things were made by Him; but he who was Creator was made from the lineage of David to be Jesus, that is, Savior. 1 [v.l]. The psalm that we have now heard, and to which we have responded by singing, is brief, but very useful. You will not strive for a long time while listening, nor will you work without fruit when acting, for it is just as stated in its title: Canticle of degree or gradual. In Greek it is written anabazmon. The steps or steps can be up or down. But as the steps are recorded in these psalms, they are ascending. Then let us take them as steps by which we must climb. But let us not seek ascents for the feet of the body, for in another psalm it is written: He prepared ascents in his heart from the valley of tears to the place he established. He talked about climbs. Where? In the heart. Why point? Through the valley of tears. Now it seems that the human word is missing to be able to explain and perhaps even think about where it should go up. You recently heard, when the Apostle was read, that the eye did not see, nor the ear hear, nor did it enter into the heart of man, It did not enter into the heart of man; So let the heart of man go up there. Therefore, since the eye has not seen, nor the ear heard, nor has it ascended into the heart of man, how can it be said where it will ascend? Then since it cannot be said or explained, he adds: to the place he established. What more should I say, adds the man through whom the Holy Spirit spoke, than to a certain place or a certain place?
